**Problem:** friends add shared expenses ('Asha paid 3,000 for dinner, split among 4'). The app tracks who owes whom, shows balances, simplifies debts, and records settlements. Asked as both HLD and LLD; the LLD version is very common in machine-coding rounds.

### Requirements

- **Functional:**
  - Users, friends, and groups (trips, flatmates).
  - Add an expense: payer(s), amount, participants, **split type**: equal, exact amounts, percentage, shares.
  - Show balance per friend and per group; overall 'you owe / you are owed'.
  - **Simplify debts** within a group (minimize number of payments).
  - Record settlements (payments between users); edit and delete expenses; expense history/activity feed.
  - Multi-currency (stretch), notifications, receipts (stretch).
- **Non-functional:** **correctness of money above all** (no rounding drift, no lost updates), strong consistency inside a group, audit trail, moderate scale, works on flaky mobile networks.

### Estimation

- 50M users, 10M DAU, 2 expenses/user/day = 20M writes/day = \~230 writes/s average, \~1,000/s peak. Reads (opening app, balances) \~10x = 10,000/s peak.
- Expense row \~1 KB with participants: 20M x 1 KB = 20 GB/day = \~7 TB/year. Needs sharding eventually, but trivial compared to social feeds.
- **Conclusion:** relational DB, sharded by group, plus cache for balances. No exotic infra needed.

### Core modeling idea (say this early)

**Store expenses as an immutable ledger; derive balances from it.** Never store only 'A owes B 50' and mutate it. Keep:

1. `expenses` and per-person `expense_splits` (what happened),
2. a maintained `balances` table as a **cache** of pairwise net amounts that can always be recomputed from the ledger.

Why: edits and deletes become 'reverse the old entries, apply the new ones', and you can audit and repair.

**Represent money as integer minor units** (paise/cents) in a `Money` class with a currency. Never use floating point.

### Data model

```
users(user_id PK, name, email, phone, default_currency)
groups(group_id PK, name, created_by, created_at)
group_members(group_id, user_id, joined_at)            PK(group_id, user_id)
expenses(expense_id PK, group_id, description, total_minor, currency,
         split_type, created_by, created_at, deleted BOOL, version)
expense_payers(expense_id, user_id, paid_minor)        -- who paid (can be several)
expense_splits(expense_id, user_id, owed_minor)        -- who owes how much
settlements(settlement_id PK, group_id, from_user, to_user, amount_minor, currency, created_at)
balances(group_id, user_a, user_b, net_minor)          -- user_a < user_b; positive = a is owed by b
activity_log(id, group_id, actor, action, payload, ts)
```

- Invariant: for every expense, `sum(paid_minor) = total_minor = sum(owed_minor)`. Enforce in code and with a DB check at write time.
- Shard by `group_id`: almost every query (balances, history, simplify) is inside one group, so there are no cross-shard transactions for the main flows. 'Friend' balances outside groups can be modeled as a hidden two-person group.

### API

```
POST /groups                         {name, memberIds}
POST /groups/{id}/expenses           {description, total, currency, payers[], splitType, splits[]}  (Idempotency-Key header)
PUT  /expenses/{id}                  {...}     DELETE /expenses/{id}
GET  /groups/{id}/balances           -> per-pair net + per-user summary
GET  /groups/{id}/simplified         -> minimal list of payments
POST /groups/{id}/settlements        {from, to, amount}
GET  /users/{id}/summary             -> total owed / owing across groups
GET  /groups/{id}/activity?cursor=
```

### HLD

```
 Mobile/Web -> LB -> API Gateway (auth) -> [Expense Service] --> SQL (sharded by group_id)
                                               |  \--> Redis (balance cache)
                                               +-> outbox -> Kafka -> [Notification Service] -> push/email
                                                              \-> [Activity/Feed Service]
                                                              \-> [Search/Export workers]
 [Balance/Simplify Service] reads ledger + balances; [Currency Service] caches FX rates
```

**Add-expense flow (write path), all in one DB transaction on the group's shard:**

1. Validate: payer and participants are group members; sums match; amounts are non-negative.
2. Split strategy computes each person's share (handling rounding, below).
3. Insert `expenses`, `expense_payers`, `expense_splits`.
4. Update `balances` for each (payer, participant) pair.
5. Write an outbox event; a relay publishes it to Kafka for notifications and activity feed.

The client sends an **idempotency key** so a retry on a flaky network doesn't add the expense twice.

### LLD: classes

Entities: `User`, `Group`, `Expense`, `Split`, `Money`, `BalanceSheet`, `Settlement`. Behaviors: `SplitStrategy` (varies), `DebtSimplifier`.

```java
class Money {                      // immutable value object
  final long minor; final String currency;
  Money plus(Money o) {...}  Money minus(Money o) {...}
}

enum SplitType { EQUAL, EXACT, PERCENT, SHARES }

interface SplitStrategy {
  // returns userId -> amount owed; must sum exactly to total
  Map<String, Money> split(Money total, Map<String, Number> input);
}

class EqualSplit implements SplitStrategy {
  public Map<String, Money> split(Money total, Map<String, Number> in) {
    List<String> users = new ArrayList<>(in.keySet());
    long base = total.minor / users.size();
    long remainder = total.minor % users.size();     // distribute leftover paise
    Map<String, Money> out = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < users.size(); i++)
      out.put(users.get(i), new Money(base + (i < remainder ? 1 : 0), total.currency));
    return out;
  }
}
// ExactSplit: validate sum == total. PercentSplit: validate sum == 100, floor each, give remainder to first.
// SharesSplit: proportional to weights, largest-remainder method.

class SplitStrategyFactory {
  static SplitStrategy of(SplitType t) { /* switch returns the right strategy */ }
}

class Expense {
  String id; String groupId; Money total; Map<String, Money> paid; Map<String, Money> owed;
}

class ExpenseService {
  void addExpense(String groupId, Money total, Map<String, Money> payers,
                  SplitType type, Map<String, Number> input) {
    Map<String, Money> owed = SplitStrategyFactory.of(type).split(total, input);
    // transaction: persist expense, then balanceSheet.apply(payers, owed)
  }
}
```

**Updating balances:** for each user compute `net = paid - owed`. Positive net = is owed money; negative = owes. Pairwise tracking: the payer is owed by each participant their share. A simple, scalable alternative is to track **only each user's net position in the group** (`net[user]`), which sums to zero, and derive 'who pays whom' at read time using the simplifier. Pairwise balances are needed only if you must show 'Bob owes Asha 400' without simplification; many real apps keep pairwise to preserve the user's mental model.

### Debt simplification (the algorithm interviewers love)

Goal: minimize the number of transactions to settle a group. Compute each member's net balance; then greedily match the biggest creditor with the biggest debtor.

```java
List<Payment> simplify(Map<String, Long> net) {
  PriorityQueue<long[]> creditors = new PriorityQueue<>((a,b)->Long.compare(b[1],a[1])); // [idx, amount] max-heap
  PriorityQueue<long[]> debtors   = new PriorityQueue<>((a,b)->Long.compare(b[1],a[1]));
  List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(net.keySet());
  for (int i = 0; i < ids.size(); i++) {
    long v = net.get(ids.get(i));
    if (v > 0) creditors.add(new long[]{i, v});
    else if (v < 0) debtors.add(new long[]{i, -v});
  }
  List<Payment> out = new ArrayList<>();
  while (!creditors.isEmpty() && !debtors.isEmpty()) {
    long[] c = creditors.poll(), d = debtors.poll();
    long pay = Math.min(c[1], d[1]);
    out.add(new Payment(ids.get((int)d[0]), ids.get((int)c[0]), pay));
    if (c[1] > pay) { c[1] -= pay; creditors.add(c); }
    if (d[1] > pay) { d[1] -= pay; debtors.add(d); }
  }
  return out;
}
```

This gives at most n-1 payments and runs in O(n log n). **Honest caveat:** the true minimum number of transactions is NP-hard (it is a subset-sum partition problem). The greedy is the accepted practical answer; mention that exact minimization means splitting into zero-sum subsets, which is exponential, only worthwhile for small groups (n up to about 15 with bitmask DP).

### Deep dive and trade-offs

- **Rounding:** 100 split 3 ways is 33.33 + 33.33 + 33.34. Always distribute remainder minor units deterministically so totals match exactly.
- **Edit/delete an expense:** mark old as deleted (or add a reversing entry), apply the new one, bump `version`; use optimistic locking on the group (`version` column) so two simultaneous edits don't corrupt balances.
- **Concurrency:** two people add expenses to the same group at once. Balance rows are updated with atomic increments (`UPDATE ... SET net = net + ?`) inside the transaction; no read-modify-write in app code.
- **Multi-currency:** store each expense in its original currency; convert for display using a rate captured at expense time (store the rate used). Don't mix currencies in one balance row.
- **Offline-first mobile:** client queues expenses with client-generated UUIDs and syncs later; server dedupes on UUID.
- **Payments integration:** 'Settle up' can deep-link to UPI or a payment provider; the app only records the settlement (and confirms it) to avoid handling money itself.
- **Privacy:** only group members see group expenses; activity log is append-only.
- **Scaling later:** shard by group\_id; cache computed balances in Redis and invalidate on write; precompute user summary asynchronously from events.

**Interview tip:** open with 'immutable ledger plus derived balances, money in integer minor units'. Then show Strategy for the four split types and the heap-based simplification. That covers design, correctness, and algorithm in one pass.

### Q3 in depth: Splitwise, every detail

#### 3.1 How the product actually behaves (so your design matches it)

- A **group** (Goa Trip) has members. Anyone can add an expense: description, total amount, who paid (one or several people), who participated, and how it is divided.
- The app shows, per group, **who owes whom** and how much; and per user, one line per friend: 'You owe Ravi 450' or 'Meera owes you 1,200'.
- **Simplify debts** is a group setting: instead of showing the raw pairwise debts, the app shows the minimum payments that settle everyone.
- A **settlement** ('Ravi paid you 450') is recorded as a payment that reduces the debt; it is not an expense and nobody 'consumed' anything.
- Expenses can be edited or deleted; every change appears in the activity log; balances must always reconcile with the ledger.

#### 3.2 Money handling rules (get these exactly right)

1. Store amounts as **integers in the smallest unit** (paise/cents). 100.00 INR = 10000. Never `float` or `double`.
2. Every split must sum **exactly** to the total. Rounding leftovers are handed out one minor unit at a time.
3. Keep the currency with every amount (`Money(minor, currency)`); refuse arithmetic across different currencies.
4. Signs: use one convention and document it. Here: `net[user] > 0` means the group owes that user; `net[user] < 0` means the user owes the group. The sum of all nets in a group is always **0** (an invariant you should assert in code and tests).

#### 3.3 The four split types with worked examples (amounts in paise)

**Equal.** Total 10000 (INR 100.00) among 3 people. 10000 / 3 = 3333 remainder 1. Hand out the one leftover paisa to the first person: 3334, 3333, 3333 (sum 10000). Rotate who receives leftovers (for example by `hash(expenseId) mod n`) so the same person is not always the one who pays the extra paisa.

**Exact.** The user enters each person's amount: 4000, 3500, 2500. Validate: sum == 10000, else reject with 'amounts must add up to the total'.

**Percentage.** Total 10001 (INR 100.01), shares 25%, 25%, 50%. Exact values: 2500.25, 2500.25, 5000.50. Take the floor of each: 2500, 2500, 5000 = 10000. Leftover = 1. Give it to the person with the largest fractional part (0.50, the third person): 2500, 2500, 5001. Validate that percentages sum to 100.

**Shares (weights).** Total 10000, weights 1:2:3 (for example nights stayed). Exact: 1666.67, 3333.33, 5000.00. Floors: 1666, 3333, 5000 = 9999. Leftover 1 goes to the largest fraction (.67): 1667, 3333, 5000 = 10000. This is the **largest remainder method** and it is also used by Percentage.

**Multiple payers.** Asha paid 2000 and Bob paid 1000 (total 3000), shared equally by Asha, Bob and Chitra (1000 each). Net per person = paid - owed: Asha +1000, Bob 0, Chitra -1000. So Chitra owes 1000 to the group, and since only Asha is owed, Chitra pays Asha 1000. The net approach handles multiple payers naturally.

**Participant who did not pay and payer who did not participate:** both are normal. Example: Dev paid 600 for a dinner for Eli and Fay only (Dev not in the split). Nets: Dev +600, Eli -300, Fay -300.

#### 3.4 Two ways to store balances

| Approach | What is stored | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Net per user per group** | `net[group][user]` (sums to 0) | Tiny, trivially atomic, simplification is natural | Cannot answer 'who exactly owes me' without running the simplifier; users see settled-looking debts that did not happen |
| **Pairwise balances** | `owes[group][A][B]` for every pair | Matches the user's mental model ('Ravi owes me 450'), no surprises | O(n^2) rows per group; must net opposite directions; multi-payer needs allocation rules |

**What Splitwise-like apps do:** keep **pairwise** balances (as the display model) and offer simplification as a computed view on top. For multiple payers, allocate each participant's share across payers proportionally to what each payer paid, then post pairwise deltas. Keep a net-per-user number too, as a cheap checksum (the sum of pairwise balances for a user must equal their net).

Pairwise delta example: Asha paid 3000 for A, B, C equally (1000 each). Pairs updated: B owes A 1000 and C owes A 1000. Next, Bob paid 600 for A and B equally (300 each). Pairs: A owes B 300. Net the opposite directions: B owes A 1000 - 300 = **700**. Store one number per unordered pair.

#### 3.5 Debt simplification, step by step

Example: after a trip, nets are A +70, B +30, C -50, D -50 (sum 0). Everyone's direct debts might involve many pairs. The algorithm: put creditors in a max-heap {A:70, B:30} and debtors in a max-heap {C:50, D:50}; repeatedly match the largest creditor with the largest debtor.

| Step | Largest creditor | Largest debtor | Payment | Remaining |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | A 70 | C 50 | C pays A 50 | A 20, B 30, D 50 |
| 2 | B 30 | D 50 | D pays B 30 | A 20, D 20 |
| 3 | A 20 | D 20 | D pays A 20 | all zero |

Three payments for four people (at most n-1 in general). **Greedy is not always optimal.** Example: nets A +6, B +5, C -5, D -3, E -3. The best solution settles {B, C} with 1 payment (5 and -5 cancel) and {A, D, E} with 2 payments = **3 payments**. Greedy pairs A (6) with C (5) first, ending with **4 payments**. Finding the true minimum means partitioning people into the largest possible number of zero-sum groups, which is NP-hard in general (a partition problem). Practical answer: use the greedy for large groups; for groups of up to about 15 people compute the optimal partition with bitmask DP (`dp[mask]` = max number of zero-sum groups, mask sum must be 0), then settle each group with n-1 payments. Say this in the interview: it shows depth.

**Display rules:** if simplify is off, show the raw pairwise balances. If simplify is on, still keep raw balances in the database (they are the truth); the simplified list is computed on demand and cached. Never delete raw data to simplify.

#### 3.6 Settlements

A settlement `{group, from, to, amount}` posts a ledger entry that moves balances as if `from` paid `to`: `balance(from, to) -= amount`. It can be partial. If it overpays, the debt flips direction. Mark settlements with a status (`PENDING_CONFIRMATION`, `CONFIRMED`) if the receiver must confirm cash payments. For UPI or card payments the app can deep-link to the payment app and record the settlement on success; the app itself never holds the money, which avoids financial licensing and risk.

#### 3.7 Edit and delete without corrupting balances

Never 'patch' balances by guesswork. Use **reverse and reapply** inside one transaction:

1. Load the expense (version v) with its payers and splits.
2. Apply the **negative** of its old contribution to pairwise/net balances.
3. Validate and store the new expense fields and splits (version v+1).
4. Apply the **positive** contribution of the new version.
5. Append an `activity_log` row ('Asha edited Dinner: 3000 -> 3200').

Use **optimistic locking**: `UPDATE expenses SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE expense_id = ? AND version = ?`. If zero rows are updated, someone else edited first: return 409 and let the client reload. Delete = mark `deleted = true` and apply the negative contribution (soft delete keeps history and lets undo work).

#### 3.8 Full relational schema

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  user_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, email TEXT UNIQUE, phone TEXT,
  default_currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'INR', created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE groups (
  group_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, created_by BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users,
  simplify_debts BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE group_members (
  group_id BIGINT REFERENCES groups, user_id BIGINT REFERENCES users,
  joined_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, left_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL, PRIMARY KEY (group_id, user_id));

CREATE TABLE expenses (
  expense_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, group_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES groups,
  description TEXT NOT NULL, total_minor BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (total_minor > 0), currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
  split_type TEXT NOT NULL, created_by BIGINT NOT NULL, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1, deleted BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
  idempotency_key UUID UNIQUE);          -- client-generated: retries do not duplicate

CREATE TABLE expense_payers (expense_id BIGINT REFERENCES expenses, user_id BIGINT, paid_minor BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (paid_minor >= 0), PRIMARY KEY (expense_id, user_id));
CREATE TABLE expense_splits (expense_id BIGINT REFERENCES expenses, user_id BIGINT, owed_minor BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (owed_minor >= 0), PRIMARY KEY (expense_id, user_id));

CREATE TABLE settlements (
  settlement_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, group_id BIGINT NOT NULL, from_user BIGINT NOT NULL, to_user BIGINT NOT NULL,
  amount_minor BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (amount_minor > 0), currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  CHECK (from_user <> to_user));

-- Pairwise balance: ONE row per unordered pair, user_lo < user_hi.
-- net_minor > 0 means user_hi owes user_lo; < 0 means user_lo owes user_hi.
CREATE TABLE balances (
  group_id BIGINT, user_lo BIGINT, user_hi BIGINT, currency CHAR(3), net_minor BIGINT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (group_id, user_lo, user_hi, currency), CHECK (user_lo < user_hi));

CREATE TABLE activity_log (id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, group_id BIGINT, actor BIGINT, action TEXT, payload JSONB, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ);
```

The invariant `SUM(paid_minor) = total_minor = SUM(owed_minor)` is verified in application code inside the transaction (a CHECK constraint cannot span rows), plus a nightly consistency job that recomputes balances from the ledger and alerts on any difference.

**Atomic balance update (no read-modify-write in application code):**

```sql
INSERT INTO balances (group_id, user_lo, user_hi, currency, net_minor)
VALUES (:g, :lo, :hi, :cur, :delta)
ON CONFLICT (group_id, user_lo, user_hi, currency)
DO UPDATE SET net_minor = balances.net_minor + EXCLUDED.net_minor;
```

To avoid deadlocks when one transaction touches many pairs, always process pairs in sorted `(lo, hi)` order.

#### 3.9 Complete in-memory implementation (the machine-coding version)

```java
final class Money {
  final long minor; final String currency;
  Money(long minor, String currency) { this.minor = minor; this.currency = currency; }
  Money plus(Money o) { check(o); return new Money(minor + o.minor, currency); }
  Money minus(Money o) { check(o); return new Money(minor - o.minor, currency); }
  private void check(Money o) { if (!currency.equals(o.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch"); }
}

interface SplitStrategy {
  /** input: userId -> weight/percent/exact amount (meaning depends on the strategy). Returns userId -> owed minor units. */
  Map<String, Long> split(long totalMinor, Map<String, Double> input);
}

class EqualSplit implements SplitStrategy {
  public Map<String, Long> split(long total, Map<String, Double> in) {
    List<String> users = new ArrayList<>(in.keySet());
    long base = total / users.size(), rem = total % users.size();
    Map<String, Long> out = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < users.size(); i++) out.put(users.get(i), base + (i < rem ? 1 : 0));
    return out;
  }
}

class ExactSplit implements SplitStrategy {
  public Map<String, Long> split(long total, Map<String, Double> in) {
    Map<String, Long> out = new LinkedHashMap<>(); long sum = 0;
    for (var e : in.entrySet()) { long v = Math.round(e.getValue()); out.put(e.getKey(), v); sum += v; }
    if (sum != total) throw new IllegalArgumentException("exact amounts must add up to the total");
    return out;
  }
}

class WeightedSplit implements SplitStrategy {            // used for PERCENT (weights sum to 100) and SHARES
  final boolean requireHundred;
  WeightedSplit(boolean requireHundred) { this.requireHundred = requireHundred; }
  public Map<String, Long> split(long total, Map<String, Double> in) {
    double sumW = in.values().stream().mapToDouble(Double::doubleValue).sum();
    if (requireHundred && Math.abs(sumW - 100.0) > 1e-9) throw new IllegalArgumentException("percentages must add up to 100");
    Map<String, Long> out = new LinkedHashMap<>(); Map<String, Double> frac = new HashMap<>(); long assigned = 0;
    for (var e : in.entrySet()) {
      double exact = total * e.getValue() / sumW;
      long fl = (long) Math.floor(exact);
      out.put(e.getKey(), fl); frac.put(e.getKey(), exact - fl); assigned += fl;
    }
    long left = total - assigned;                          // largest remainder method
    List<String> order = new ArrayList<>(in.keySet());
    order.sort((a, b) -> Double.compare(frac.get(b), frac.get(a)));
    for (int i = 0; i < left; i++) out.merge(order.get(i), 1L, Long::sum);
    return out;
  }
}

class SplitStrategyFactory {
  static SplitStrategy of(SplitType t) {
    switch (t) {
      case EQUAL: return new EqualSplit();
      case EXACT: return new ExactSplit();
      case PERCENT: return new WeightedSplit(true);
      case SHARES: return new WeightedSplit(false);
      default: throw new IllegalArgumentException();
    }
  }
}

class Group {
  final String id; final Set<String> members = new HashSet<>();
  final Map<String, Long> net = new HashMap<>();                         // userId -> net minor (sum is always 0)
  final Map<String, Map<String, Long>> owes = new HashMap<>();           // A -> (B -> amount A owes B), only positive
  final List<Expense> expenses = new ArrayList<>();

  synchronized void addExpense(Expense e) {                              // one lock per group = strong consistency inside a group
    validate(e);
    apply(e, +1); expenses.add(e);
  }
  synchronized void removeExpense(Expense e) { apply(e, -1); expenses.remove(e); }

  private void apply(Expense e, int sign) {
    for (String u : e.paid.keySet()) net.merge(u, sign * e.paid.get(u), Long::sum);
    for (String u : e.owed.keySet()) net.merge(u, -sign * e.owed.get(u), Long::sum);
    if (e.paid.size() == 1) {                                            // single payer: also keep pairwise view
      String payer = e.paid.keySet().iterator().next();
      for (var en : e.owed.entrySet())
        if (!en.getKey().equals(payer)) transfer(en.getKey(), payer, sign * en.getValue());
    }
  }
  /** debtor owes creditor 'amt' more (negative amt reduces the debt); nets opposite directions. */
  private void transfer(String debtor, String creditor, long amt) {
    long forward = owes.computeIfAbsent(debtor, k -> new HashMap<>()).getOrDefault(creditor, 0L);
    long backward = owes.computeIfAbsent(creditor, k -> new HashMap<>()).getOrDefault(debtor, 0L);
    long result = forward - backward + amt;                              // positive: debtor owes creditor
    owes.get(debtor).put(creditor, Math.max(result, 0));
    owes.get(creditor).put(debtor, Math.max(-result, 0));
  }
  synchronized void settle(String from, String to, long amt) { transfer(from, to, -amt); net.merge(from, amt, Long::sum); net.merge(to, -amt, Long::sum); }

  private void validate(Expense e) {
    long p = e.paid.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum();
    long o = e.owed.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum();
    if (p != e.total || o != e.total) throw new IllegalArgumentException("payments and shares must equal the total");
    if (!members.containsAll(e.paid.keySet()) || !members.containsAll(e.owed.keySet())) throw new IllegalArgumentException("not a member");
  }
}

class DebtSimplifier {
  static List<Payment> simplify(Map<String, Long> net) {
    PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Long>> cred = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Long.compare(b.getValue(), a.getValue()));
    PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Long>> debt = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Long.compare(b.getValue(), a.getValue()));
    for (var e : net.entrySet()) {
      if (e.getValue() > 0) cred.add(new AbstractMap.SimpleEntry<>(e));
      else if (e.getValue() < 0) debt.add(new AbstractMap.SimpleEntry<>(e.getKey(), -e.getValue()));
    }
    List<Payment> out = new ArrayList<>();
    while (!cred.isEmpty() && !debt.isEmpty()) {
      var c = cred.poll(); var d = debt.poll();
      long pay = Math.min(c.getValue(), d.getValue());
      out.add(new Payment(d.getKey(), c.getKey(), pay));
      if (c.getValue() > pay) { c.setValue(c.getValue() - pay); cred.add(c); }
      if (d.getValue() > pay) { d.setValue(d.getValue() - pay); debt.add(d); }
    }
    return out;
  }
}
```

**Tests you should mention:** (1) every split type sums to the total, including awkward remainders; (2) `sum(net) == 0` after any sequence of add, edit, delete and settle; (3) add then delete returns balances to the exact previous state; (4) simplify output, applied as settlements, brings every net to zero; (5) a concurrency test adding 1,000 expenses from 20 threads gives the same result as sequential execution.

#### 3.10 Extra features and how they fit

- **Recurring expenses (rent):** a scheduler (Q24) creates the expense on a schedule using a stored template with an idempotency key `(template, period)`.
- **Friends outside groups:** model a hidden two-person group so there is only one code path.
- **Multi-currency:** expense stored in original currency; display converts using a rate captured at creation and saved with the expense so history never changes. A balance row exists per currency; settle per currency or convert with an explicit conversion entry.
- **Receipts and OCR:** upload to object storage; async OCR suggests the total and items; item-level splits ('Bob had the fish') are just an exact split derived from selected items.
- **Comments and reactions:** separate table keyed by expense id; push notifications via Q13.
- **Offline-first mobile:** the app writes locally with client-generated UUIDs, syncs when online; the server deduplicates by `idempotency_key`; conflicting edits resolved by version check.
- **Leaving a group with unsettled balances:** block leaving until balance is zero, or allow leaving but keep the balance record and show it on the friends list.
- **Search and export:** Elasticsearch for expense search; CSV export from the ledger.

#### 3.11 Scaling plan

- Start: one PostgreSQL primary with replicas; everything for a group is on one node, so every operation is a single-node transaction.
- Growth: shard by `group_id`. Friends-outside-groups are hidden groups, so they shard the same way. A user's 'total balance across groups' is the one cross-shard read: precompute it asynchronously from events into a per-user summary table (eventually consistent, refreshed within seconds).
- Cache balances in Redis keyed by group; invalidate on write.
- Hot groups (a 500-member community) are rare; keep the per-group lock short, and move heavy work (notifications, search indexing) off the transaction path via the outbox pattern.

#### 3.12 Follow-up questions and model answers

1. **How do you prevent duplicate expenses on a flaky network?** Client-generated idempotency key stored with a unique constraint; a retry returns the original result.
2. **How do you keep balances correct under concurrent edits?** One transaction per operation, atomic increments, optimistic version check on edits, and a nightly job that recomputes balances from the ledger.
3. **Why not store only 'who owes whom'?** It loses history and cannot be repaired. Store the ledger, derive balances.
4. **Is the minimum number of payments always achievable?** No; it is NP-hard. Greedy gives at most n-1; exact optimization is exponential and only worth it for small groups.
5. **How do you handle rounding fairly?** Largest remainder method for weighted splits; rotating leftover cents for equal splits; always sums exactly.
6. **What happens when the payer is not in the split?** Their net is +total; participants each owe their share to the payer.
7. **How do you show 'you owe in total' across groups at scale?** Event-driven summary table per user, eventually consistent.
8. **How would you add item-level bill splitting?** Items with assigned people; shared items split equally among their assignees; tax and tip allocated proportionally; produces an exact split.
9. **How do you secure it?** Membership check on every group call; activity log is append-only; only the creator or payer can delete (policy), with audit.
10. **How would you test the simplifier?** Property-based tests: random nets summing to zero must produce payments that zero everyone out, with at most n-1 payments.

## Q4. Cleartrip / MakeMyTrip (online travel booking)

**Problem:** let users search and book flights and hotels (also trains, buses, cabs). This is a favourite because it combines **search over third-party inventory**, **price volatility**, and a **multi-step booking with payment**.

### The key insight (say it first)

The platform usually **does not own inventory**. Airlines (directly or through GDS systems like Amadeus and Sabre), hotel chains and channel managers do. So:

- **Search** is a fan-out to many supplier APIs that are slow (1 to 5 s) and rate-limited, so we cache and aggregate aggressively.
- **Booking** must hold the supplier's seat/room, take payment, then confirm with the supplier. If any step fails we must undo the others (saga), and prices can change between search and book.

### Requirements

- **Functional:** search flights (origin, destination, dates, passengers, class) and hotels (city, dates, rooms); filters and sorting; fare details; select, enter traveller info, pay; get e-ticket/voucher; view/cancel/modify booking; refunds; price alerts; offers/coupons.
- **Non-functional:** search p95 under 2-3 s; **no double charge, no paid-but-unticketed booking**; high availability at sales peaks; handle supplier outages gracefully; strong auditability for money.

### Estimation

- 20M MAU, 2M DAU, 20 searches per booking session. Say 10M searches/day = \~115 searches/s average, \~1,000/s at peak (festival sales).
- Each search fans out to \~10 suppliers, so up to 10,000 supplier calls/s at peak if uncached. That cost is why caching and result reuse matter.
- Bookings: \~100K/day (about 1-2/s average, \~50/s peak). Tiny compared with search. **Search is the scale problem; booking is the correctness problem.** Design them as separate paths.

### API

```
GET  /flights/search?from=DEL&to=BOM&date=2026-12-20&adults=2&class=ECONOMY  -> results[], searchId
GET  /flights/{offerId}/price                -> revalidated fare (price check before booking)
POST /bookings                               {offerId, travellers[], contact}   (Idempotency-Key) -> bookingId, status=PENDING_PAYMENT
POST /bookings/{id}/pay                      {paymentMethod}                      -> payment redirect/status
GET  /bookings/{id}                          -> status, ticket(s)
POST /bookings/{id}/cancel                   -> refund quote / confirmation
GET  /hotels/search?city=&checkin=&checkout=&rooms=
```

### HLD

```
 Client -> CDN -> API Gateway -> [Search Service] -> Search Cache (Redis, TTL 5-15 min)
                                      |    \-> Supplier Adapters (Airline A, B, GDS, Hotel X...)  [parallel, timeouts]
                                      |    \-> Ranking/Filter/Dedupe -> response (streamed)
                                      +-> Elasticsearch (static data: airports, hotels, content, images)
                                      
 Client -> [Booking Service] (orchestrator / saga) --> Booking DB (SQL)
                |-> [Pricing/Offers Service] (revalidate fare, coupons, taxes)
                |-> [Inventory Hold via Supplier Adapter] (create PNR / hold room)
                |-> [Payment Service] -> PSP (Razorpay/Stripe/bank)
                |-> [Ticketing Service] -> supplier confirm -> e-ticket (PDF) -> object store
                '-> Kafka events -> Notification (email/SMS/WhatsApp), Analytics, Refund/Recon, Price alerts
```

### Search path (read-heavy)

1. **Parallel fan-out** to supplier adapters, each with a strict timeout (e.g. 2 s). Slow suppliers are skipped, so the page shows what we have; late results can stream in via SSE/WebSocket.
2. **Normalize** each supplier's response to one internal `Offer` model (each supplier has a different format, so use the Adapter pattern).
3. **Cache** results keyed by `(route, date, pax, class)` with a short TTL (5 to 15 minutes). Fares change, so the TTL is a trade-off between cost and freshness. Popular routes (DEL-BOM) hit the cache constantly.
4. **Dedupe and rank:** merge identical itineraries from several suppliers keeping the cheapest; rank by price, duration, stops, and a blend score. Apply filters server-side.
5. **Static data** (airports, airlines, hotel descriptions, images, reviews) lives in a normal DB plus Elasticsearch for hotel search by name/location. These change rarely, so cache heavily and serve images via CDN.
6. **Pre-warming:** a batch job refreshes fares for the top routes ahead of peak periods.

### Booking path (write-heavy on correctness): the saga

Booking states: `CREATED -> FARE_VERIFIED -> HELD -> PAYMENT_PENDING -> PAID -> TICKETED -> CONFIRMED`, with failure branches `FAILED`, `CANCELLED`, `REFUND_PENDING`, `REFUNDED`.

1. **Revalidate price** with the supplier (the cached fare may be stale). If the price changed, show the user the new fare and ask to continue. Never silently charge a different amount.
2. **Hold inventory:** create a provisional reservation at the supplier (airline PNR / hotel hold) with an expiry (typically 10 to 30 minutes).
3. **Take payment** through the payment service with an idempotency key. Payment can succeed, fail, or be **unknown** (timeout).
4. **Issue ticket / confirm** with the supplier.
5. **Compensation:** if payment fails, release the hold. If payment succeeded but ticketing fails, **auto-refund** (or retry ticketing / try an alternative fare) and notify the user.
6. The dangerous case is **payment unknown or ticketing unknown**: a reconciliation job queries the PSP and the supplier for every booking stuck in an intermediate state for more than N minutes and fixes it. Mention reconciliation explicitly; it is what interviewers listen for.

Use an **orchestration saga** (a booking orchestrator persisting state transitions) because the flow is long, has external parties, and needs clear audit. Persist every state change; make each step idempotent so the orchestrator can resume after a crash.

### Data model (core)

```
bookings(booking_id PK, user_id, type[FLIGHT|HOTEL], status, total_minor, currency,
         supplier, supplier_ref(PNR), idempotency_key UNIQUE, created_at, hold_expires_at)
booking_items(item_id, booking_id, offer_snapshot JSON, fare_breakdown JSON)   -- snapshot what the user agreed to
travellers(traveller_id, booking_id, name, dob, passport, ...)                 -- encrypt PII
payments(payment_id, booking_id, psp_ref, status, amount_minor, attempt_no)
refunds(refund_id, booking_id, amount_minor, status, reason)
booking_events(booking_id, from_state, to_state, ts, detail)                   -- audit trail
```

Relational DB (strong consistency, transactions), sharded by `user_id` or `booking_id` when needed. Offers during search are **not** stored in the DB, only in cache, with a snapshot saved at booking.

### LLD: how the code is structured

```java
interface SupplierAdapter {
  List<Offer> search(SearchRequest r);
  PriceQuote revalidate(String offerId);
  HoldResult hold(Offer o, List<Traveller> t);
  Ticket issue(HoldResult h);
  void release(HoldResult h);
}
class AirlineXAdapter implements SupplierAdapter { ... }   // Adapter pattern per supplier

class SearchService {
  List<SupplierAdapter> adapters; Cache cache; Ranker ranker;
  List<Offer> search(SearchRequest r) {
    return cache.getOrCompute(r.key(), () -> {
      // submit all adapters in parallel with timeout; collect successes
      List<Offer> all = fanOut(adapters, r, Duration.ofSeconds(2));
      return ranker.rank(dedupe(all), r);
    });
  }
}

interface BookingState { BookingState next(Event e); }     // State pattern: Created, Held, Paid, Ticketed, Failed...

class BookingOrchestrator {
  void process(String bookingId) {
    Booking b = repo.load(bookingId);
    switch (b.state) {
      case CREATED: verifyPrice(b); // fallthrough via events
      case FARE_VERIFIED: hold(b); ...
      case HELD: charge(b); ...
      case PAID: issueTicket(b); ...
    }
  }
  // each step: perform side effect idempotently, persist next state in same transaction, publish event via outbox
}
```

Patterns to name: **Adapter** (suppliers), **Strategy** (ranking, pricing/markup rules, coupon types), **State** (booking lifecycle), **Saga/Orchestrator** (booking), **Chain of Responsibility** (price components: base fare, taxes, convenience fee, discount).

### Deep dive and trade-offs

- **Fare freshness vs cost:** a short cache TTL means more supplier calls (cost, rate limits); a long TTL means more 'price changed' surprises. Cache by popularity: short TTL for hot routes, deterministic revalidation at checkout.
- **Price change at checkout:** common. UX shows 'fare updated from X to Y'; the booking records the final agreed price.
- **Seat inventory contention:** we don't own it, so the supplier arbitrates. Our job is to hold quickly and release cleanly. For hotels we own allotments with some partners, so we use a DB row with `available_rooms` decremented conditionally (`WHERE available_rooms > 0`).
- **Double booking by user (double click):** unique `idempotency_key` per checkout attempt; a duplicate returns the existing booking.
- **Supplier outage:** circuit breaker per adapter; the search still returns results from healthy suppliers.
- **Cancellation and refunds:** airline fare rules define fees; compute with a rules engine; refund via PSP asynchronously; track in `refunds`. Reconcile daily with supplier and PSP settlement files.
- **Dynamic pricing and markup:** a pricing service applies supplier price + platform margin - coupons; keep the breakdown for invoices and GST/tax compliance.
- **Peak sales:** queue-based admission or rate limiting at checkout, autoscale stateless search, protect suppliers with per-supplier rate limiters.
- **Security and compliance:** PCI scope stays with the PSP (never store raw card data); encrypt passport and ID data; mask in logs.
- **Price alerts:** store alerts, a periodic job re-searches popular routes, pushes via the notification service on drop.

**Interview tip:** split the problem into 'search = scale and caching' and 'booking = saga and reconciliation'. Say 'we don't own inventory' in your first minute; it shows you understand the domain.

### Q4 in depth: Cleartrip / MakeMyTrip, every detail

#### 4.1 What makes travel booking hard (say this first)

A travel platform owns almost **no inventory**. Flights, hotels, buses and trains belong to airlines, hotel chains and operators. You are an aggregator and a booking orchestrator on top of **slow, unreliable, rate-limited, inconsistent third-party APIs**. The three hard problems are: (1) **search** across many suppliers within a second or two, (2) **price/availability drift** between search and payment, and (3) a **multi-step booking** (hold, pay, confirm, ticket) that spans your system, a payment gateway and a supplier, any of which can fail halfway.

#### 4.2 Requirements and scale

- Functional: search flights/hotels, filters and sorting, price display, seat/room selection, hold, pay, issue ticket/voucher, cancel/refund, change/reschedule, notifications, loyalty and offers.
- Non-functional: search p95 under 2 s; booking never double-charges; booking and payment states always reconcile; 99.9 percent on search, higher on booking; graceful degradation when a supplier is slow.
- Scale example: 20M searches/day = about 230/s average, 2,000/s peak. 150k bookings/day = about 2/s average, 20/s peak. Search is **read-heavy by roughly 100:1**, so search and booking are separate services with separate scaling.
- Each search fans out to maybe 10 suppliers: 2,000 search/s becomes **20,000 supplier calls/s** if uncached. This is why caching and rate-limiting suppliers dominate the design.

#### 4.3 Two kinds of supplier, two designs

| Type | Example | How inventory is obtained | Design consequence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Live-search (pull)** | Airline GDS / NDC APIs (Amadeus, Sabre) | Real-time call per search | Slow (1-5 s), costly per call (GDS charges per search), must cache and throttle |
| **Inventory-feed (push)** | Hotels via channel managers, bus operators | Supplier pushes availability and rates; you store them | You own a local copy, search is fast, but copy can be stale; verify at booking |

Building an **adapter layer** (one interface, one adapter per supplier) lets the core system ignore supplier differences. Each adapter normalizes request, response, error codes and currencies into your canonical model, and carries its own timeout, retry and circuit breaker.

#### 4.4 Flight search pipeline, step by step

1. **Parse the request:** origin, destination, date(s), passengers, cabin, flexible dates.
2. **Resolve airports:** a city code may map to several airports (DEL; NYC = JFK + EWR + LGA). Use an airports table plus a typeahead service (a trie or search index).
3. **Choose suppliers:** a routing table decides which airlines/GDS to call for this route; skip suppliers that do not serve it.
4. **Fan out in parallel with a deadline:** call every adapter at once with a per-supplier timeout (for example 1.5 s). Collect whatever returns in time; **do not wait for stragglers**. Return partial results and stream late ones (SSE/WebSocket) so the page fills in progressively.
5. **Normalize** to a canonical `Itinerary`: segments, flight numbers, times in UTC plus local, fare components, baggage, refundability.
6. **Merge and dedupe:** the same flight can come from two suppliers at different prices; keep the cheapest per fare class but remember all sources.
7. **Rank and filter:** price, duration, stops, departure window, airline, with a scoring function (price + weighted duration + stop penalty); sort and paginate.
8. **Cache and respond.**

**Round trips and multi-city:** a round trip is two one-way searches combined; combining outbound and return options is a cross product, so prune (take the top K per leg, then combine and re-price).

#### 4.5 Search caching: the biggest lever

Cache key: `origin:destination:date:pax:cabin`. Values are lists of itineraries with fares.

- **Short TTL** because fares change: for departures within 7 days TTL 2-5 min; for far-future dates, 15-30 min. Hot routes (DEL-BOM) are always warm.
- **Cache is for browsing, not for booking.** Showing a cached price is fine; **re-price against the supplier before payment**. Tell the user clearly: 'Fare has changed from X to Y' if drift is detected.
- **Popularity-driven pre-warming:** a background job refreshes the top N routes and dates continuously.
- **Request coalescing:** if 500 users search DEL-BOM tomorrow at the same moment on a cold cache, send one supplier call and let the 500 requests await the same future.
- Estimated hit rate for a well-tuned system: 70-90 percent, cutting 20,000 supplier calls/s to 2,000-6,000.
- **Protect suppliers:** per-supplier rate limiter (token bucket, Q2) and a circuit breaker that opens when error rate crosses a threshold, so a dead supplier costs a fast fail instead of a timeout on every search.

#### 4.6 Hotel search

Hotels differ: the data is mostly **static content** (name, photos, amenities, location) plus **dynamic rates and availability** per date and room type.

- Static content in a document store, indexed in Elasticsearch/OpenSearch for text, filters (stars, amenities, price range) and **geo queries** (within 5 km of a point, via geohash/BKD tree).
- Dynamic rates stored as `rate[hotel][room][date]` in a fast store (Redis/Cassandra) fed by supplier pushes; a search computes the sum for the date range.
- Two-phase search: Elasticsearch narrows by location and filters to a few hundred hotels, then the rate service prices and checks availability for those hotels only, then ranking.
- Ranking blends price, rating, distance, conversion history, margin and personalization.

#### 4.7 Booking flow as a state machine

```
SEARCH_SELECTED -> PRICE_VERIFIED -> HELD -> PAYMENT_PENDING -> PAID -> CONFIRMING
    -> CONFIRMED (ticket issued)
    -> FAILED_AFTER_PAYMENT -> REFUND_PENDING -> REFUNDED
HELD -> EXPIRED  (hold timer ran out)
CONFIRMED -> CANCEL_REQUESTED -> CANCELLED -> REFUND_PENDING -> REFUNDED
```

Each transition is a database update guarded by the current state (`UPDATE bookings SET state='PAID' WHERE id=? AND state='PAYMENT_PENDING'`), so a duplicate payment callback or a retry cannot move the booking twice.

**Step by step:**

1. **Verify price** with the supplier (a pre-booking call). If price differs, show the new price and ask for consent.
2. **Hold / block** the inventory at the supplier where supported (airlines allow a time-limited hold, PNR created in 'on hold' state; hotels via 'pre-book'). The hold has a TTL (say 15 min). If the supplier has no hold API, there is a risk window: be honest in the design and mention 'book-then-refund' as the fallback.
3. **Create the booking** record in `HELD` with `expires_at`, and an **idempotency key** supplied by the client.
4. **Payment:** redirect/SDK to the gateway; amount is taken from the server-side booking, never from the client. Gateway webhook plus a status poll both feed the same idempotent handler.
5. **Confirm with supplier** (ticketing). Only after payment is captured.
6. **Success:** state CONFIRMED, store supplier reference (PNR), generate e-ticket PDF, email/SMS/push.
7. **Failure after payment** (supplier says sold out or ticketing times out): refund automatically, tell the user, and optionally offer alternatives.

#### 4.8 The saga: coordinating without a distributed transaction

There is no transaction spanning your DB, a payment gateway and an airline. Use a **saga** with compensating actions, driven by a **booking orchestrator** (a workflow engine such as Temporal/Cadence, or a state machine fed by Kafka events):

| Step | Action | Compensation if a later step fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Hold inventory at supplier | Release the hold |
| 2 | Capture payment | Refund payment |
| 3 | Confirm/ticket at supplier | Cancel at supplier, then refund |
| 4 | Issue voucher, notify | Retry; non-critical, never rolls back money |

**Rules:** every step is **idempotent** (safe to retry), every call has a timeout and a retry with backoff, every outcome is persisted before the next step, and any step whose result is **unknown** (timeout) is resolved by a **reconciliation query** ('does supplier have a booking with my reference?') rather than a blind retry. Unknown-outcome handling is the single most important thing to state in this interview.

**Payment taken but ticketing timed out - what now?** Mark `CONFIRMING_UNKNOWN`. A reconciler polls the supplier with the booking reference every 30 s for up to N minutes. If a ticket exists, move to CONFIRMED. If not, cancel at supplier and refund. A human-visible status 'We are confirming your booking' avoids panic and duplicate attempts.

#### 4.9 Seat selection and ancillaries

Seat maps come from the supplier per flight. Seats chosen are added to the hold. For hotels, room choice is made before the hold. Ancillaries (baggage, meals, insurance) are separate line items with their own price and are priced into the total at verification. Model the booking as **one order with many items**: `orders`, `order_items(type, supplier_ref, price, state)`. Partial failure (the meal fails but the flight succeeds) is handled per item.

#### 4.10 Data model

```sql
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  booking_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, user_id BIGINT NOT NULL, state TEXT NOT NULL,
  total_minor BIGINT NOT NULL, currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
  idempotency_key UUID UNIQUE NOT NULL, hold_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1);
CREATE TABLE booking_items (
  item_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, booking_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES bookings,
  type TEXT NOT NULL,                 -- FLIGHT / HOTEL / BUS / ANCILLARY
  supplier TEXT NOT NULL, supplier_ref TEXT, price_minor BIGINT NOT NULL, state TEXT NOT NULL, details JSONB NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE passengers (booking_id BIGINT, seq INT, name TEXT, dob DATE, passport_no_enc BYTEA, PRIMARY KEY (booking_id, seq));
CREATE TABLE payments (
  payment_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, booking_id BIGINT NOT NULL, gateway TEXT, gateway_txn_id TEXT UNIQUE,
  amount_minor BIGINT, state TEXT, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ);
CREATE TABLE refunds (refund_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, payment_id BIGINT, amount_minor BIGINT, reason TEXT, state TEXT, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ);
CREATE TABLE booking_events (id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, booking_id BIGINT, from_state TEXT, to_state TEXT, payload JSONB, at TIMESTAMPTZ);  -- audit trail
```

Shard bookings by `user_id` (a user's trips are together) with a secondary lookup by `booking_id`. Passport and card-adjacent data is encrypted at rest with field-level keys.

#### 4.11 Pricing, fees, offers

Final price = base fare + taxes + supplier fee + platform convenience fee - coupon/loyalty discount. Keep the **price breakdown** itself stored with the booking (needed for refunds and invoices). Offer engine: rules (min amount, route, bank card BIN, first booking) evaluated at checkout; a coupon redemption is a counted resource, so decrement atomically (Q17 flash-sale pattern) and release on payment failure. Currency shown to the user is converted at a rate locked for the booking session.

#### 4.12 Cancellation, refund, reschedule

Rules come from the fare (non-refundable, refundable with penalty, free within 24 h). Store the **fare rule snapshot** at booking time so the refund calculation is deterministic. Refund = paid amount - supplier penalty - platform fee, computed by a rules service, executed as a refund saga (cancel at supplier first, then refund through the gateway, which may take days). Reschedule = cancel plus rebook as one orchestrated change with a price difference.

#### 4.13 Failure scenarios

| Failure | Handling |
| --- | --- |
| Supplier slow in search | Per-supplier deadline; show partial results; stream the rest |
| Supplier down | Circuit breaker, skip supplier, alert; do not fail the whole search |
| Fare changed at verify | Show new price, require consent; log drift for supplier-quality metrics |
| Hold expires during payment | Re-verify before capture; if inventory still there, extend/rehold; else refund |
| Duplicate payment webhook | Idempotent handler keyed by `gateway_txn_id`; state guard |
| User double-clicks Pay | Idempotency key on booking creation returns the existing booking |
| Payment success but app crashed before saving | Gateway webhook is the source of truth; reconciler matches unmatched gateway transactions to bookings |
| Ticketing unknown outcome | Reconcile with supplier before any retry or refund |
| Overbooking by supplier | Immediate refund plus compensation policy; alternatives search |

#### 4.14 Architecture (HLD)

```
Client -> API Gateway/BFF -> Search Service -> Supplier Adapter Pool -> GDS / airlines / hotel feeds
                                |-> Redis (search cache) | Elasticsearch (hotels) | Rate Service
                          -> Booking Orchestrator (workflow engine)
                                |-> Inventory/Hold Service -> suppliers
                                |-> Payment Service -> Gateway (webhooks back in)
                                |-> Ticketing Service -> suppliers
                                |-> Notification Service (Kafka -> email/SMS/push)
                          -> Bookings DB (sharded) | Kafka (events) | Reconciliation jobs
```

#### 4.15 LLD: supplier adapters with resilience, and the booking state machine

```java
interface FlightSupplier {
  String name();
  List<Itinerary> search(SearchRequest req) throws SupplierException;
  PriceQuote verifyPrice(String offerId);
  HoldResult hold(String offerId, List<Passenger> pax);
  TicketResult ticket(String holdRef, PaymentProof proof);
  void cancel(String ref);
  Optional<TicketResult> lookup(String clientRef);    // reconciliation: did the booking actually happen?
}

class ResilientSupplier {                               // decorator: timeout + circuit breaker + rate limit
  private final FlightSupplier delegate; private final CircuitBreaker breaker; private final RateLimiter limiter;
  List<Itinerary> search(SearchRequest r, Duration timeout) {
    if (!breaker.allowRequest()) return List.of();        // fail fast
    if (!limiter.tryAcquire(delegate.name()).isAllowed()) return List.of();
    try {
      List<Itinerary> out = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> delegate.search(r)).get(timeout.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
      breaker.recordSuccess(); return out;
    } catch (Exception e) { breaker.recordFailure(); return List.of(); }
  }
}

class SearchService {
  List<Itinerary> search(SearchRequest req) {
    String key = req.cacheKey();
    return cache.getOrCompute(key, ttlFor(req), () -> {                // also coalesces concurrent identical requests
      List<CompletableFuture<List<Itinerary>>> fs = suppliers.stream()
          .map(s -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> s.search(req, Duration.ofMillis(1500)), pool)).toList();
      List<Itinerary> all = new ArrayList<>();
      for (var f : fs) { try { all.addAll(f.getNow(List.of())); } catch (Exception ignore) {} }   // whatever is done by now
      return ranker.rank(dedupe(all), req);
    });
  }
}

enum BookingState { HELD, PAYMENT_PENDING, PAID, CONFIRMING, CONFIRMED, FAILED_AFTER_PAYMENT, REFUND_PENDING, REFUNDED, EXPIRED, CANCELLED }

class BookingStateMachine {
  private static final Map<BookingState, Set<BookingState>> ALLOWED = Map.of(
    BookingState.HELD, Set.of(BookingState.PAYMENT_PENDING, BookingState.EXPIRED),
    BookingState.PAYMENT_PENDING, Set.of(BookingState.PAID, BookingState.EXPIRED),
    BookingState.PAID, Set.of(BookingState.CONFIRMING),
    BookingState.CONFIRMING, Set.of(BookingState.CONFIRMED, BookingState.FAILED_AFTER_PAYMENT),
    BookingState.FAILED_AFTER_PAYMENT, Set.of(BookingState.REFUND_PENDING),
    BookingState.CONFIRMED, Set.of(BookingState.CANCELLED),
    BookingState.CANCELLED, Set.of(BookingState.REFUND_PENDING),
    BookingState.REFUND_PENDING, Set.of(BookingState.REFUNDED));
  boolean transition(long id, BookingState from, BookingState to) {
    if (!ALLOWED.getOrDefault(from, Set.of()).contains(to)) throw new IllegalStateException(from + " -> " + to);
    return repo.updateIfState(id, from, to) == 1;        // compare-and-set in SQL; false means someone else moved it
  }
}

class PaymentWebhookHandler {                           // idempotent: safe if the gateway calls 5 times
  void onPaymentSuccess(String gatewayTxnId, long bookingId, long amountMinor) {
    if (!payments.insertIfAbsent(gatewayTxnId, bookingId, amountMinor)) return;          // unique constraint
    Booking b = bookings.get(bookingId);
    if (amountMinor != b.totalMinor) { refunds.initiate(gatewayTxnId, "amount mismatch"); return; }
    if (sm.transition(bookingId, BookingState.PAYMENT_PENDING, BookingState.PAID)) orchestrator.startTicketing(bookingId);
    else if (b.state == BookingState.EXPIRED) refunds.initiate(gatewayTxnId, "paid after expiry");
  }
}
```

#### 4.16 Reconciliation, the safety net

Nightly and continuous jobs compare three sources: **your bookings, gateway settlement files, and supplier statements**. Categories to flag: paid but not confirmed, confirmed but not paid, refunded at gateway but booking active, supplier charged but no booking. Every mismatch becomes a ticket with an owner. This is what real travel companies spend engineering time on.

#### 4.17 Follow-up questions and model answers

1. **How do you keep search fast with 10 slow suppliers?** Parallel fan-out with a deadline, partial and streamed results, caching with short TTL, circuit breakers, request coalescing.
2. **Cached price differs from the real price. What do you do?** Cache is advisory; always re-verify before hold and payment; show the change and get consent; track drift per supplier.
3. **How do you prevent double booking and double charge?** Idempotency key on booking creation, state guard (compare-and-set) on every transition, unique gateway transaction id, supplier hold before payment.
4. **Payment succeeded but ticketing failed.** Saga compensation: cancel at supplier if needed, auto-refund, notify; unknown outcomes resolved by reconciliation lookup, never blind retry.
5. **How do you design hotel search with maps and filters?** Elasticsearch with geo and facet queries for static data; separate rate/availability store queried only for the shortlisted hotels.
6. **Why a workflow engine instead of plain code?** Durable state, timers (hold expiry), retries, visibility, and resuming after crashes without custom plumbing.
7. **How would you handle flash sales and festival peaks?** Pre-scale search, aggressive caching, queue-based admission to booking, per-supplier throttles, degrade features (recommendations off) before core flows.
8. **How do you support multi-currency?** Prices stored in supplier currency and converted at a locked rate; store both amounts; round per the currency's minor unit.
9. **How do you test it?** Supplier simulators with injected latency and failures, contract tests per adapter, chaos tests for crash-between-steps, replayable event logs.
10. **What do you monitor?** Search latency per supplier, cache hit rate, fare-drift rate, booking funnel conversion, payment success rate, count of bookings stuck in each state, reconciliation mismatches.

#### 4.18 One-page summary

Aggregator over unreliable suppliers. Search = adapters + parallel fan-out + deadline + short-TTL cache + circuit breakers. Booking = idempotent saga (verify, hold, pay, ticket) with compensations. State machine with compare-and-set. Reconcile everything against gateway and supplier. Hotels = Elasticsearch plus a rate store. Never trust a cached price at payment time.

## Q5. WhatsApp / Chat system

**Problem:** one-to-one and group messaging with delivery receipts, online presence, media sharing, and offline delivery.

### Requirements

- **Functional:** 1:1 chat, group chat (up to \~1,000 members), sent/delivered/read receipts, last seen/online status, media (image, video, document), push notification when offline, multi-device sync, message history.
- **Non-functional:** low latency (under 200 ms online delivery), **no message loss**, **per-conversation ordering**, high availability, end-to-end encryption (E2EE) so servers can't read content.

### Estimation

- 500M DAU x 40 messages/day = 20B messages/day = \~230,000 messages/s average, \~600,000/s peak.
- Message \~100 bytes of text: 2 TB/day of text. Media dominates (stored in blob storage, not the chat DB).
- Concurrent connections: \~200M+ online. One server holds \~100K to 1M idle WebSockets, so you need thousands of **gateway** servers.

### API (over WebSocket, plus REST for media)

```
WS  connect /ws?token=...            persistent bidirectional connection
 -> send   {clientMsgId, chatId, to, ciphertext, type}
 <- ack    {clientMsgId, serverMsgId, status=SENT}
 <- deliver{serverMsgId, chatId, from, ciphertext, ts}
 -> receipt{serverMsgId, status=DELIVERED|READ}
POST /media/upload  -> mediaId (encrypted blob in object store), then message carries mediaId + key
GET  /chats/{id}/messages?before=
```

### HLD

```
 Phone A <==WS==> [Chat Gateway A] --\                               /-- [Chat Gateway B] <==WS==> Phone B
                       |              \                             /
                       v               v                           v
                 [Session Registry: userId -> gatewayId]  (Redis)
                       |
                 [Chat Service] --> Message Store (Cassandra/HBase, partition by chatId)
                       |         \-> Kafka (fan-out, receipts, analytics)
                       |          \-> Inbox/Offline queue per user
                       +--> [Push Notification Service] -> APNs / FCM (when recipient offline)
 Media: Client -> Upload Service -> Object Store (S3) -> CDN     Presence: [Presence Service] (Redis, heartbeats)
```

### Message flow (1:1)

1. A sends over its WebSocket to Gateway A with a client-generated `clientMsgId` (for dedupe/retries).
2. Chat Service assigns a **server message id** (monotonic per chat, e.g. timestamp + sequence), persists the message, and returns an ack (**one grey tick: sent**).
3. Chat Service looks up B in the session registry.
   - **B online:** forward to Gateway B, which pushes over B's socket. B's app acks, producing **two ticks (delivered)**, sent back to A.
   - **B offline:** message is stored in B's inbox/offline queue and a push notification is sent via APNs/FCM. When B reconnects it pulls everything after its last seen sequence number.
4. When B opens the chat, a **read receipt** flows back (**blue ticks**).

Persist **before** acking, and delete from the server only after the recipient acks delivery. That gives at-least-once delivery; clients dedupe by `serverMsgId`.

### Data model

```
messages(chat_id PARTITION KEY, msg_id CLUSTERING KEY (time-ordered), sender_id, body_or_media_ref, type, created_at)
inbox(user_id PARTITION KEY, msg_id, chat_id, status)         -- undelivered / unsynced messages
chats(chat_id, type[1:1|group], members[], created_at)
users(user_id, phone, public_keys, last_seen)
group_members(group_id, user_id, role)
```

Cassandra/HBase suit this: very high write throughput, and the access pattern is 'recent messages of one chat'. WhatsApp-style systems also delete the server copy after delivery, which keeps storage small.

### Group chat

- Small groups: **fan-out on write** (server delivers a copy of the message to each member's inbox/socket). Simple and fast to read.
- Very large groups/channels: fan-out cost grows with members, so cap group size or use **fan-out on read** with per-group timelines and sequence numbers.
- Group membership is cached; delivery to members on different gateways goes through Kafka or a direct gateway-to-gateway publish.

### Presence and last seen

Clients send a heartbeat every \~5 to 30 s; Presence Service writes `userId -> lastHeartbeat` in Redis with a TTL. Online = key exists. Don't broadcast every change to everyone: fetch presence lazily when a chat is opened, or subscribe only to the contacts currently visible on screen.

### Ordering and ids

Ordering matters **within a chat**, not globally. Partition by `chat_id`, and assign monotonically increasing ids per chat (one writer per chat partition, or hybrid logical clock/Snowflake). Clients display by server order, falling back to client time for unsent messages.

### LLD: connection and delivery classes

```java
class ChatGateway {                         // holds the sockets
  Map<String, WebSocketSession> sessions = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();   // userId -> socket
  void onMessage(String userId, ClientMessage m) { chatService.send(userId, m); }
  void deliver(String userId, ServerMessage m) { sessions.get(userId).send(m); }
}

class ChatService {
  SessionRegistry registry; MessageStore store; InboxStore inbox; PushService push; GatewayClient gateways;

  Ack send(String from, ClientMessage m) {
    if (store.existsByClientId(from, m.clientMsgId)) return store.ackFor(m);     // idempotent retry
    ServerMessage sm = store.append(m);                                          // assign id, persist
    for (String to : membersOf(m.chatId, from)) {
      String gw = registry.gatewayOf(to);
      if (gw != null) gateways.forward(gw, to, sm);
      else { inbox.add(to, sm); push.notifyOffline(to, sm); }
    }
    return new Ack(sm.id, SENT);
  }
}
```

### Deep dive and trade-offs

- **E2EE:** Signal protocol; each device has keys, the server routes ciphertext only. Consequence: server-side search and spam scanning on content are impossible, and multi-device needs per-device encryption of each message.
- **Why WebSocket not polling:** persistent connection gives push with minimal overhead; fall back to long polling on bad networks.
- **Gateway failure:** clients reconnect (with jittered backoff) to another gateway and pull missed messages by last sequence number. Nothing is lost because messages are persisted first.
- **Hot group / reconnect storm:** rate-limit reconnects, spread with jitter, scale gateways horizontally.
- **Multi-device:** each device has its own inbox cursor; sender encrypts per device or uses a shared sender key.
- **Media:** upload to object storage first, send only a reference and decryption key; thumbnails inline; CDN for downloads; auto-expire.
- **Retention:** keep messages on device; the server holds them only until delivered (plus backups encrypted by the user).
- **Spam/abuse:** rate limits, metadata-based detection, user reports (since content is encrypted).

**Interview tip:** be precise about the tick states and the 'persist, then ack, then deliver, then delete after delivery ack' pipeline. Mention gateway + session registry; that is the core scaling idea.

### Q5 in depth: WhatsApp / chat system, every detail

#### 5.1 Requirements and scale

- Functional: 1:1 chat, group chat (up to 1024 members), delivery status (sent, delivered, read), online/last-seen, media, offline delivery, multi-device, push notifications, end-to-end encryption.
- Non-functional: low latency (under 200 ms same region), **no message loss**, **per-conversation ordering**, high availability, millions of concurrent long-lived connections.
- Scale example: 1B users, 500M DAU, 40 messages/user/day = 20B messages/day = **230k msgs/s average, 700k peak**. Concurrent connections: 200M. At about 10 KB of memory per connection (socket buffers + session), 200M connections need **2 TB RAM**, so about **2,000 gateway servers at 100k connections each**.
- Storage: 100 bytes metadata + 100 bytes text average = 200 B x 20B = **4 TB/day** for text. Media dominates (go to object storage, Q8).

#### 5.2 Why WebSocket and how a connection works

HTTP polling wastes requests; long polling holds threads; **WebSocket** gives one persistent, full-duplex TCP connection upgraded from HTTP, so the server can push the instant a message arrives. Mobile networks drop connections constantly, so the client sends a heartbeat (ping every 30-60 s), reconnects with exponential backoff and jitter, and **resumes from the last message id it has** so nothing is lost.

**Connection layer is stateful**, which makes everything else harder: a user is connected to *one specific gateway server*. You need a **session registry** `user_id/device_id -> gateway_id` (Redis, TTL refreshed by heartbeat) so any service can route a message to the right gateway.

#### 5.3 Message flow, hop by hop (1:1)

1. Alice's app generates `client_msg_id` (UUID) and sends `{conversation_id, client_msg_id, body, ts}` over her WebSocket to Gateway A.
2. Gateway A forwards to the **Chat Service**, which assigns a **per-conversation sequence number** (monotonic) and persists the message. Persist **before** acknowledging.
3. Chat Service replies to Alice with `ACK(client_msg_id, seq)` -> Alice sees **one tick (sent)**.
4. Chat Service looks up Bob's sessions in the registry. If Bob is online on Gateway B, it publishes the message to Gateway B (via Kafka topic partitioned by gateway, or Redis pub/sub or gRPC). Gateway B pushes it down Bob's socket.
5. Bob's app stores it and sends `DELIVERED(seq)`. Chat Service updates state and notifies Alice -> **two ticks**.
6. When Bob opens the chat, the app sends `READ(upto_seq)` -> **blue ticks** (a cumulative marker, not one event per message).
7. If Bob is **offline**: the message stays in his per-user inbox; a push notification (APNs/FCM) wakes the device; on reconnect the app asks 'give me everything after my last seq per conversation' and the server streams it. After delivery, the server **deletes** its copy (WhatsApp keeps messages on devices, not on servers).

#### 5.4 Ordering and ids

Global ordering across the world is neither needed nor possible cheaply. You need **order within a conversation**. Options:

| Approach | How | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Per-conversation counter | Conversation shard owns an incrementing `seq` | Simple and strict; the shard is the serialization point (fine, one chat is low rate) |
| Snowflake-style id (time + node + counter) | ids sort roughly by time | No coordination, but ties and clock skew break strict order across nodes |
| Hybrid logical clock | Timestamp that respects causality | Good for multi-writer, more complex |

Pick: route all messages of a conversation to the same Chat Service partition (hash of `conversation_id`), which assigns `seq`. The client displays by `seq`, and uses `client_msg_id` for **deduplication** (a retry after a lost ACK must not create a duplicate).

**Delivery guarantee:** at-least-once on the wire + idempotent receive (dedupe by `client_msg_id`) = **effectively once**. Never claim exactly-once transport.

#### 5.5 Groups

A message to a group of N is stored **once** and delivered N-1 times.

- **Small groups (under \~100):** fan out per member on write: for each member, deliver to online ones via gateway and add to the offline inbox of others.
- **Large groups / channels:** store once in the group log; each member tracks `last_read_seq`; online members get a lightweight notification and fetch; this is the same fan-out-on-read idea as feeds (Q6).
- Group membership and admin rules live in a Group Service (membership list cached; changes are events). A message must be authorized against membership **at send time**.
- Delivery/read receipts in large groups are aggregated (a counter) rather than N separate events.

#### 5.6 Presence (online / last seen / typing)

Presence is high-volume and low-value per event, so treat it as ephemeral:

- Heartbeat updates `presence:{user}` in Redis with TTL (for example 60 s). Absence of heartbeat = offline; `last_seen` = last heartbeat time.
- **Do not broadcast** presence changes to all contacts (500 contacts x 200M users = disaster). Fetch presence **on demand** when a user opens a chat, and subscribe only to the contacts currently on screen.
- Typing indicators are fire-and-forget through the gateway, never stored, rate-limited, and sent only to the other party's open chat.

#### 5.7 Data model

Message store needs: write-heavy, append-only, reads by (conversation, range). A wide-column store (Cassandra/ScyllaDB/HBase) fits.

```
Table messages: PRIMARY KEY ((conversation_id, bucket), seq)
  columns: sender_id, client_msg_id, body_ciphertext, type, media_ref, sent_at, status
  -- bucket = e.g. month, so a hot conversation does not make one giant partition
  -- reads: WHERE conversation_id=? AND bucket=? AND seq > :last ORDER BY seq LIMIT 50

Table inbox (undelivered):     PRIMARY KEY (user_id, conversation_id, seq)  -- deleted after delivery ack
Table conversations_by_user:   PRIMARY KEY (user_id, last_activity DESC)    -- chat list screen
Table receipts:                PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, user_id) -> delivered_upto, read_upto
Table devices:                 PRIMARY KEY (user_id, device_id) -> push_token, platform, keys
```

User, contacts and group metadata go in a relational or key-value store (smaller, consistency matters more).

#### 5.8 Multi-device

Each device has its own connection and keys. A message is delivered to **every device** of the recipient and also to the sender's other devices ('sent' sync). Each device tracks its own `last_seq`. For E2EE, the sender encrypts a copy for each recipient device (fan-out of ciphertexts, as WhatsApp's multi-device design does). Read state is synced across a user's devices through the receipts table.

#### 5.9 End-to-end encryption in one page

Servers must not be able to read content. Signal-protocol outline: each device uploads an **identity key**, a **signed prekey** and a batch of **one-time prekeys** to the server. To start a chat, Alice fetches Bob's prekey bundle, performs an **X3DH** key agreement to derive a shared secret, then uses the **Double Ratchet** to derive a fresh key per message (forward secrecy: leaking today's key does not expose yesterday's messages; post-compromise security: it heals). The server only relays ciphertext plus routing metadata. Groups use **sender keys**: one symmetric key per sender, distributed to members pairwise, so a group message is encrypted once. Trade-offs to state: server-side search and spam detection are impossible on content (use metadata and user reports), and backups need a separate user-held key.

#### 5.10 Media

Never send media through the chat path. The client uploads the encrypted file to object storage via a pre-signed URL (resumable, chunked), gets a `media_ref` and key, and sends a small message carrying the reference, thumbnail and decryption key. Recipients download from a CDN edge. Compress and generate thumbnails client-side. Deduplicate forwarded media by content hash.

#### 5.11 Gateway design and scaling

- Gateways are stateless in logic but stateful in connections. Use L4 load balancing (TCP) with least-connections and connection draining on deploy.
- Tune the OS: file descriptor limits, epoll/kqueue event loops (Netty, Erlang/BEAM which WhatsApp famously used), small per-connection buffers.
- **Reconnect storms:** when a gateway dies, 100k clients reconnect at once. Use jittered backoff and admission control so the rest of the fleet is not overwhelmed.
- Routing between services and gateways: Chat Service publishes `deliver(user, device, msg)` to a topic keyed by gateway id; each gateway consumes its own partition. Alternative: a consistent-hash ring decides which gateway owns a user so the registry lookup is cheaper.
- Geo: users connect to the nearest region; cross-region messages travel over backbone links; user home region holds the inbox.

#### 5.12 Reliability scenarios

| Scenario | Handling |
| --- | --- |
| ACK lost, client resends | Same `client_msg_id`, server returns existing `seq` (idempotent) |
| Gateway crashes | Registry entries expire; clients reconnect elsewhere and sync from last seq; unacked pushes are retried from inbox |
| Recipient offline for weeks | Inbox with retention (e.g. 30 days) then dropped; push tells device to sync |
| Chat Service partition leader fails | Kafka/DB replica takes over; sequence assignment resumes from the persisted max seq |
| Duplicate delivery to device | Device dedupes by `(conversation_id, seq)` |
| Out-of-order arrival | Client sorts by `seq`; if a gap is seen, it requests the missing range |
| User blocks sender | Checked at send time in Chat Service; message dropped or silently not delivered |
| Spam / abuse | Rate limit sends (Q2), report-based signals, new-account throttles |

#### 5.13 LLD: core classes

```java
record Message(String convId, long seq, String clientMsgId, String senderId, byte[] body, long sentAt) {}

class ChatService {
  private final MessageStore store; private final SessionRegistry sessions;
  private final GatewayRouter router; private final InboxStore inbox; private final PushService push;
  private final ConcurrentMap<String, AtomicLong> seqPerConv = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();  // in real life: owned by the partition leader, recovered from store

  Ack send(String convId, String clientMsgId, String sender, byte[] body) {
    Optional<Message> dup = store.findByClientId(convId, clientMsgId);
    if (dup.isPresent()) return new Ack(dup.get().seq());                 // idempotent retry
    authorize(convId, sender);
    long seq = seqPerConv.computeIfAbsent(convId, c -> new AtomicLong(store.maxSeq(c))).incrementAndGet();
    Message m = new Message(convId, seq, clientMsgId, sender, body, System.currentTimeMillis());
    store.append(m);                                                        // durable BEFORE ack
    for (String member : members(convId)) if (!member.equals(sender)) deliver(member, m);
    return new Ack(seq);
  }
  private void deliver(String user, Message m) {
    List<Session> live = sessions.activeSessions(user);
    if (live.isEmpty()) { inbox.add(user, m); push.notifyUser(user, m.convId()); return; }
    for (Session s : live) router.sendToGateway(s.gatewayId(), s.deviceId(), m);
    inbox.add(user, m);                                                     // removed when device acks delivery
  }
  void onDeliveryAck(String user, String deviceId, String convId, long seq) { inbox.remove(user, convId, seq); receipts.markDelivered(convId, user, seq); }
  List<Message> sync(String user, String convId, long afterSeq, int limit) { return store.range(convId, afterSeq, limit); }
}

class SessionRegistry {                       // backed by Redis: SET session:{user}:{device} gatewayId EX 90
  void register(String user, String device, String gatewayId) {...}
  void heartbeat(String user, String device) {...}     // refresh TTL
  List<Session> activeSessions(String user) {...}
}
```

Client-side state machine for one outgoing message: `PENDING (local) -> SENT (server ACK) -> DELIVERED -> READ`, with `FAILED` and a retry button; pending messages are persisted locally and resent after reconnect.

#### 5.14 HLD diagram

```
Mobile client <==WebSocket==> L4 LB -> Gateway fleet <-> Session Registry (Redis)
                                   |  (user events)
                                   v
```
