```
POST /v1/notify  {userId | userIds[] | segmentId, templateId, params, channels?, priority, sendAt?, dedupeKey}
GET  /v1/notifications/{id}/status
PUT  /v1/users/{id}/preferences  {channel settings, quiet hours, topics}
```

### HLD

```
 Producers (services) -> [Notification API] -> validate, dedupe (Redis SET NX dedupeKey), check preferences
                                  -> Kafka topics by PRIORITY: high (OTP/transactional), medium, low (marketing)
                                  -> [Orchestrator] : resolve recipients (user service / segment), pick channels, render template (i18n)
                                  -> per-channel queues: push-q, sms-q, email-q, inapp-q
                                  -> [Channel Workers] -> Providers: APNs/FCM, Twilio/SMS aggregator, SES/SendGrid, WebSocket gateway
                                  -> provider callbacks/webhooks -> [Status Tracker] -> DB / analytics
 [Scheduler] for sendAt;  [Retry/DLQ]; [Rate limiter per user and per provider]; [Template Service]; [Device Token Registry]
```

### Key design points

1. **Separate queues by priority and channel.** OTPs never wait behind a 50M-user campaign. Dedicated worker pools per queue.
2. **Fan-out for campaigns:** the orchestrator expands a segment into per-user messages in batches (paged reads), writing to the channel queue. The segment query itself is a data-platform job, not on the hot path.
3. **Preferences and compliance:** check opt-in/opt-out, quiet hours (hold until morning), and legal rules (DND registries for SMS, unsubscribe links in email). Always honor transactional vs marketing categories.
4. **Dedupe:** the caller provides a `dedupeKey`; also per-user per-template window (e.g. no more than 1 'cart reminder' per 24 h).
5. **Rate limiting:** per user (avoid spamming), per provider (respect their limits), and global backpressure through the queue.
6. **Retries:** exponential backoff with jitter; retry on provider 5xx/timeouts; do not retry on permanent errors (invalid number, uninstalled app). After N attempts go to the DLQ. Fallback channel: if push fails or isn't delivered in 60 s, send SMS for important messages.
7. **Device tokens:** keep a registry per user (multiple devices); remove tokens APNs/FCM report as invalid.
8. **Providers behind an interface:** switch or load-balance among SMS vendors for cost and reliability.

### Data model

```
notifications(notif_id PK, user_id, template_id, channel, priority, status[QUEUED|SENT|DELIVERED|FAILED|OPENED], created_at, sent_at, provider_ref, dedupe_key UNIQUE)
user_prefs(user_id, channel, category, enabled, quiet_start, quiet_end)
device_tokens(user_id, device_id, platform, token, updated_at)
templates(template_id, channel, locale, body, version)
```

Write-heavy event data (status updates) in Cassandra/ClickHouse; preferences in SQL or KV with cache.

### LLD sketch

```java
interface NotificationChannel { SendResult send(Notification n); }                // Strategy / Adapter
class PushChannel implements NotificationChannel { ... FCM/APNs ... }
class SmsChannel implements NotificationChannel { ... pick vendor via ProviderRouter ... }
class EmailChannel implements NotificationChannel { ... }

class ChannelFactory { NotificationChannel of(ChannelType t) { ... } }

class NotificationProcessor {
  void handle(NotifyRequest r) {
    if (!dedupe.firstTime(r.dedupeKey)) return;
    UserPrefs p = prefs.get(r.userId);
    for (ChannelType ct : planner.channelsFor(r, p)) {                           // respects opt-outs, priority, fallback order
      if (!limiter.allow(r.userId, ct)) continue;
      Notification n = renderer.render(r, ct, p.locale);
      queue.publish(ct, r.priority, n);
    }
  }
}
class RetryPolicy { Duration nextDelay(int attempt) { return Duration.ofSeconds((long)Math.min(300, Math.pow(2, attempt)) + jitter()); } }
```

Patterns: **Strategy/Adapter** (channels, providers), **Factory** (channel creation), **Observer** (status callbacks), **Template Method** (render then send then record), **Chain of Responsibility** (preference, quiet-hours, rate-limit filters).

### Deep dive and trade-offs

- **Exactly-once is a myth:** you get at-least-once; make send idempotent using the provider's message id where supported and dedupe on your side.
- **Ordering:** rarely needed; if so, partition Kafka by userId.
- **Delivery tracking:** providers send delivery receipts via webhook; map `provider_ref` back to the notification. Opens and clicks via tracking pixel / link redirect.
- **Hot campaigns:** throttle outbound to what providers allow; scale workers by queue depth; spread sends over time to avoid thundering-herd app opens hitting your backend.
- **Scheduled / recurring:** a time-bucketed scheduler (store by minute bucket, a poller loads due items) or a delay queue.
- **Observability:** per-channel success rate, queue lag, provider latency; alert on lag, not on every failure.

**Interview tip:** talk about priority isolation, fan-out, provider rate limits, retries with DLQ, and user preferences. These are the five things graders listen for.

### Q13 in depth: Notification system, every detail

#### 13.1 Requirements and scale

- Functional: send **push** (APNs/FCM), **SMS**, **email**, **in-app** messages; triggered by events (order shipped), scheduled (reminders), or bulk campaigns (sale announcement to 50M users); templates with localization; user preferences (channel opt-in/out, quiet hours, frequency caps); delivery tracking (sent, delivered, opened, clicked); unsubscribe/compliance.
- Non-functional: **no notification lost** for critical ones (OTP, payment), but **no duplicates** for any; low latency for transactional (OTP within seconds); high throughput for bulk; fairness so a marketing blast cannot delay OTPs; graceful degradation when a provider is down.
- Scale example: 10M notifications/day transactional (115/s) plus campaigns of 50M in two hours (7k/s) plus peaks 10x = **\~100k/s capacity**. Vendor rate limits (e.g. an SMS provider allowing 500/s per account) become the real bottleneck, so throttling per provider is central.

#### 13.2 Architecture in layers

1. **Ingress API / event consumers:** services call `POST /notifications` or publish events to Kafka. Payload: `{user_id | audience, type, channel hints, template_id, params, priority, idempotency_key, scheduled_at}`.
2. **Notification Service (orchestrator):** validates, dedupes (idempotency key), loads user preferences and contact info, applies rules (opt-out, quiet hours, frequency cap), renders the template, decides channels, and writes a `notification` record.
3. **Per-channel queues** (Kafka topics or SQS): `push`, `sms`, `email`, `inapp`, each split by **priority** (`critical`, `high`, `normal`, `bulk`) so a bulk campaign never starves OTPs. Separate consumer groups per queue.
4. **Channel workers:** pull from their queue, call the provider adapter, handle provider-specific limits, record the result.
5. **Provider adapters:** APNs/FCM (push), Twilio/MSG91/SNS (SMS), SES/SendGrid (email), WebSocket/inbox (in-app). Multiple providers per channel with failover.
6. **Feedback loop:** provider callbacks/webhooks (delivered, bounced, complaint, click) update status and prune bad tokens.

#### 13.3 Priority isolation and fairness

Three techniques, combined: (a) **separate topics/queues per priority** with dedicated worker pools (OTP workers are never shared with bulk); (b) **weighted consumption** inside shared pools (e.g. 70/20/10); (c) **per-tenant or per-campaign rate limits** (token bucket, Q2) so one campaign cannot monopolize provider quota. Critical channel capacity is over-provisioned and reserved.

#### 13.4 Reliability: at-least-once with idempotent sends

Exactly-once delivery to a phone is impossible (the provider may accept the message and the response may get lost). Aim for **at-least-once processing plus deduplication** so the user rarely sees a duplicate:

1. Each notification has a stable `notification_id` (and per-channel `delivery_id`).
2. Before sending, the worker does an atomic check-and-claim: `INSERT INTO deliveries(delivery_id, status='SENDING') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`; if the row already exists and is `SENT`, skip. If it exists as `SENDING` for too long (worker died), retry with the same `delivery_id`.
3. Pass the `delivery_id` as the provider's own idempotency/reference id when supported (APNs `apns-collapse-id`, FCM collapse key, email Message-ID).
4. Retry with **exponential backoff and jitter**, max N attempts; then send to a **dead-letter queue (DLQ)** with alerting and a replay tool.
5. After provider acceptance: mark `SENT`; later callback marks `DELIVERED`/`FAILED`.

For critical OTPs, fail over across providers (SMS provider A times out -> B), accepting rare duplicate SMS over a lost OTP.

#### 13.5 User preferences, compliance, and suppression

- Preference store: `(user_id, category, channel) -> enabled`, plus quiet hours with timezone, and global do-not-disturb. Cached in Redis; the orchestrator consults it for **every** non-critical message. Critical categories (security, OTP, legal) bypass marketing opt-outs but follow channel availability.
- **Frequency caps:** at most N marketing messages per user per day/week across all campaigns; implemented with a Redis counter `INCR key; EXPIRE` (or a sliding window, Q2).
- **Suppression lists:** hard-bounced emails, unsubscribed users, invalid or uninstalled push tokens, DND-registered numbers (TRAI rules in India, TCPA in US, GDPR consent). Always check at send time, not only at enqueue time (a campaign may sit in queue for hours).
- Email specifics: SPF/DKIM/DMARC for deliverability, one-click unsubscribe header, separate sending domains/IPs for transactional versus marketing to protect reputation, warm-up new IPs, handle bounce and complaint feedback loops.

#### 13.6 Templates and localization

Templates stored with versions: `(template_id, channel, locale, version, subject, body, variables_schema)`. Rendering with a safe engine (Handlebars/Mustache; never evaluate arbitrary code), locale fallback chain (`hi-IN -> hi -> en`), variable validation (missing variable fails fast and is not sent). Content approvals and SMS DLT template registration where regulation requires a pre-registered text. Rendering happens in the orchestrator so queues carry final, small payloads (or ids plus params to render at the worker for huge campaigns to save memory).

#### 13.7 Bulk campaigns / audience fan-out

A campaign targets a **segment** (query over user attributes), not a list passed in one API call. Flow: campaign service resolves the audience in **pages** (stream 10k users at a time from the user store/data warehouse), enqueues notifications in batches to the bulk queue, and tracks progress `(campaign_id, cursor, sent, failed)` so it can pause, resume, or cancel. Throttle enqueue rate to the provider quota. Scheduling by user timezone ('send at 9:00 local') is done by partitioning the audience by timezone and scheduling each slice. A/B variants assign users deterministically by `hash(user_id, campaign_id) mod 100`.

#### 13.8 Scheduling and delayed delivery

Reminders and scheduled sends need a **scheduler** (see Q24): store `(notification_id, fire_at)` in a time-partitioned table or a sorted set / hierarchical timing wheel; a poller picks due items each second (or each minute bucket) with a lease to prevent two pollers sending the same one; due items are pushed to the normal queue. Cancellation = flag checked at send time.

#### 13.9 Push notification specifics

Devices register a token with the backend (`device_tokens(user_id, device_id, platform, token, last_seen)`). A user may have several devices; push to all active ones (or the most recent). APNs/FCM respond with 'unregistered/invalid token': delete it immediately. Use **collapse keys** so a burst of 'new message' pushes updates one visible notification. Payload limits (\~4 KB) mean you send identifiers and let the app fetch details. Silent/data pushes trigger background sync (careful with OS throttling). Connection pooling to APNs (HTTP/2 multiplexed streams) matters for throughput.

#### 13.10 In-app notifications / inbox

Store per-user inbox items: `inbox(user_id, notification_id DESC, title, body, read, created_at)` in a wide-column/KV store; unread badge count cached in Redis (increment on create, decrement/reset on read). Real-time delivery to an open app through the WebSocket gateway (Q5), otherwise visible next open. Retention (e.g. 90 days).

#### 13.11 Data model

```sql
notifications(notification_id PK, idempotency_key UNIQUE, user_id, category, priority, template_id, params JSONB, status, scheduled_at, created_at)
deliveries(delivery_id PK, notification_id, channel, provider, status, attempts, last_error, provider_msg_id, sent_at, delivered_at)
user_prefs(user_id, category, channel, enabled, PRIMARY KEY(user_id, category, channel)) ; quiet_hours(user_id, start, end, tz)
device_tokens(user_id, device_id, platform, token, last_seen) ; suppression(contact_hash, channel, reason, created_at)
campaigns(campaign_id, segment_query, template_id, schedule, status, cursor, stats JSONB)
templates(template_id, channel, locale, version, subject, body)
```

#### 13.12 LLD: orchestrator, channel strategy, retry worker

```java
interface ChannelSender {                                     // Strategy per channel/provider
  Channel channel();
  SendResult send(Delivery d) throws ProviderException;
}

class NotificationOrchestrator {
  void handle(NotificationRequest req) {
    if (!idempotency.claim(req.idempotencyKey())) return;                            // dedupe duplicate API calls
    UserContext u = users.load(req.userId());
    List<Channel> channels = router.channelsFor(req, u);                             // preference + priority + availability
    for (Channel ch : channels) {
      if (req.priority() != Priority.CRITICAL) {
        if (!prefs.allows(u, req.category(), ch) || quietHours.active(u) || !caps.tryConsume(u.id(), req.category())) continue;
      }
      if (suppression.blocked(u, ch)) continue;
      Rendered msg = templates.render(req.templateId(), ch, u.locale(), req.params());
      Delivery d = deliveries.create(req.id(), ch, msg);                              // unique (notification, channel)
      queues.publish(topicFor(ch, req.priority()), d);
    }
  }
}

class ChannelWorker implements Runnable {
  public void run() {
    for (Delivery d : queue.poll(100)) {
      if (!deliveries.claimForSend(d.id())) continue;                                // atomic SENDING claim
      if (!providerLimiter.tryAcquire(d.provider())) { queue.requeueWithDelay(d, 1_000); continue; }   // respect provider quota
      try {
        SendResult r = senders.get(d.channel()).send(d);
        deliveries.markSent(d.id(), r.providerMsgId());
      } catch (RetryableException e) {
        if (d.attempts() >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) { dlq.publish(d, e); deliveries.markFailed(d.id(), e); }
        else queue.requeueWithDelay(d, backoffWithJitter(d.attempts()));
      } catch (PermanentException e) {                                               // invalid number / bad token
        suppression.add(d.contact(), e.reason()); deliveries.markFailed(d.id(), e);
      }
    }
  }
  static long backoffWithJitter(int attempt) { long base = Math.min(60_000, 500L << attempt); return ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(base / 2, base); }
}

class FailoverSender implements ChannelSender {                                       // provider failover with circuit breaker (see Q4)
  List<ChannelSender> providers; List<CircuitBreaker> breakers;
  SendResult send(Delivery d) {
    for (int i = 0; i < providers.size(); i++) {
      if (!breakers.get(i).allowRequest()) continue;
      try { SendResult r = providers.get(i).send(d); breakers.get(i).recordSuccess(); return r; }
      catch (ProviderException e) { breakers.get(i).recordFailure(); }
    }
    throw new RetryableException("all providers failing");
  }
}
```

#### 13.13 HLD diagram

```
Services / Kafka events / Campaign Service / Scheduler
   -> Notification API -> Orchestrator (idempotency, prefs, caps, suppression, templates)
        -> priority topics per channel: [push-critical, push-bulk, sms-critical, sms-bulk, email-*, inapp]
             -> Channel workers (rate-limited per provider) -> Provider adapters (APNs/FCM, SMS A/B, SES/SendGrid)
   <- Provider callbacks/webhooks -> Status service -> Delivery store, analytics (Kafka -> warehouse)
   DLQ + replay tool ; Preference/Suppression service (Redis + DB) ; Template service ; Inbox store + WebSocket gateway
```

#### 13.14 Failure scenarios

| Failure | Handling |
| --- | --- |
| SMS provider outage | Circuit breaker, failover provider, queue absorbs backlog; critical first |
| Worker crashes mid-send | Lease/claim expires; retry with same delivery id; provider-level dedupe where supported |
| Campaign floods queues | Separate bulk topics, enqueue throttling, per-campaign limits; critical lane unaffected |
| Invalid tokens/numbers | Permanent error handling, prune suppression |
| Duplicate API call | Idempotency key at ingress |
| User opts out while queued | Re-check suppression at send time |
| Template variable missing | Validation fails fast, DLQ with reason, alert owner |
| Callback lost | Periodic status polling for unresolved deliveries; mark 'unknown' after TTL |

#### 13.15 Follow-up questions and model answers

1. **How do you guarantee an OTP arrives?** Dedicated critical lane, multiple providers with failover, fast retries, delivery receipts, fallback to voice call or another channel.
2. **How do you avoid duplicates?** Idempotency keys, delivery claim rows, provider collapse/message ids; accept rare duplicates over losses.
3. **How do you rate limit per provider?** Token bucket per provider (Q2) in workers; requeue with delay when exhausted.
4. **How do you handle 50M-user campaigns?** Paged audience resolution, bulk queues, throttling, resumable progress cursors, time-zone slices.
5. **How do you respect user preferences at scale?** Cached preference store checked at send time, frequency caps in Redis, suppression lists.
6. **Why separate queues per channel and priority?** Isolation of failure and load, independent scaling and quotas, no head-of-line blocking.
7. **How do you track opens and clicks?** Tracking pixel and wrapped links hitting a redirect service that logs events to Kafka; push open events from the app SDK.
8. **How do you schedule millions of reminders?** Time-bucketed storage with leased pollers or timing wheel; push to queues at fire time.
9. **How do you test it?** Provider sandbox/mocks, replay of production traffic shapes, chaos tests for provider failure, end-to-end canary notifications.
10. **What do you monitor?** Queue lag per lane, provider success and latency, delivery rate, bounce/complaint rate, DLQ depth, time-to-deliver for OTP.

#### 13.16 One-page summary

Orchestrator (idempotency, preferences, caps, suppression, templates) -> per-channel, per-priority queues -> rate-limited workers -> provider adapters with failover. At-least-once plus dedupe via delivery ids. Critical lane isolated from bulk. Campaigns stream audience in pages with resumable cursors. Provider callbacks update status; DLQ with replay. Scheduler for delayed sends.

## Q14. Distributed cache / Key-Value store (Redis, DynamoDB style)

**Problem:** design a distributed in-memory cache or a durable key-value store that scales to millions of ops/second across many machines, with replication and fault tolerance. Covers the classic Dynamo paper ideas.

### Requirements

- **Functional:** `put(key, value, ttl?)`, `get(key)`, `delete(key)`; optionally atomic ops (INCR, CAS).
- **Non-functional:** latency under 1 ms (cache) or \~10 ms (durable store); horizontally scalable; highly available (survive node failure); tunable consistency; automatic data distribution and rebalancing.

### Estimation

- Target: 1M ops/s, 10 TB data, values \~1 KB. One node does \~50K to 100K ops/s and holds \~100 GB in RAM, so we need at least 20 to 100 nodes. Use replication factor 3.

### Building blocks

1. **Partitioning with consistent hashing.** Hash both keys and nodes onto a ring (0 to 2^32). A key belongs to the first node clockwise. Adding/removing a node moves only \~1/N of keys. Use **virtual nodes** (each physical node owns many ring points) to balance load and let stronger machines take more (Q21).
2. **Replication.** Store each key on the next N=3 distinct nodes clockwise (the 'preference list'), ideally in different racks/zones.
3. **Tunable consistency with quorums.** With N replicas, write waits for W acks, read queries R replicas. If **R + W > N**, reads overlap the latest write (e.g. N=3, W=2, R=2). Lower W or R for speed; set W=N for durability.
4. **Conflict resolution** when replicas diverge: last-write-wins by timestamp (simple, can lose writes) or **vector clocks** (detect concurrent writes and let the client/app merge, as in Dynamo).
5. **Failure handling:**
   - *Failure detection:* gossip protocol; nodes exchange heartbeats and spread membership info.
   - *Hinted handoff:* if a replica is down, another node temporarily stores the write with a hint, and forwards it when the replica returns (keeps writes available).
   - *Anti-entropy / read repair:* replicas compare data with **Merkle trees** to find and fix differences; a read that sees stale replicas fixes them.
6. **Local storage engine.** For durable KV: **LSM tree** (write to commit log + memtable, flush sorted SSTables, compact in the background, Bloom filters to skip files). For a pure cache: a hash map in RAM with eviction.

### HLD

```
 Client library (knows ring) or Proxy/Router
    |  hash(key) -> coordinator node
    v
 [Node A] --replicate--> [Node B] --> [Node C]        each node: API + replication + gossip + storage engine
   | commit log + memtable -> SSTables (disk) ; or in-memory hash table + LRU (cache)
   '-- gossip membership with all nodes ; optional: coordination service (etcd/ZooKeeper) for config
```

**Write path (Dynamo style):** client contacts any node (coordinator); coordinator forwards to the N replicas, waits for W acks, replies. **Read path:** coordinator reads from R replicas, returns the newest (or siblings), triggers read repair.

### Cache-specific design (Redis/Memcached)

- **Eviction:** LRU implemented with a hash map + doubly linked list (Q81) for O(1); Redis uses approximated LRU/LFU by sampling.
- **TTL expiry:** lazy (check on access) + periodic sampling sweep.
- **Sharding:** client-side (consistent hashing) or server-side cluster slots (Redis Cluster uses 16,384 hash slots, with slot ownership moving between nodes).
- **Persistence (optional):** RDB snapshots and AOF append log.
- **Cache patterns:** cache-aside, write-through, write-back (Part 3.4). Prevent stampede with request coalescing / per-key lock or probabilistic early refresh.

### LLD sketch: ring + node

```java
class ConsistentHashRing {
  private final TreeMap<Long, Node> ring = new TreeMap<>();
  private final int vnodes;
  void addNode(Node n) { for (int i = 0; i < vnodes; i++) ring.put(hash(n.id + "#" + i), n); }
  void removeNode(Node n) { for (int i = 0; i < vnodes; i++) ring.remove(hash(n.id + "#" + i)); }
  List<Node> preferenceList(String key, int replicas) {
    List<Node> out = new ArrayList<>(); Set<Node> seen = new HashSet<>();
    Long start = ring.ceilingKey(hash(key)); if (start == null) start = ring.firstKey();
    for (Long k : tailThenHead(start)) {                     // walk clockwise
      Node n = ring.get(k);
      if (seen.add(n)) out.add(n);
      if (out.size() == replicas) break;
    }
    return out;
  }
}

class Coordinator {
  boolean put(String key, byte[] val, int W) {
    List<Node> replicas = ring.preferenceList(key, N);
    int acks = 0;
    for (Node r : replicas) if (r.writeAsync(key, val, clock.next()).await(timeout)) acks++;
    return acks >= W;
  }
}
```

### Deep dive and trade-offs

- **CP vs AP:** Dynamo/Cassandra style is AP (available under partition, eventually consistent); etcd/ZooKeeper/Spanner style is CP (consensus via Raft/Paxos, single leader per shard). Pick by use case: a cache wants AP, a lock service wants CP.
- **Hot keys:** one key getting 100K req/s melts one node. Fixes: replicate hot keys to many nodes, add a client-side near-cache with short TTL, split a key into sub-keys (counter sharding).
- **Rebalancing:** when adding a node, stream only the affected ranges; throttle to avoid hurting live traffic.
- **Memory:** use compact encodings; eviction policy chosen by workload (LFU suits skewed popularity).
- **Consistency of cache vs DB:** delete-on-write (invalidate) is safer than update-on-write; use TTL as a safety net.
- **Multi-region:** async replication between regions; conflict resolution by LWW or CRDTs.

**Interview tip:** walk the story: consistent hashing with vnodes, replication N, quorum R+W>N, gossip, hinted handoff, Merkle trees, LSM storage. That is the whole Dynamo toolbox.

### Q14 in depth: Distributed cache and key-value store, every detail

#### 14.1 Two related problems (clarify which one is asked)

- **Distributed cache** (Redis/Memcached): in-memory, loses data acceptably, sits in front of a database, eviction policies, sub-millisecond latency.
- **Distributed key-value store** (DynamoDB, Cassandra, Riak, etcd for strong): durable, replicated, tunable consistency, the system of record.

They share the same machinery (partitioning, replication, failure detection); the cache adds eviction and TTL; the store adds durability (WAL, SSTables) and anti-entropy. Say which you are designing, then cover shared parts once.

#### 14.2 Requirements and scale

- Functional: `get(key)`, `put(key, value, ttl?)`, `delete(key)`; optional atomic ops (incr, CAS); value sizes up to \~1 MB; namespaces/tenants.
- Non-functional: p99 latency under \~5 ms; horizontally scalable to petabytes and millions of ops/s; highly available through node failures; tunable consistency; adding/removing nodes without moving most data.
- Scale example: 10M ops/s, 100 TB dataset, 1 KB average value. One node serves \~100k ops/s and holds \~1 TB on SSD (or \~256 GB RAM for a cache) => at least 100 nodes for throughput and 100 for capacity; with replication factor 3, plan **\~300 nodes**.

#### 14.3 Partitioning with consistent hashing

Naive `hash(key) mod N` moves almost every key when N changes (adding a 4th node to 3 relocates \~75 percent). **Consistent hashing** places nodes and keys on a hash ring (0 to 2^32-1); a key belongs to the first node clockwise. Adding a node takes only \~1/N of the keys from its neighbor.

**Virtual nodes:** each physical node owns many (100-256) points on the ring. Benefits: even load despite random placement, smoother rebalancing (a joining node takes small slices from many nodes, so streaming happens in parallel), heterogeneous machines (bigger nodes get more vnodes). Example: 3 nodes with 1 token each can be badly unbalanced (one may own 60 percent); with 128 vnodes each the spread falls to a few percent.

Alternative: **fixed slots** (Redis Cluster uses 16,384 hash slots mapped to nodes; moving slots moves data). Slots make rebalancing explicit and routing tables small.

```java
class ConsistentHashRing<N> {
  private final TreeMap<Long, N> ring = new TreeMap<>(); private final int vnodes;
  ConsistentHashRing(int vnodes) { this.vnodes = vnodes; }
  void addNode(N node) { for (int i = 0; i < vnodes; i++) ring.put(hash(node + "#" + i), node); }
  void removeNode(N node) { for (int i = 0; i < vnodes; i++) ring.remove(hash(node + "#" + i)); }
  N nodeFor(String key) {
    if (ring.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException();
    Map.Entry<Long, N> e = ring.ceilingEntry(hash(key));
    return (e != null ? e : ring.firstEntry()).getValue();                   // wrap around
  }
  /** First 'count' distinct physical nodes clockwise = the replica set (preference list). */
  List<N> replicasFor(String key, int count) {
    LinkedHashSet<N> out = new LinkedHashSet<>();
    Long start = Optional.ofNullable(ring.ceilingKey(hash(key))).orElse(ring.firstKey());
    for (N n : concat(ring.tailMap(start, true).values(), ring.headMap(start, false).values())) {
      out.add(n); if (out.size() == count) break;
    }
    return new ArrayList<>(out);
  }
  private long hash(String s) { return Hashing.murmur3_128().hashString(s, UTF_8).asLong(); }
}
```

#### 14.4 Replication and quorums

Each key is stored on N nodes (the **preference list**: the next N distinct physical nodes on the ring, ideally in different racks/AZs). Dynamo-style quorum: a write succeeds when **W** replicas acknowledge, a read queries **R** replicas. If **R + W > N**, read and write sets overlap, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write (strong-ish consistency, barring sloppy quorums and clock issues).

| N | R | W | Property |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | 2 | 2 | Balanced; tolerates 1 node failure for both reads and writes |
| 3 | 1 | 3 | Fast reads, writes need all replicas (write availability poor) |
| 3 | 3 | 1 | Fast writes, slow reads |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | Eventual consistency, max speed and availability (stale reads possible) |

Another model: **leader-based per partition** (Raft/Paxos group per shard, as in etcd, Spanner, Redis with replicas): one leader orders writes, followers replicate; gives linearizability at the cost of leader failover time. State the choice: Dynamo-style = AP-leaning, tunable; Raft-per-shard = CP.

**Sloppy quorum and hinted handoff:** if a preference-list node is down, the write goes to the next healthy node on the ring with a **hint** ('belongs to node X'); when X returns, the hint is replayed. Keeps writes available during failures.

#### 14.5 Conflicts: versioning and reconciliation

With multiple writers and partitions, replicas diverge. Options:

- **Last-write-wins (LWW)** by timestamp: simple, may silently lose a concurrent update, vulnerable to clock skew. Good for caches and idempotent data.
- **Vector clocks:** each value carries `{nodeA:2, nodeB:1}`; two versions are either ordered (one dominates) or **concurrent** (siblings). Concurrent versions are returned to the client/application to merge (Dynamo's shopping cart: union of items). Cost: clock growth (prune by size), complexity.
- **CRDTs** (counters, sets, registers) merge automatically and commutatively, ideal for counters/sets.

**Read repair:** on a read of R replicas, if one is stale, send it the newest version in the background. **Anti-entropy with Merkle trees:** each replica builds a hash tree over key ranges; replicas compare roots and descend only into differing subtrees to find and sync divergent keys cheaply, so a background process heals long-term drift without scanning everything.

#### 14.6 Failure detection and membership: gossip

Nodes exchange heartbeat tables with a few random peers every second (**gossip protocol**). Each entry has a heartbeat counter; if a node's counter has not advanced for T seconds it is suspected down; with enough suspicion it is marked down (phi-accrual detectors adapt the threshold to network behavior instead of using a fixed timeout). Gossip also spreads membership changes (join/leave), token assignments and schema, with no central coordinator and convergence in O(log N) rounds. Alternatives: a coordination service (ZooKeeper/etcd) holding membership; simpler but a dependency.

Clients either (a) are **partition-aware** (hold the ring and route directly: lowest latency), (b) go through any node that **coordinates** the request (Cassandra/Dynamo), or (c) use a **proxy** layer (Twemproxy, Envoy, mcrouter) that hides topology.

#### 14.7 Single-node storage engine (for the durable KV store)

Use an **LSM tree** (write-optimized, used by Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB):

1. Write goes to the **commit log (WAL)** (sequential disk write, durability) and to the in-memory **memtable** (sorted).
2. When the memtable fills (say 64 MB), it is flushed as an immutable sorted file (**SSTable**).
3. Reads check memtable, then SSTables newest to oldest; a **Bloom filter** per SSTable skips files that definitely lack the key; an index finds the block.
4. Background **compaction** merges SSTables, drops overwritten values and tombstones past their grace time, keeping read amplification bounded.

Trade-off vs B-tree (update in place): LSM has high write throughput and sequential I/O but read and space amplification; B-trees have predictable reads but random writes. Deletes are **tombstones**, only purged after all replicas have seen them (gc\_grace), otherwise deleted data can resurrect.

#### 14.8 Cache-specific design

**Eviction policies:** LRU (evict least recently used; doubly linked list + hash map, O(1)), LFU (least frequently used; resists scans, needs frequency tracking, e.g. TinyLFU), FIFO, random, TTL-based. Redis uses approximated LRU/LFU by sampling a few keys, avoiding global structures.

**Caching patterns:**

| Pattern | Flow | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cache-aside | App reads cache; on miss reads DB, fills cache | Most common; app owns logic; risk of stale data |
| Read-through | Cache loads from DB on miss itself | Simplifies apps |
| Write-through | Write to cache and DB synchronously | Consistent, slower writes |
| Write-back (behind) | Write to cache, flush to DB asynchronously | Fast, risk of loss on cache failure |
| Write-around | Write to DB only, cache fills on read | Avoids polluting cache with write-once data |

**Classic cache failure modes and fixes:**

- **Stampede / dogpile:** a hot key expires and 10,000 requests hit the DB. Fix: per-key mutex/single-flight (one loader, others wait), **stale-while-revalidate**, TTL jitter (randomize expiry so keys do not expire together), probabilistic early refresh.
- **Penetration:** requests for non-existent keys always miss. Fix: cache negative results with short TTL, Bloom filter in front.
- **Hot key:** one celebrity key overloads one node. Fix: replicate the hot key across several nodes with suffixes (`key#0..k`) and read randomly, local in-process cache (near cache) with short TTL.
- **Cache avalanche:** many keys expire at once or a node dies. Fix: jitter, multi-layer caches, gradual warm-up, rate limiting to the DB.
- **Inconsistency between cache and DB:** update DB then **delete** the cache key (not update it), and use short TTL as a safety net; for strict needs use CDC (change data capture) to invalidate from the DB log.

**Atomic operations:** `INCR`, `SETNX`, CAS with version, Lua scripts (Q2) for multi-step atomic logic. Distributed locks via `SET key token NX PX ttl` with token-checked release (and Redlock caveats; use fencing tokens for correctness-critical cases).

#### 14.9 Resharding and rebalancing

Adding a node: it takes ownership of vnode ranges; existing owners **stream** the affected key ranges to it while still serving (double-write or read-forward during transfer), then ownership flips and old copies are cleaned up. Throttle streaming so production traffic is unaffected. Removing a node: reverse. Use many small partitions (e.g. 10k logical partitions mapped to nodes) so moves are fine-grained.

#### 14.10 Multi-datacenter

Async replication across regions (low write latency, possible conflicts, resolve with LWW/CRDT) or synchronous quorum across regions (high latency, strong). Per-key home region for locality; local reads, global writes; `LOCAL_QUORUM` vs `EACH_QUORUM` choices in Cassandra terms.

#### 14.11 LLD: LRU cache with TTL and a minimal KV node

```java
class LruCache<K, V> {                                   // O(1) get/put with TTL; thread-safe via one lock (shard it for throughput)
  private final int capacity; private final LinkedHashMap<K, Entry<V>> map;
  private static class Entry<V> { V value; long expiresAt; }
  LruCache(int capacity) {
    this.capacity = capacity;
    this.map = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) {                    // accessOrder=true gives LRU ordering
      protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, Entry<V>> e) { return size() > LruCache.this.capacity; }
    };
  }
  synchronized V get(K k) {
    Entry<V> e = map.get(k);
    if (e == null) return null;
    if (e.expiresAt != 0 && e.expiresAt < System.currentTimeMillis()) { map.remove(k); return null; }   // lazy expiry
    return e.value;
  }
  synchronized void put(K k, V v, long ttlMs) {
    Entry<V> e = new Entry<>(); e.value = v; e.expiresAt = ttlMs > 0 ? System.currentTimeMillis() + ttlMs : 0; map.put(k, e);
  }
  synchronized void delete(K k) { map.remove(k); }
}

class StripedCache<K, V> {                               // reduce lock contention: N independent LRUs
  private final LruCache<K, V>[] stripes;
  V get(K k) { return stripes[(k.hashCode() & 0x7fffffff) % stripes.length].get(k); }
}

class QuorumCoordinator {                                // coordinator logic for a Dynamo-style write/read
  private final ConsistentHashRing<Node> ring; private final int N = 3, R = 2, W = 2;
  boolean put(String key, byte[] val, VectorClock vc) {
    List<Node> replicas = ring.replicasFor(key, N);
    CountDownLatch acks = new CountDownLatch(W); AtomicInteger ok = new AtomicInteger();
    for (Node n : replicas) async(() -> { if (n.write(key, val, vc)) { ok.incrementAndGet(); acks.countDown(); } else hints.store(n, key, val, vc); });
    return await(acks, 50) && ok.get() >= W;             // success after W acks within the timeout
  }
  Versioned get(String key) {
    List<Versioned> replies = readFrom(ring.replicasFor(key, N), R);
    Versioned newest = VectorClock.pickDominant(replies);        // siblings returned if concurrent
    readRepair(key, replies, newest);                            // fix stale replicas in the background
    return newest;
  }
}
```

#### 14.12 HLD diagram

```
Client (smart client / proxy) -> any Coordinator node
   Ring (vnodes, gossip membership) -> Replica set [Node A, Node B, Node C] in different AZs
   Each node: commit log (WAL) + memtable -> SSTables (Bloom filters, compaction) ; hinted handoff store
   Background: gossip, failure detector, read repair, Merkle-tree anti-entropy, streaming for rebalance, compaction
   Cache mode: memory store + eviction (LRU/LFU) + TTL ; persistence optional (snapshot/AOF)
```

#### 14.13 Failure scenarios

| Failure | Handling |
| --- | --- |
| Replica node dies | Quorum still met with N-1; hinted handoff; replace node and stream data |
| Network partition | AP mode: both sides accept writes, reconcile with vector clocks/LWW later; CP mode: minority side rejects |
| Stale read | Raise R, use read repair; or leader-based reads |
| Hot partition | Split partition, replicate hot keys, add near cache |
| Disk corruption | Checksums per block; repair from replicas |
| Whole cache cluster restarts (cold) | Gradual warm-up, DB protected by rate limits, persistence snapshot |
| Clock skew breaking LWW | Hybrid logical clocks or vector clocks; NTP monitoring |
| Split brain | Quorum rules, leases/fencing tokens |

#### 14.14 Follow-up questions and model answers

1. **Why consistent hashing?** Minimal key movement on scale changes, balanced with vnodes.
2. **How do you choose N, R, W?** From availability and consistency needs; R+W>N for read-your-writes; mention latency impacts.
3. **How do you detect failed nodes?** Gossip with phi-accrual detection.
4. **How do you keep replicas in sync long-term?** Read repair for hot data, Merkle-tree anti-entropy for cold data, hinted handoff for short outages.
5. **How do you resolve write conflicts?** LWW for simplicity; vector clocks with app merge; CRDTs for counters/sets.
6. **LRU or LFU?** LRU for recency patterns; LFU/TinyLFU for scan resistance and skew; mention approximation by sampling.
7. **What is a cache stampede and how do you stop it?** Many simultaneous misses on a hot key; single-flight, jitter, stale-while-revalidate.
8. **Cache and DB consistency?** Delete-on-write with short TTL, or CDC-based invalidation; accept bounded staleness.
9. **Why LSM over B-tree for a KV store?** Sequential writes and high ingest rate; Bloom filters and compaction manage reads.
10. **How would you add transactions?** Per-partition Raft with 2PC across partitions (Spanner-like), or restrict to single-key CAS.

#### 14.15 One-page summary

Consistent hashing with vnodes (or fixed slots) for partitioning; N replicas on distinct racks; tunable quorum (R+W>N) or Raft per shard; gossip for membership; hinted handoff, read repair, Merkle trees for healing; LSM storage engine for durability; cache layer adds LRU/LFU, TTL jitter, single-flight, and delete-on-write invalidation. State the CAP stance explicitly.

## Q15. Web crawler

**Problem:** starting from seed URLs, download billions of web pages, extract links, and keep discovering and refreshing pages (for a search engine or data mining), without overloading any website.

### Requirements

- **Functional:** fetch pages, extract links, store content, avoid duplicates, respect `robots.txt`, re-crawl pages periodically.
- **Non-functional:** **scalable** (1B pages/month), **polite** (don't hammer one host), **robust** (bad HTML, traps, timeouts), **extensible** (new content types), freshness for important pages.

### Estimation

- 1B pages/month = \~400 pages/s. At 100 KB per page: 100 TB/month of raw content; storage in object store with compression.
- 400 pages/s with \~500 ms per fetch means \~200+ concurrent fetches. In practice, hundreds of machines with thousands of async fetch slots each, because DNS and network latency dominate.

### HLD

```
 Seed URLs -> [URL Frontier] --(by host queue, priority)--> [Fetcher Workers] -> [DNS cache] -> Internet
                  ^                                           |
                  |                                  raw HTML -> [Content Store] (S3/HDFS)  + Kafka 'page.fetched'
                  |                                           v
           [URL Filter / Normalizer / Dedup]  <-- extracted links -- [Parser / Link Extractor] -> [Content Dedup (simhash)]
                  |  Bloom filter + KV store of seen URLs                    \-> Indexer, Spam/Quality classifiers
           [robots.txt cache]   [Scheduler for re-crawl]
```

### Components

1. **URL Frontier** (the heart). Not a simple queue. It enforces two things:
   - **Priority:** important pages (high PageRank, news sites, frequently changing) first. Multiple priority queues; a prioritizer assigns scores.
   - **Politeness:** one queue per host with a single worker draining it and a delay (e.g. 1 request/second/host, or the site's `Crawl-delay`). A router maps hostname to queue so the same host always goes to the same worker.
2. **Fetcher:** async HTTP client with timeouts, redirect limits, size limits (abort 100 MB responses), and retries with backoff. Local **DNS cache** since DNS lookups are a notorious bottleneck.
3. **robots.txt:** fetch and cache per host (refresh daily); skip disallowed paths.
4. **Parser/extractor:** parse HTML, extract links and text. Handle malformed HTML, relative URLs (resolve to absolute), and optionally render JavaScript pages with a headless browser (expensive; only for selected sites).
5. **URL normalization & dedupe:** canonicalize (lowercase host, remove fragments, sort query params, strip tracking params). Check the 'seen' set using a **Bloom filter** in memory in front of a persistent store (false positives mean we occasionally skip a new URL, which is acceptable; no false negatives).
6. **Content dedup:** many pages are near-duplicates. Hash the content for exact duplicates; use **simhash/minhash** to find near-duplicates.
7. **Storage:** raw pages to object storage (compressed); metadata (url, fetch time, status, hash, outlinks) in a wide-column or KV store.
8. **Re-crawl scheduling:** estimate each page's change rate from history; adaptive intervals (news homepage hourly, static page monthly).

### Crawler traps and hazards

- Infinite calendars/session-id URLs: limit URL length and depth per host, cap pages per domain, detect repeating patterns.
- Spider traps and spam farms: domain-level quotas and quality scoring.
- Slow or malicious servers: strict timeouts, concurrency caps, blacklist.
- Legal/ethical: honor robots.txt, identify with a User-Agent, provide opt-out contact.

### Distribution

Partition hosts across crawler nodes by `hash(host)` with consistent hashing, so each host is owned by one node (politeness is local, no coordination). When a node fails, its hosts move to others; frontier state is persisted (disk-backed queues with a small in-memory buffer) so work is not lost.

### Data model

```
url_metadata(url_hash PK, url, host, last_fetched, next_fetch, status, content_hash, depth, priority)
host_state(host PK, robots_txt, robots_fetched_at, crawl_delay, last_request_at)
```

### LLD sketch

```java
class UrlFrontier {
  PriorityQueue<HostQueue> ready;                       // ordered by next-allowed-time
  Map<String, HostQueue> byHost = new HashMap<>();
  synchronized void add(Url u, int priority) { byHost.computeIfAbsent(u.host(), HostQueue::new).add(u, priority); }
  synchronized Optional<Url> next(Instant now) {
    HostQueue hq = ready.peek();
    if (hq == null || hq.nextAllowed.isAfter(now)) return Optional.empty();   // politeness: not yet
    ready.poll(); Url u = hq.pop(); hq.nextAllowed = now.plus(hq.delay);
    if (!hq.isEmpty()) ready.add(hq);
    return Optional.of(u);
  }
}
class Crawler {
  void run() { while (true) { Url u = frontier.nextBlocking(); if (!robots.allowed(u)) continue;
      Page p = fetcher.fetch(u); store.save(p);
      for (Url l : parser.links(p)) if (filter.accept(l) && !seen.mightContain(l)) { seen.add(l); frontier.add(l, scorer.score(l)); } } }
}
```

### Deep dive and trade-offs

- **BFS vs DFS vs best-first:** BFS from seeds with priority scoring is standard; pure DFS gets stuck in deep sites.
- **Freshness vs coverage:** limited bandwidth; spend it on pages likely to have changed and likely to matter.
- **Bloom filter sizing:** 10B URLs at 1% false-positive needs \~12 GB; shard it across nodes.
- **Exactly-once fetch isn't required;** at-least-once with dedupe is fine.
- **Observability:** pages/s, error rates by host, queue depth per priority, DNS latency.

**Interview tip:** emphasize the frontier with politeness + priority, the Bloom filter, and trap handling.

### Q15 in depth: Web crawler, every detail

#### 15.1 Requirements and scale

- Functional: starting from seed URLs, discover and download pages; extract links; store content for indexing; recrawl to keep it fresh; respect `robots.txt` and politeness; avoid duplicates and traps; prioritize important pages; support new content types (HTML, PDF, images) as plug-ins.
- Non-functional: **scalable** (billions of pages), **polite** (never hammer one site), **robust** (the web is full of malformed HTML, infinite loops, slow servers), **extensible**, high throughput.
- Scale example: crawl 1B pages/month = 385 pages/s average; to refresh the web monthly plus fresh news hourly aim for **\~1,000-2,000 pages/s**. Average page 100 KB => 1B x 100 KB = **100 TB/month raw**; compressed \~30 TB. URL frontier: assume 10B known URLs x 100 B = **1 TB** of URL metadata. Bandwidth: 2,000 pages/s x 100 KB = 200 MB/s = 1.6 Gbps. DNS: 2,000 lookups/s without caching would hurt, so cache aggressively.

#### 15.2 The crawl loop

```
Seed URLs -> URL Frontier -> Fetcher (DNS, robots.txt, HTTP GET) -> Content Parser/Validator
   -> Content-seen check (dedup) -> Content store -> Link Extractor -> URL Filter/Normalizer
   -> URL-seen check (Bloom filter + store) -> back into URL Frontier
```

Every box is a horizontally scalable service connected by queues, so each stage scales independently and a slow stage back-pressures instead of crashing.

#### 15.3 The URL Frontier (the most interesting component)

The frontier is not a simple FIFO queue. It must enforce three things: **priority** (important pages first), **politeness** (at most one request at a time per host, with a delay between requests), and **freshness** (recrawl changing pages).

**Design: two layers of queues.**

1. **Front queues (priority):** F queues, one per priority level (1 = highest). A *prioritizer* assigns a score from signals such as PageRank estimate, domain authority, change frequency, depth from seed, link count, sitemap `priority` tag. Higher priority URLs are selected more often (weighted random choice among front queues).
2. **Back queues (politeness):** B queues, **each queue holds URLs of a single host only**, enforced by a mapping table `host -> queue_id`. A worker thread is bound to a back queue (one thread per queue), so only one connection per host at a time. After fetching from host H, record `next_allowed_time[H] = now + crawl_delay` (from `robots.txt` Crawl-delay or a default like 1-5 s, adaptive to server response time: slow server = longer delay). A min-heap keyed by `next_allowed_time` yields the next host that may be fetched.
3. When a back queue empties, refill it by pulling the next URL from a front queue, route by host, and assign the host to this queue.

The frontier is too big for memory: keep the hot head of each queue in RAM and the rest on disk (or in a distributed store/Kafka partitions keyed by host hash). Partition the whole frontier across crawler nodes by `hash(host) mod N` (consistent hashing) so one node owns a host and politeness is local.

#### 15.4 Fetcher details

- **DNS resolution:** a custom asynchronous resolver with a large local cache (DNS is a classic bottleneck). Pre-resolve hosts when URLs enter back queues.
- **robots.txt:** fetch once per host, cache for \~24 h (respect `Cache-Control`), obey `Disallow`, `Crawl-delay`, `Sitemap`. If robots.txt is unreachable (5xx) treat the site as temporarily disallowed; if 404, allow all. Always identify with a clear `User-Agent` and contact URL.
- **HTTP:** async I/O (epoll/Netty) to hold thousands of connections per node; timeouts (connect 5 s, total 30 s), maximum response size (for example 10 MB) to avoid tarpits, follow a limited number of redirects (e.g. 5) and record the redirect chain, support gzip, HTTP keep-alive per host, conditional GET using `ETag`/`If-Modified-Since` for recrawls (304 saves bandwidth).
- **Rendering JavaScript:** a large share of the modern web needs a headless browser to see content; it is 10-100x more expensive, so use it selectively (a second-wave crawler for known JS-heavy domains).
- Retries with backoff for transient errors (5xx, timeouts), permanent failure after N attempts; per-host error rates feed back into delay (back off hard when seeing 429/503).

#### 15.5 Deduplication, two kinds

**URL-seen test:** have we already queued this URL? Billions of entries. Normalize first (lowercase host, remove default port, remove fragments `#...`, sort/drop tracking query params like `utm_*`, resolve `.`/`..`, decode percent-encoding consistently, strip session ids). Then check a **Bloom filter** (fast, memory-light, no false negatives; false positives mean skipping a few unseen URLs, acceptable) backed by a persistent set for exact checks if needed. Sizing: 10B URLs at 1 percent false-positive rate needs about 9.6 bits per element = **12 GB**, shardable across nodes by URL hash. Alternative: store 8-byte URL fingerprints in a sharded key-value store.

**Content-seen test:** different URLs often serve the same content (mirrors, printer versions). Compute a hash (SHA-1/MD5) of the normalized content and look it up; for **near-duplicates** use **SimHash**: a 64-bit fingerprint where similar documents differ in few bits (compare using Hamming distance <= 3 with bit-permuted tables for fast lookup) or MinHash/shingling. Near-duplicate detection stops you from indexing 500 copies of the same article.

#### 15.6 Avoiding crawler traps

Infinite calendars (`/calendar?month=+1`), session-id URLs, dynamically generated infinite paths, and malicious sites. Defenses: maximum URL length (2,000 chars), maximum depth per site (e.g. 15-20), cap pages per host (budget by importance), detect repeating path segments (`/a/b/a/b/a/b`), query parameter whitelist per domain learned from content duplication, skip hosts with abnormal link-to-content ratios, and manual blacklist. Track **per-host crawl budgets** so one site cannot consume the whole crawl.

#### 15.7 Freshness and recrawl scheduling

Pages change at different rates. Estimate each URL's **change rate** from history (compare content hashes across visits; if a page changed in 8 of last 10 visits it's volatile). Model changes as a Poisson process: optimal recrawl interval is roughly proportional to the observed change rate but capped by importance (do not spend crawl budget on rapidly changing, low-value pages like a clock page). Policy: news homepages every few minutes, active blogs daily, static pages monthly. The scheduler periodically scans the URL metadata store for items whose `next_crawl_time <= now` and pushes them to the frontier. Use sitemaps (`lastmod`) and feeds (RSS) as free change signals; use `If-None-Match` to cut bandwidth.

#### 15.8 Storage

```sql
urls(url_hash BIGINT PK, url TEXT, host_id, priority, status ENUM('NEW','QUEUED','FETCHED','FAILED','BLOCKED'),
     last_crawl TIMESTAMPTZ, next_crawl TIMESTAMPTZ, change_rate REAL, content_hash BIGINT, etag TEXT, fail_count INT, depth INT)
hosts(host_id PK, host, robots_txt TEXT, robots_fetched_at, crawl_delay_ms, avg_response_ms, error_rate, pages_crawled, budget)
links(src_url_hash, dst_url_hash)                 -- graph for PageRank (wide-column or graph store)
```

Raw pages go to a distributed object/file store (HDFS/S3) as compressed WARC-style files (hundreds of pages per file, with metadata), keyed by crawl date and content hash; downstream indexers/MapReduce jobs read them in bulk. URL metadata lives in a sharded KV/wide-column store (Bigtable/Cassandra) keyed by `url_hash`, sharded consistent with the frontier partitioning.

#### 15.9 Extracting links

Parse HTML with a tolerant parser (real pages are broken), extract `a href`, `link rel=canonical` (use canonical URL for dedup), `iframe`, `form action` (usually skip), `sitemap` entries; resolve relative URLs against `base href`; filter schemes (http/https only), file extensions (skip binaries you do not want), and domains (allow/deny lists); respect `nofollow` and `noindex` meta tags. Record anchor text (valuable ranking signal).

#### 15.10 Distributed architecture and failure handling

- **Crawler nodes** each own a shard of hosts (consistent hash). Each node runs the frontier shard, fetchers, and parsers. Newly discovered URLs belonging to another shard are sent to the owner via message queue (Kafka topic partitioned by host hash).
- **Node failure:** its shard is reassigned (consistent hashing) and the frontier state is recovered from the durable log/disk checkpoints; in-flight URLs time out back to `QUEUED` (at-least-once crawling, tolerated because fetching is idempotent).
- **Checkpointing:** periodically snapshot frontier state and Bloom filter to durable storage; replay recent URL events after crash.
- **Backpressure:** bounded queues between stages; if the parser lags, fetchers slow down.
- **Monitoring:** pages/s, fetch success rate, queue depths, per-host errors, DNS latency, duplicate rate, average freshness, robots violations (should be zero).

#### 15.11 Legal and ethical considerations

Obey robots.txt and terms, rate-limit, identify yourself, respect copyright when storing/redistributing, honor `noindex`, privacy laws (GDPR) on personal data, and provide a webmaster contact/opt-out. Mention that large crawlers publish IP ranges for verification.

#### 15.12 LLD: frontier with politeness, normalizer, and crawler worker

```java
class PoliteFrontier {
  private final Map<String, Queue<CrawlUrl>> hostQueues = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
  private final PriorityQueue<HostSlot> ready = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingLong(h -> h.nextAllowedAt));   // min-heap by time
  private final Map<String, Long> delayMs = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

  synchronized void add(CrawlUrl u) {
    Queue<CrawlUrl> q = hostQueues.computeIfAbsent(u.host(), h -> { ready.add(new HostSlot(h, 0)); return new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(CrawlUrl::priority)); });
    q.add(u);
  }
  /** Blocks until some host is allowed and has work. */
  synchronized CrawlUrl next() throws InterruptedException {
    while (true) {
      HostSlot slot = ready.peek();
      if (slot == null) { wait(); continue; }
      long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
      if (slot.nextAllowedAt > now) { wait(slot.nextAllowedAt - now); continue; }
      ready.poll();
      Queue<CrawlUrl> q = hostQueues.get(slot.host);
      if (q == null || q.isEmpty()) { hostQueues.remove(slot.host); continue; }  // drop idle hosts
      CrawlUrl u = q.poll();
      slot.nextAllowedAt = now + delayMs.getOrDefault(slot.host, 1000L);   // enforce politeness gap
      ready.add(slot);
      return u;
    }
  }
  void reportResponse(String host, long responseMs, int status) {      // adapt: slow/erroring servers get longer gaps
    long d = (status == 429 || status >= 500) ? Math.min(60_000, delayMs.getOrDefault(host, 1000L) * 2) : Math.max(1000, responseMs * 10);
    delayMs.put(host, d);
  }
}

final class UrlNormalizer {
  static String normalize(String raw, String base) {
    URI u = URI.create(base).resolve(raw.trim());
    String host = u.getHost().toLowerCase(); int port = u.getPort();
    if (port == 80 && "http".equals(u.getScheme()) || port == 443 && "https".equals(u.getScheme())) port = -1;
    String path = u.getPath().isEmpty() ? "/" : removeDotSegments(u.getPath());
    String query = sortAndFilterParams(u.getRawQuery());               // drops utm_*, sessionid, sorts keys
    return u.getScheme() + "://" + host + (port == -1 ? "" : ":" + port) + path + (query.isEmpty() ? "" : "?" + query);   // fragment dropped
  }
}

class CrawlerWorker implements Runnable {
  public void run() {
    while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
      CrawlUrl u = frontier.next();
      if (!robots.allowed(u)) continue;
      FetchResult r = fetcher.fetch(u);                                 // async client, timeouts, size cap
      frontier.reportResponse(u.host(), r.millis(), r.status());
      if (r.status() == 304) { meta.touch(u); continue; }
      if (!r.ok()) { meta.recordFailure(u); retryOrGiveUp(u); continue; }
      long fp = SimHash.of(r.text());
      if (contentIndex.nearDuplicate(fp)) { meta.markDuplicate(u); continue; }
      store.append(u, r);
      for (String link : LinkExtractor.extract(r.html(), u.url())) {
        String n = UrlNormalizer.normalize(link, u.url());
        if (urlFilter.accept(n) && urlSeen.addIfAbsent(n)) router.sendToOwner(n, priorityEstimator.estimate(n, u));
      }
      meta.update(u, r, changeRateEstimator.update(u, fp));
    }
  }
}
```

#### 15.13 HLD diagram

```
Seed list / Sitemaps / Feeds / Recrawl scheduler
          |
   URL Frontier (sharded by host hash): Prioritizer -> front queues -> Router -> back queues (one host each) + politeness timers
          |
   Fetcher fleet (async HTTP) <-> DNS cache, robots cache
          |
   Parser (HTML, links, canonical) -> Content dedup (SimHash index) -> Raw store (HDFS/S3 WARC)
          |                                                             |-> Indexing pipeline / PageRank (batch)
   Link extractor -> Normalizer -> URL filter -> URL-seen (Bloom + KV) -> Kafka by host hash -> Frontier
   URL metadata store (Bigtable/Cassandra) ; Monitoring ; Blacklist/Trap detector
```

#### 15.14 Failure scenarios

| Failure | Handling |
| --- | --- |
| Host slow or hangs | Timeouts, size caps, longer delay, skip temporarily |
| Crawler node crash | Shard reassigned; in-flight URLs requeue; fetch is idempotent |
| Bloom filter false positive | A small fraction of new URLs skipped; periodic re-discovery from other pages |
| robots.txt unreachable | Treat as disallow temporarily; retry later |
| Infinite URL space | Depth limits, per-host budget, pattern detection |
| DNS outage | Multiple resolvers, local cache with stale-if-error |
| IP blocked by sites | Slow down, rotate legitimate egress IPs only if allowed by policy, contact owners; never evade bans abusively |
| Duplicate storms (mirrors) | SimHash content-seen filter |

#### 15.15 Follow-up questions and model answers

1. **BFS or DFS?** BFS-style (queue) with priority scoring; DFS risks deep traps and is unfair across hosts.
2. **How do you ensure politeness?** One back queue per host, one connection at a time, adaptive delay, robots Crawl-delay.
3. **How do you detect duplicates at scale?** URL normalization plus Bloom filter for URL-seen; SimHash for content near-duplicates.
4. **How do you prioritize?** Score by PageRank-like importance, freshness need and depth; weighted selection among front queues.
5. **How do you recrawl efficiently?** Per-URL change-rate estimates, conditional GET, sitemaps/RSS hints.
6. **How do you partition the crawl?** Consistent hash by host so politeness and robots caches stay local.
7. **How do you handle JavaScript sites?** Selective headless rendering in a separate, smaller fleet.
8. **What storage do you choose?** Object store for raw pages, wide-column for URL metadata, Bloom filters in memory.
9. **How do you extend to images or PDFs?** Pluggable content-type handlers after fetch, same frontier and storage.
10. **What if the crawler is overwhelming a site?** Adaptive backoff on latency/errors, respect 429 and Retry-After, per-host rate caps.

#### 15.16 One-page summary

Frontier = priority front queues + per-host back queues with timers. Fetchers are async with DNS and robots caches. Normalize URLs, Bloom filter for seen-URLs, SimHash for near-duplicate content. Partition by host hash. Traps defended by depth and budgets. Recrawl by estimated change rate with conditional requests. Raw pages to object store; metadata to wide-column store.

## Q16. Search autocomplete (typeahead)

**Problem:** as the user types 'sys', show the top \~5 suggestions ('system design', 'sysco', ...) within \~50 ms.

### Requirements

- **Functional:** return top-K (5 to 10) completions for a prefix, ranked by popularity (and optionally personalization/recency); support multiple languages; filter offensive terms.
- **Non-functional:** very low latency (under 100 ms end-to-end, aim for \~20 ms server); highly available; suggestions can be slightly stale (updated hourly/daily is fine); read-heavy.

### Estimation

- 10B searches/day, avg 4 words, \~20 characters; the client sends a request per keystroke (minus debounce), \~5 requests per search = 50B/day = \~580K QPS average, \~1M+ peak.
- Unique queries: say 100M distinct popular queries x 50 bytes = 5 GB for the index. **It fits in memory.** The challenge is QPS and latency, not storage.

### API

```
GET /suggest?q=sys&limit=5&lang=en   ->  ["system design", "sysco", ...]
```

### Core data structure: trie with top-K cached at each node

A **trie** (prefix tree) stores queries; each node represents a prefix. Walking to the prefix node is O(length). To avoid scanning the whole subtree for the best completions, **store the top-K suggestions at every node** (precomputed). Lookup = walk to node, return its list: O(prefix length).

```
          (root)
           s
           y
           s   -> top5: [system design (9M), sysco (2M), syscall (1M), ...]
          / \
        t     c ...
```

Memory trade-off: storing top-K at every node multiplies memory; mitigate by storing only ids/pointers to query strings and storing top-K only for nodes above a frequency threshold.

**Alternatives:** sorted array + binary search for prefix range; Elasticsearch completion suggester (FST based); for small datasets, a Redis sorted set per prefix (`ZREVRANGE prefix:sys 0 4`).

### HLD

```
 ONLINE:  Browser -(debounced requests)-> CDN/edge cache -> LB -> [Suggestion Service] (trie in memory, replicated)
                                                                      \-> Redis (hot prefixes) as fallback
 OFFLINE: search logs -> Kafka -> [Aggregation job (Spark/Flink)] counts per query (weighted by recency)
          -> [Trie Builder] builds new trie/snapshot -> uploaded to storage -> Suggestion servers load it and swap atomically
          -> filter banned words / PII / low-quality queries
```

### Details that earn points

- **Client-side:** debounce keystrokes (wait \~100 to 150 ms), cancel in-flight requests when a new key arrives, cache results for prefixes already requested, and prefetch.
- **Server-side cache:** results for short, popular prefixes are identical for everyone: cache at the CDN/edge with a short TTL (minutes). One- and two-letter prefixes are extremely hot.
- **Sharding:** if the trie doesn't fit one machine, partition by first character(s) with load-aware ranges (e.g. 'a-c', 'd', ...), because 's' and 'q' are not equally common. Or shard by hash of prefix with a router.
- **Updating:** building the trie online per query is too slow and write-heavy. Rebuild periodically (hourly/daily) from aggregated logs and swap atomically (blue/green). For trending/breaking news, add a small real-time layer: a streaming job (Count-Min Sketch, windowed counts) pushes fresh hot queries into an overlay merged at query time.
- **Ranking:** score = frequency x recency decay (+ personalization from the user's history, locale, location). Keep personalized suggestions in a separate small per-user store and merge.
- **Safety:** blocklist for offensive/sensitive queries, minimum count threshold so rare private queries (names, emails) never surface.

### LLD sketch

```java
class TrieNode {
  Map<Character, TrieNode> children = new HashMap<>();
  List<Suggestion> top = new ArrayList<>();                 // sorted by score, size <= K
}
class Trie {
  TrieNode root = new TrieNode(); int K = 5;
  void insert(String q, long score) {
    TrieNode cur = root;
    for (char ch : q.toCharArray()) {
      cur = cur.children.computeIfAbsent(ch, c -> new TrieNode());
      updateTop(cur, q, score);                               // insert/update, keep top K by score
    }
  }
  List<Suggestion> suggest(String prefix) {
    TrieNode cur = root;
    for (char ch : prefix.toCharArray()) { cur = cur.children.get(ch); if (cur == null) return List.of(); }
    return cur.top;
  }
}
```

The built trie is **immutable at serving time** (read-only snapshot), so reads need no locks. Writers build a new one off to the side and swap a reference.

### Deep dive and trade-offs

- **Typos / fuzzy:** add edit-distance matching ('sytem' -> 'system') using n-gram indexes or a BK-tree; run only when exact prefix returns too few results.
- **Multi-language:** per-locale tries; handle Unicode normalization, CJK (no spaces; index by character or by segmented tokens).
- **Freshness vs cost:** hourly rebuild is cheap; real-time overlay costs more. Choose by product need.
- **Consistency:** none needed; each server independently serves its loaded snapshot version.
- **Availability:** replicate shards across zones; serve stale snapshot if the builder is down.

**Interview tip:** say 'trie with precomputed top-K per node, built offline, served from memory, cached at the edge, debounced on the client'. That one sentence hits all the markers.

### Q16 in depth: Search autocomplete (typeahead), every detail

#### 16.1 Requirements and scale

- Functional: as the user types a prefix, return the top K (5-10) suggested completions ranked by popularity/relevance; update with trending queries; personalization (optional); multi-language; typo tolerance (optional); filter offensive/illegal suggestions.
- Non-functional: **very low latency** (under 100 ms end to end; ideally under 50 ms server side because it fires on every keystroke), high availability, eventual freshness (new trends within minutes to hours is fine).
- Scale example: 500M DAU, each performs 10 searches/day, types \~5 characters before selecting a suggestion. Requests = 500M x 10 x 5 = 25B/day = **290k QPS average, \~600k peak**. Reduce load: the client **debounces** (waits 100-200 ms after the last keystroke) and caches results per prefix, cutting calls by 3-5x. Data size: 1B unique queries in the log, but distinct popular queries \~100M x average 25 bytes = 2.5 GB of strings plus counts: the **suggestion corpus fits in memory** of a single large machine, so replicate rather than shard by size (shard only for throughput or very large corpora).

#### 16.2 Core data structure: trie with precomputed top-K

A **trie** (prefix tree) stores strings by shared prefixes. Naively, to answer prefix `ap`, find the node for `a -> p` and traverse its entire subtree to collect all completions and sort by frequency: too slow for short prefixes (the subtree of `a` is huge).

**Optimization: store the top-K completions at every node.** Each node keeps a small array of the best K (say 10) query strings (or ids) with scores for all words in its subtree. A lookup is `O(len(prefix))` to find the node plus `O(1)` to return its cached list. Cost: memory. Estimate: 100M queries, average 25 chars, compressed trie shares prefixes giving maybe 400M nodes; 10 pointers/ids x 8 bytes x 400M = 32 GB. Mitigations: store ids not strings (strings live in a separate table), store top-K only for nodes whose subtree is large (small subtrees can be scanned at query time), use a compressed (radix/Patricia) trie, cap depth (suggest only for the first 20 characters), prune very rare queries (frequency below threshold).

Example: queries and counts: `apple 100`, `app store 80`, `application 60`, `apply 40`, `banana 70`. Node `a-p-p` stores top-3 `[apple 100, app store 80, application 60]`. Typing `app` returns instantly; typing `appl` node stores `[apple 100, application 60, apply 40]`.

**Alternative: Elasticsearch/Solr completion suggester or an FST (finite state transducer)** with weights: the same idea, packaged. Or a sorted array of queries with binary search for the prefix range plus a range-max structure; simpler but slower for hot prefixes. In the interview, trie-with-top-K is the expected answer, with the FST/ES as the pragmatic production alternative.

#### 16.3 Where scores come from (data pipeline)

The trie is a read-only serving structure **rebuilt offline**, not updated per query (per-query updates under 600k QPS would make the hot path slow and add lock contention).

1. **Log collection:** each completed search is logged to Kafka (query text normalized, timestamp, locale, user bucket).
2. **Aggregation:** a batch job (Spark/MapReduce) or streaming job (Flink) counts queries per window: hourly/daily counts with **time-decay** weighting, e.g. `score = sum(count_d x 0.9^(age_days))` so recent behavior outweighs old. Separate trending signal: ratio of last-hour count to baseline.
3. **Filtering:** remove offensive, adult, legal-takedown terms, personal data (phone numbers, emails), and low-count queries (privacy: suggest only queries searched by at least N distinct users, to prevent leaking an individual's private query).
4. **Build:** construct the trie (or FST) with top-K per node; write it to blob storage as a snapshot file (e.g. `trie-2026-11-10-14.bin`).
5. **Deploy:** serving nodes download the new snapshot, load it into memory, then **atomically swap** the pointer from old to new (blue/green in memory), so no query ever sees a half-built trie.
6. **Fast path for trending:** every few minutes, a streaming job computes the top rising queries and pushes a small **overlay** (a tiny second trie or hash map of hot queries) merged at query time with the main trie's results. This gives freshness for breaking news without a full rebuild.

Rebuild cadence: full rebuild daily or hourly (a 100M-query trie builds in minutes), overlay every 1-5 minutes.

#### 16.4 Serving architecture

- **Client:** debounce keystrokes (150 ms), cancel in-flight stale requests, local cache keyed by prefix (previous results reused when the user types the next letter or backspaces), prefetch for common prefixes, show instantly from cache. HTTP/2 with keep-alive; small JSON payloads (a few hundred bytes).
- **CDN/edge cache:** responses for popular short prefixes (1-3 characters) are identical for all users in a locale and cacheable for minutes: `GET /suggest?q=ap&locale=en-US` with `Cache-Control: max-age=300`. This absorbs a large share of traffic since most keystrokes are short prefixes.
- **Suggestion service:** stateless servers each holding the full trie in memory; load-balance by round-robin (no sharding needed if corpus fits). For huge corpora or per-language tries shard by first character or by language/locale; avoid sharding by hash of prefix because the hot prefix problem leads to imbalance; instead shard by prefix range with weights, or replicate hot ranges.
- **Redis fallback:** for very small deployments precompute `prefix -> top-K` pairs for all prefixes up to length N in a key-value store (billions of keys: memory heavy); the trie is more compact.

#### 16.5 Personalization and context

Blend global suggestions with personal ones: recent searches of the user (stored per user in a small KV store, a few dozen entries), plus context (location: 'restaurants near me', language, device, time of day, current page). Implementation: fetch up to K global candidates from the trie and up to M personal ones, merge using a lightweight scoring function (`score = w_g x global + w_p x personal_recency + w_ctx x context_match`), dedupe and return the top K. Personalization must stay under the latency budget: personal data cached in memory on the session server or sent by the client in the request.

#### 16.6 Typo tolerance and ranking improvements

For misspelled prefixes (`appel`), options: (1) edit-distance-1 candidate expansion by exploring neighboring trie branches with a bounded edit budget (Levenshtein automaton over the FST); (2) phonetic keys (Soundex/Metaphone); (3) learned spelling correction from query logs ('appel' is frequently followed by a click on 'apple'). Ranking beyond raw frequency: click-through rate on suggestions, freshness, a learned-to-rank model with features (prefix length, position, click history), diversity (avoid 10 near-identical suggestions), and business rules (promoted terms).

Multi-language and Unicode: normalize (NFKC, lowercase, strip diacritics when appropriate), tokenization for languages without spaces (Chinese/Japanese) using n-grams or segmenters; transliteration for Hinglish ('namaste' -> Devanagari).

#### 16.7 Data model and storage

```text
query_log (Kafka -> object store): {ts, query_norm, locale, user_bucket, clicked_suggestion?}
query_stats (warehouse): (query_norm, locale, day, count, distinct_users)
suggest_snapshot (blob): trie nodes serialized: [char | children offsets | topK (ids) ], plus string table: id -> query text, score
blocklist (DB + cache): normalized terms and regexes
user_recent (KV): user_id -> last 50 queries (LRU)
```

Trie serialization: nodes in contiguous arrays (cache-friendly, memory-mappable) rather than pointer-heavy objects, which matters in Java/Go for GC pressure and memory: e.g. a flat `int[] children`, `byte[] chars`, `int[] topK` layout loaded via memory mapping.

#### 16.8 LLD: trie with top-K, and atomic snapshot swap

```java
class SuggestTrie {
  static final int K = 10;
  static class Node {
    Map<Character, Node> children = new HashMap<>();
    List<Suggestion> top = new ArrayList<>(K);        // best K in this subtree, sorted by score desc
  }
  record Suggestion(String text, long score) {}
  private final Node root = new Node();

  /** Offline build: insert each query with its score and update top-K along the path. */
  void insert(String query, long score) {
    Node cur = root;
    for (char c : query.toCharArray()) {
      cur = cur.children.computeIfAbsent(c, k -> new Node());
      update(cur.top, new Suggestion(query, score));
    }
  }
  private void update(List<Suggestion> top, Suggestion s) {
    top.removeIf(t -> t.text().equals(s.text()));                                   // avoid duplicates
    top.add(s);
    top.sort((a, b) -> Long.compare(b.score(), a.score()));
    if (top.size() > K) top.remove(top.size() - 1);
  }
  /** Online lookup: O(prefix length). */
  List<Suggestion> suggest(String prefix) {
    Node cur = root;
    for (char c : prefix.toLowerCase().toCharArray()) {
      cur = cur.children.get(c);
      if (cur == null) return List.of();
    }
    return cur.top;                                                                 // precomputed
  }
}

class SuggestService {
  private final AtomicReference<SuggestTrie> current = new AtomicReference<>();
  private volatile Map<String, List<Suggestion>> trendingOverlay = Map.of();

  List<Suggestion> suggest(String prefix, UserContext ctx) {
    List<Suggestion> base = current.get().suggest(prefix);
    List<Suggestion> hot = trendingOverlay.getOrDefault(prefix.toLowerCase(), List.of());
    List<Suggestion> personal = ctx.recentMatching(prefix, 3);
    return Ranker.merge(base, hot, personal, blocklist, 10);
  }
  void reload(String snapshotPath) {                                                // runs on a background thread
    SuggestTrie fresh = SnapshotLoader.load(snapshotPath);
    validate(fresh);                                                                // sanity: size, sample queries
    current.set(fresh);                                                             // atomic swap, readers never block
  }
}
```

#### 16.9 HLD diagram

```
Search app --keystroke (debounced)--> CDN/Edge cache (short prefixes) --miss--> Load balancer --> Suggestion service (trie in memory)
                                                                                      |-> Personalization (recent queries KV) |-> Blocklist
Query logs --> Kafka --> Stream job (trending overlay, every few min) -----------------------+
                     --> Batch aggregation (daily/hourly, decay, filtering) --> Trie builder --> Snapshot (blob) --> rolling load + atomic swap
```

#### 16.10 Failure scenarios and edge cases

| Case | Handling |
| --- | --- |
| Bad snapshot (corrupt or tiny) | Validate before swap; keep serving the previous trie; alert |
| Node restart | Load latest snapshot from blob before joining the LB (readiness probe) |
| Traffic spike on breaking news | Overlay picks up trend within minutes; CDN and client caching absorb load |
| Offensive or legal-takedown suggestion | Blocklist checked at serve time (instant effect), removed at next build |
| Privacy leak of rare personal queries | Minimum distinct-user threshold, PII filters, no per-user data in global trie |
| Prefix with no results | Return empty fast; optionally spelling-corrected prefix suggestions |
| Hot prefix imbalance | Replicate rather than shard by prefix; CDN for popular prefixes |
| Stale personalization data | Short TTL; fall back to global |

#### 16.11 Follow-up questions and model answers

1. **Why a trie rather than SQL `LIKE 'ap%'`?** `LIKE` scans or needs an index range plus sorting by frequency; at 600k QPS the latency and cost are too high. A trie with precomputed top-K answers in O(prefix length).
2. **Memory too large?** Compress with radix tree/FST, store ids not strings, cap depth, prune rare queries, store top-K only on big nodes.
3. **How do you keep results fresh?** Hourly/daily rebuild plus a minutes-fresh trending overlay; time-decayed scores.
4. **How do you update a live trie safely?** Build new snapshot offline, load in the background, atomic pointer swap; never mutate the live structure.
