**Follow-ups.** (1) *Why Kafka in the middle?* Absorb spikes, decouple, replay after an indexing bug. (2) *How do you trace a request?* trace\_id propagation plus tracing backend. (3) *How do you keep costs sane?* Sampling, tiering, label-only indexes, short retention. (4) *Logs versus metrics versus traces?* Logs for detail, metrics for trends and alerts, traces for latency across services. (5) *Security/audit logs?* Separate immutable pipeline (WORM storage, hash chaining), strict access.

**Summary.** Structured JSON with trace ids, node-local agents with bounded spooling, Kafka buffering, stream processing for parsing, redaction and sampling, tiered indexed storage (hot/warm/cold), time-pruned queries, and strict cost and volume controls.

### Q31. CDN

- **Idea:** cache content at edge locations near users.
- **HLD:** DNS/anycast routes a user to the nearest edge PoP; edge checks cache; on miss goes to a regional/shield cache then origin; cache keyed by URL + selected headers; TTL via `Cache-Control`; purge/invalidate API; TLS terminated at edge. **Push CDN** (you upload) vs **pull CDN** (edge fetches on miss).
- **Data / LLD:** edge cache = hash map + LRU over disk/memory; request coalescing so 1,000 simultaneous misses cause one origin fetch.
- **Watch out:** cache poisoning, versioned asset names (`app.3f2a.js`) instead of purging, dynamic/personalized content bypass, origin shielding to protect the origin from thundering herds.

#### Q31 in depth: CDN

**Purpose.** A Content Delivery Network is a globally distributed set of cache servers (edge PoPs) that serve content from near the user. It cuts latency (a 150 ms intercontinental round trip becomes 10-20 ms), offloads the origin (often 90-99 percent of bytes), absorbs traffic spikes and DDoS, and terminates TLS close to users. Examples: Cloudflare, Akamai, CloudFront, Fastly.

**Requirements and scale.** 100+ PoPs worldwide, 50 Tbps peak egress, p95 time-to-first-byte under 50 ms for cached content, cache hit ratio above 95 percent for static assets, purge in seconds, TLS everywhere, support for HTTP/2/3, streaming video segments (Q9), dynamic acceleration.

**How a request flows.** 1) User resolves `static.example.com`; DNS (GeoDNS or **anycast**) returns the IP of a nearby/healthy PoP. 2) Edge server checks its cache (RAM then SSD). **Hit:** serve immediately. 3) **Miss:** edge asks a **parent/regional cache** (tiered caching), which asks the **origin shield** (a designated layer that collapses misses from all PoPs into one origin fetch), which finally asks the origin. 4) Response is stored according to cache rules and returned. Each layer reduces origin load: with 100 PoPs missing the same new file, the shield turns 100 origin fetches into 1.

**Routing users to PoPs.** *DNS-based:* authoritative DNS answers with the best PoP by resolver location, latency measurements and load (limitation: resolver location, not client; mitigated by EDNS Client Subnet). *Anycast:* the same IP is announced via BGP from every PoP, so network routing sends each user to the topologically nearest one, with automatic failover when a PoP withdraws (simple and DDoS-resilient, but BGP routes can shift flows mid-connection, so TCP needs care; QUIC helps).

**Cache semantics.** Cache key: scheme + host + path + normalized query string + selected headers (`Accept-Encoding`, device class); carefully avoid keying on cookies for static content. Freshness from `Cache-Control: max-age`, `s-maxage` (CDN-specific), `Expires`; validation with `ETag`/`If-None-Match` or `Last-Modified` (304 saves bytes). `stale-while-revalidate` and `stale-if-error` serve old content while refreshing or when origin is down. Don't cache responses with `Set-Cookie` or `private`. **Versioned URLs** (`app.3f9a1c.js`, hash in filename) allow year-long TTLs and instant 'invalidation' by changing the URL, which is the best practice for static assets.

**Invalidation/purge.** Purge by URL, tag (surrogate keys: tag all pages of product 17 with `product-17`, purge the tag when it changes) or prefix. Propagate purge to thousands of servers in seconds via a control-plane broadcast (pub/sub fan-out to all PoPs); each edge removes or marks stale; consistency window of a few seconds. Soft purge marks stale (serve stale while revalidating) to avoid origin stampede.

**Eviction and storage.** Two-tier cache: hot objects in RAM (LRU/LFU variants such as TinyLFU/ARC), the rest on SSD/NVMe; avoid caching **one-hit wonders** (objects requested once) by admission control with a Bloom filter: cache only on the second request, which preserves capacity for repeat content. Large files use range requests and segment/chunk caching so partial downloads and seeks cache well. Consistent hashing across servers within a PoP (Q21) gives each object one home server, multiplying effective cache size instead of duplicating objects on every machine; hot objects are replicated to several servers.

**Origin protection and request collapsing.** When 10,000 users request an uncached object simultaneously, the edge sends **one** request to the origin and holds the others (request coalescing). Negative caching for 404/5xx short TTLs. Per-origin connection pools, circuit breaker, and rate limits so a CDN miss storm cannot flatten the origin.

**Dynamic content and security.** Dynamic acceleration: persistent optimized connections to the origin, TCP/QUIC tuning, route optimization. Edge compute (Workers, Lambda@Edge) for A/B tests, auth checks, personalization at the edge. Security: TLS termination with managed certificates (SNI), WAF, bot management, rate limiting, signed URLs/cookies (`?exp=...&sig=...`) for private content, geo-blocking, DDoS scrubbing because attack traffic is absorbed across a distributed network.

**Push versus pull CDN.** *Pull (origin pull):* CDN fetches on first miss; simplest; first user pays the miss. *Push:* you upload content to the CDN storage in advance; good for large, predictable releases (game patches, movie premieres) and pre-warming. Many do both (pre-positioning popular content in advance, as Netflix Open Connect does).

```java
class EdgeCache {
  private final LruCache<String, CachedObject> ram; private final DiskCache disk; private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<CachedObject>> inflight = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
  Response handle(Request req) {
    String key = cacheKey(req); CachedObject o = ram.get(key);
    if (o == null && (o = disk.get(key)) != null) ram.put(key, o);
    if (o != null && o.isFresh()) return o.toResponse();
    if (o != null && o.canServeStale()) { refreshAsync(key, req, o); return o.toResponse().withHeader("Warning", "110 stale"); }
    CachedObject fetched = inflight.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchFromParent(req, o)))   // request coalescing
                                    .join();
    inflight.remove(key);
    if (fetched.isCacheable() && admission.shouldAdmit(key)) { ram.put(key, fetched); disk.put(key, fetched); }
    return fetched.toResponse();
  }
  private CachedObject fetchFromParent(Request req, CachedObject stale) {
    Request r = req.copy(); if (stale != null) r.header("If-None-Match", stale.etag());       // conditional revalidation
    Response p = parent.fetch(r);
    return p.status() == 304 ? stale.refreshed(p.headers()) : CachedObject.from(p);
  }
}
class SignedUrl { static boolean verify(String path, long exp, String sig, byte[] secret) { return exp > now() && constantTimeEquals(hmacSha256(secret, path + "|" + exp), sig); } }
```

**Failure cases.** PoP failure: anycast withdraws the route or DNS health check removes it; users go to the next PoP. Origin down: serve stale, negative-cache errors briefly, fail over to a secondary origin. Cache poisoning (attacker gets a bad response cached): strict cache keys, ignore unkeyed headers, validate origin responses. Purge storm: rate-limit purges, prefer versioned URLs. Thundering herd after purge: soft purge, coalescing. Certificate expiry: automated renewal and monitoring.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *What should not be cached?* Personalized, authenticated, or rapidly changing content unless keyed and short-TTL. (2) *Cache hit ratio improvement?* Normalize query strings, versioned assets, longer TTL, origin shield, consolidate cache keys. (3) *How do you update a file immediately?* Versioned URL or purge by tag. (4) *Anycast versus GeoDNS?* Anycast gives instant failover and DDoS dispersion; DNS gives fine control. (5) *Cost drivers?* Egress bandwidth and request counts; negotiate peering, embed caches in ISPs.

**Summary.** Edge PoPs with tiered caching and an origin shield, anycast/GeoDNS routing, correct cache keys and headers, versioned URLs plus tag purges, request coalescing and stale serving to protect the origin, consistent hashing inside PoPs, admission control for one-hit wonders, and signed URLs for private content.

### Q32. Object store (S3)

- **Idea:** store immutable blobs of any size by key with extreme durability (11 nines) and availability.
- **HLD:** **Metadata service** (bucket/key -> object id, size, version, locations; sharded KV/DB) separate from **data nodes** that store the bytes. Objects split into chunks, replicated 3x or **erasure coded** (e.g. 8+4: survive 4 failures with 1.5x overhead vs 3x). Placement across racks/AZs. Background scrubbing verifies checksums and repairs.
- **Data / LLD:** API: PUT/GET/DELETE/LIST (prefix listing needs ordered metadata), multipart upload for big files, versioning, lifecycle rules (move to cold tier), pre-signed URLs.
- **Watch out:** strong read-after-write consistency requires careful metadata design; listing at scale; hot prefixes; small-object overhead.

#### Q32 in depth: Object store (S3)

**What it is.** A flat-namespace store of immutable-ish **objects** (bytes + metadata) addressed by `bucket/key`, accessed over HTTP (PUT, GET, DELETE, LIST, multipart upload), built for **11 nines of durability**, virtually unlimited capacity, and high aggregate throughput. Not a filesystem (no in-place edits, no atomic rename, no POSIX semantics) and not a database.

**Requirements and scale.** Trillions of objects, exabytes, millions of requests/s; object size from 1 byte to 5 TB; durability 99.999999999 percent; availability 99.99 percent; strong read-after-write consistency (S3 became strongly consistent in 2020); versioning, lifecycle rules, encryption, access control, events.

**Core split.** Separate **metadata plane** (bucket/key -> object id, size, checksum, version, ACL, location) from **data plane** (the bytes, stored as chunks on storage nodes). Reason: they scale and fail differently; metadata is small and hot with strong consistency needs, data is huge and sequential.

**Request path.** Client -> load balancer -> **front-end/API server** (authenticate via signed request, authorize via policy/ACL, validate) -> for PUT: ask the **placement service** which storage nodes get the data, stream the bytes to them, wait for durability, then commit metadata -> respond 200 with ETag. For GET: look up metadata, read chunks from storage nodes (parallel, range reads), verify checksum, stream back.

**Metadata store.** Needs: lookup by `(bucket, key)`, ordered **LIST with prefix and delimiter** (so `photos/2026/` behaves like a folder), versioning, transactional commit. Implementation: a sharded, replicated, strongly consistent key-value store (LSM or B-tree) keyed by `(bucket_id, key)`; shards split automatically when hot (range partitioning keeps LIST efficient; hash prefixing would break ordered LIST). Prefix-heavy workloads (all keys beginning `logs/2026-11-10/`) concentrate on one shard: the system must **auto-split hot key ranges**; advise clients to randomize leading key characters for extreme write rates.

**Data durability: replication versus erasure coding.** Triple replication: 3x storage, simple reads, survives 2 losses. **Erasure coding (Reed-Solomon, e.g. 10 data + 4 parity shards across 14 nodes/racks/AZs)**: 1.4x overhead, survives any 4 shard losses; reads fetch any 10 shards; repair rebuilds missing shards from survivors. Use replication for small/hot objects, erasure coding for large/cold. Place shards in different failure domains (disk, host, rack, AZ). Compute availability: with shards in 3 AZs, losing a whole AZ must still leave enough shards to reconstruct (design parity accordingly).

**Integrity.** Compute checksums (MD5/CRC32C/SHA-256) at the client and on arrival; store them with metadata; verify on read; **background scrubbers** continuously read all data to detect bit rot and trigger repair. Durability math: annual failure rate of a disk \~2 percent; repair time matters more than replica count: faster re-replication shrinks the window where additional failures cause loss.

**Multipart upload.** Large objects (GBs): `CreateMultipartUpload` returns an upload id; parts (5 MB to 5 GB) upload in parallel and independently retriable, `UploadPart` returns each part's ETag; `CompleteMultipartUpload` lists parts, the system stitches the manifest atomically (no copy of bytes needed: the object is a list of chunk references). Incomplete uploads are garbage-collected by lifecycle rules. Benefits: parallelism, resume, bounded retry cost.

**Versioning and deletes.** Each PUT creates a new version id when versioning is on; DELETE adds a **delete marker**; permanent delete targets a version id. Lifecycle policies transition objects between storage classes (Standard -> Infrequent Access -> Glacier archive) and expire them by age/prefix/tag. MFA delete and **object lock (WORM)** for compliance.

**Consistency.** The metadata commit is the linearization point: after PUT returns, any GET/LIST sees it (achieved by a consensus-replicated metadata layer). Overwrite of the same key is atomic last-writer-wins by commit order. No cross-object transactions.

**Security.** IAM policies, bucket policies, ACLs; requests authenticated with HMAC-SHA256 signatures (SigV4) over method, path, headers, timestamp; presigned URLs delegate temporary access; server-side encryption with per-object data keys wrapped by KMS master keys (envelope encryption); TLS in transit; block-public-access guardrails; access logs.

**Events and integrations.** Object create/delete events publish to queues/functions (Lambda), enabling pipelines such as video processing (Q9) or image resizing; replication rules for cross-region copies; inventory reports.

```java
record ObjectMeta(String bucket, String key, String versionId, long size, String etag, List<ChunkRef> chunks, Instant created, Map<String,String> userMeta) {}
class PutHandler {
  ObjectMeta put(String bucket, String key, InputStream data, long len) {
    authz.check(principal(), "s3:PutObject", bucket, key);
    List<Node> nodes = placement.chooseNodes(len, ErasureScheme.RS_10_4);
    MessageDigest md = MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5"); List<ChunkRef> refs = new ArrayList<>();
    for (byte[] stripe : ChunkReader.stripes(data, 64 << 20)) {
      md.update(stripe);
      List<byte[]> shards = ReedSolomon.encode(stripe, 10, 4);
      for (int i = 0; i < shards.size(); i++) nodes.get(i).write(shardId(stripe, i), shards.get(i));        // wait for >= 13 of 14 acks (write quorum)
      refs.add(new ChunkRef(stripeId(stripe), nodes));
    }
    ObjectMeta m = new ObjectMeta(bucket, key, newVersionId(), len, hex(md.digest()), refs, Instant.now(), Map.of());
    metadata.commit(m);                                                       // linearization point
    return m;
  }
}
class ListHandler {
  ListResult list(String bucket, String prefix, String delimiter, String continuation, int max) {
    NavigableMap<String, ObjectMeta> range = metadata.scan(bucket, prefix, continuation, max * 4);
    Set<String> commonPrefixes = new TreeSet<>(); List<ObjectMeta> objs = new ArrayList<>();
    for (var e : range.entrySet()) {
      String rest = e.getKey().substring(prefix.length()); int i = delimiter.isEmpty() ? -1 : rest.indexOf(delimiter);
      if (i >= 0) commonPrefixes.add(prefix + rest.substring(0, i + delimiter.length())); else objs.add(e.getValue());   // folder emulation
    }
    return new ListResult(objs, commonPrefixes);
  }
}
```

**Failure cases.** Storage node/disk failure: detect via heartbeat, mark shards missing, rebuild in the background from parity, prioritize objects with the fewest remaining shards. AZ outage: reads reconstruct from remaining AZs. Partial write (client disconnect mid-PUT): metadata not committed, orphan chunks garbage-collected. Metadata shard hot spot: auto-split. Request storms on one key: front-end caching of metadata, CDN. Accidental deletion: versioning + MFA delete + lifecycle holds. Silent corruption: checksums and scrubbing.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you get 11 nines?* Erasure coding across failure domains, fast repair, checksums and scrubbing. (2) *How does LIST work on a flat namespace?* Ordered metadata index with prefix/delimiter scan. (3) *Why is rename expensive?* Copy + delete, since keys are the identity. (4) *How do you serve a 5 TB object?* Multipart upload, ranged parallel reads. (5) *Strong consistency how?* Consensus-replicated metadata commit point. (6) *Cost control?* Storage classes, lifecycle, dedupe by checksum, compression.

**Summary.** Metadata plane (consistent sharded KV with ordered keys) separate from data plane (erasure-coded chunks across failure domains), checksums plus scrubbing, multipart uploads, versioning and lifecycle, SigV4 and presigned URLs, envelope encryption, event notifications.

### Q33. Distributed file system (GFS / HDFS)

- **Idea:** store huge files (GB to TB) across commodity machines for batch analytics; optimize for large sequential reads and appends.
- **HLD:** one **master/NameNode** holds namespace and file->block mapping in memory (with a replicated edit log and standby); many **ChunkServers/DataNodes** store 64 to 128 MB blocks replicated 3x (rack-aware: 2 racks). Clients ask the master where blocks are, then talk directly to data nodes. Heartbeats + block reports; the master re-replicates under-replicated blocks.
- **Data / LLD:** write pipeline: client sends to replica 1 which forwards to 2 then 3; lease chooses a primary to order mutations.
- **Watch out:** master is a single point of failure/bottleneck (use HA standby, federation); small files problem (each consumes master memory); not for low-latency random access.

#### Q33 in depth: Distributed file system (GFS / HDFS)

**Goal.** Store very large files (GBs to TBs) across thousands of commodity machines, optimized for **large sequential reads and appends** (batch analytics, MapReduce), with automatic fault tolerance. Not for low-latency random updates or many tiny files.

**Design assumptions (from the GFS paper).** Component failures are the norm (with 10,000 disks something fails daily); files are huge; most writes are appends, most reads are large streams; bandwidth matters more than latency; relaxed consistency is acceptable if well-defined.

**Architecture.** One **master / NameNode** holds all *metadata* in memory: the namespace tree, file-to-block mapping, and block locations (learned from DataNode reports, not persisted). Many **chunkservers / DataNodes** store the *data* as fixed-size blocks (64 MB in GFS, 128-256 MB in modern HDFS) in local files, replicated (default 3). Clients ask the master only *where* the data is, then talk to DataNodes directly for the bytes, so the master is not on the data path.

**Why big blocks.** Fewer blocks means less metadata (1 PB / 128 MB = 8M blocks x \~150 B = 1.2 GB of NameNode RAM), fewer client-master interactions, long sequential reads that amortize seeks, and persistent TCP connections. Cost: small files waste metadata (10M tiny files = 10M objects in RAM), so pack small files into larger containers (SequenceFiles/HAR/Parquet).

**Read path.** Client -> master: `open(path)` returns block ids and DataNode addresses ordered by network distance. Client reads from the closest replica; checksum each chunk of data (every 512 bytes or 64 KB); on checksum failure, report to the master and read another replica. The client caches block locations.

**Write path (pipeline).** Client asks the master to create the file/allocate a block; master returns a list of 3 DataNodes (placement policy). Client streams data to the first DataNode; **each DataNode forwards to the next in a chain** (pipeline replication; uses the full bandwidth of each node's outbound link instead of the client sending 3 copies); acks flow back. After the block fills, the client asks for the next block. In GFS the master grants a **lease** to one replica (the *primary*) which orders concurrent mutations for the chunk; data flow and control flow are decoupled. *Record append* lets many clients append concurrently with at-least-once semantics (an offset chosen by the primary; duplicates/padding possible, readers dedupe by record ids).

**Replica placement (rack awareness).** Replica 1 on the writer's node (or a random node), replica 2 on a **different rack**, replica 3 on a different node of the same rack as replica 2. Balances write bandwidth (one cross-rack hop), read locality, and survival of a rack failure.

**Master metadata durability.** The namespace and file-to-block map are persisted via an **operation log (edit log)** replicated to local and remote disks, plus periodic **checkpoints** (FsImage). On restart, load the checkpoint and replay the log. Block locations are rebuilt from DataNode **block reports** at startup. Single master is a bottleneck and SPOF: HDFS adds a **Standby NameNode** (shared edit log via JournalNodes/Quorum Journal Manager with ZooKeeper-based failover), and **federation** (multiple independent NameNodes owning different namespace subtrees) to scale metadata horizontally.

**Fault handling.** DataNodes send **heartbeats** every 3 s; missing for \~10 minutes marks it dead and triggers **re-replication** of its blocks from surviving replicas to restore the replication factor (rate-limited, prioritizing blocks with the fewest replicas). Corrupt replicas are detected by checksum scans and replaced. **Rebalancer** moves blocks from full to empty nodes. Decommissioning drains a node gracefully. Erasure coding (HDFS EC, RS-6-3) cuts overhead from 3x to 1.5x for cold data.

**Consistency model.** Namespace operations (create, delete, rename) are atomic via the single master (a serialization point). File data: HDFS supports single-writer, append-only semantics (no random writes), which removes most consistency problems. GFS allows concurrent record appends with defined but possibly interleaved/duplicated regions. Readers see data only after the writer flushes (`hflush`/`hsync`) or closes.

**Data locality.** Compute frameworks (MapReduce/Spark) schedule tasks on nodes that hold the block (or same rack) so computation moves to the data instead of data over the network.

```java
class NameNode {
  private final Map<String, FileMeta> namespace = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();           // path -> block ids
  private final Map<Long, Set<DataNodeId>> blockLocations = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();   // rebuilt from block reports
  private final EditLog editLog;
  synchronized AllocatedBlock addBlock(String path, String clientHost) {
    long blockId = idGen.next();
    List<DataNodeId> targets = placement.choose(3, clientHost);                        // rack-aware
    editLog.append(new AddBlockOp(path, blockId));                                      // durable BEFORE mutating memory
    namespace.get(path).blocks.add(blockId); return new AllocatedBlock(blockId, targets);
  }
  void onBlockReport(DataNodeId dn, List<Long> blocks) { for (long b : blocks) blockLocations.computeIfAbsent(b, k -> ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()).add(dn); }
  void replicationMonitor() {                                                           // every few seconds
    for (var e : blockLocations.entrySet()) {
      int live = (int) e.getValue().stream().filter(heartbeats::isAlive).count();
      if (live < TARGET_REPLICAS && live > 0) scheduleCopy(e.getKey(), pickSource(e.getValue()), pickNewTarget(e.getValue()));
    }
  }
}
class DataNode {
  void writeBlock(long blockId, InputStream in, List<DataNodeId> downstream) {
    try (OutputStream local = store.create(blockId); OutputStream next = downstream.isEmpty() ? OutputStream.nullOutputStream() : connect(downstream.get(0), downstream.subList(1, downstream.size()), blockId)) {
      byte[] buf = new byte[64 * 1024]; int n;
      while ((n = in.read(buf)) > 0) { checksum.update(buf, 0, n); local.write(buf, 0, n); next.write(buf, 0, n); }   // pipeline forward
    }
    store.writeChecksums(blockId, checksum.finish());
  }
}
```

**Failure cases.** NameNode crash: standby takes over from shared journal; clients retry. DataNode crash: re-replication. Rack failure: replicas on other racks keep data available. Network partition: NameNode safe mode when too few blocks are reported at startup. NameNode memory exhaustion: federation, merge small files. Slow DataNode (straggler): hedged reads from another replica. Corruption: checksums on read and background scans.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *Why a single master?* Simplifies placement and consistency; made safe by keeping it off the data path, in-memory metadata and standby failover. (2) *Why 3 replicas and how placed?* Failure tolerance and read bandwidth; rack-aware. (3) *Small files problem?* Metadata blowup; bundle files. (4) *How is the master's state recovered?* Checkpoint + edit log + block reports. (5) *HDFS versus object store?* HDFS offers data locality and filesystem semantics with append; object stores offer elastic storage, no locality, simpler operations.

**Summary.** In-memory master metadata with durable edit log and standby, big replicated blocks on DataNodes, pipeline replication with rack-aware placement, heartbeats and automatic re-replication, checksums, single-writer append model, and locality-aware compute.

### Q34. Webhook delivery system

- **Idea:** reliably POST events to customers' HTTP endpoints, which are slow, flaky, or down.
- **HLD:** event source -> Kafka -> **dispatcher** (looks up subscriptions) -> per-endpoint queues -> delivery workers with timeouts (5 to 10 s) -> record attempt result. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter for \~24 to 72 hours, then DLQ and a replay UI. Sign each request with HMAC (`X-Signature`) and timestamp for replay protection.
- **Data / LLD:** `deliveries(event_id, endpoint_id, attempt, status, next_attempt_at, response_code)`; event ids let receivers dedupe (at-least-once).
- **Watch out:** one slow customer must not delay others (isolation per endpoint, circuit breaker that pauses failing endpoints); SSRF protection (block internal IPs); ordering usually not guaranteed.

#### Q34 in depth: Webhook delivery system

**What it does.** Your platform notifies customers' servers about events (payment captured, order shipped, code pushed) by sending an HTTP POST to a URL they registered. You do not control those servers: they are slow, down, misconfigured, or hostile. The design problem is **reliable, secure, fair delivery to unreliable third parties** at scale (Stripe, GitHub, Shopify and Twilio all run such systems).

**Requirements and scale.** Register endpoints per customer with event-type subscriptions; deliver each event **at least once**, signed, within seconds when the endpoint is healthy; retry with backoff for days when it is down; one slow customer must never delay others; delivery logs and manual resend; auto-disable endpoints that fail for too long. Scale example: 50k events/s peak, 10M endpoints, p99 first-attempt latency under 5 s.

**Pipeline.**

1. **Event creation:** the business service writes the event and an outbox row in one DB transaction (Q12); a relay publishes `event.created` to Kafka. Event = `{event_id, type, created_at, data, api_version}`.
2. **Fan-out:** for each event, look up subscribed endpoints of the account (cached) and create one **delivery task** per endpoint: `{delivery_id, event_id, endpoint_id, attempt, next_attempt_at}`.
3. **Dispatch queues** partitioned by `endpoint_id` so concurrency limits and isolation are per endpoint; separate lanes for first attempts and retries.
4. **Workers** POST with a short timeout (5-10 s) and classify the result: 2xx success; 410 Gone disables the endpoint; 429/5xx/timeout/connection error retryable; other 4xx usually permanent failure after a few tries. Record every attempt (status, latency, response snippet).
5. **Retry schedule:** exponential backoff with jitter, e.g. 5 s, 30 s, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 6 h, then every 12 h up to 3 days (about 15 attempts). Stored as `next_attempt_at` in a delay queue or scheduler (Q24). After exhaustion mark `FAILED`, notify the customer, keep for manual replay.

**Isolation and fairness.** Per-endpoint concurrency cap (e.g. 5 in flight) and rate cap (token bucket, Q2) so a customer cannot be hammered and a slow customer holds only its own workers. Use **bulkheads**: separate worker pools for large tenants and the long tail. Circuit breaker per endpoint: after N consecutive failures stop sending live traffic and probe occasionally (so 10,000 events do not pile up retrying a dead URL; they wait in a backlog). Priority: transactional events (payments) above bulk/analytics events.

**Security.** HMAC signature: header `X-Signature: t=1731200000,v1=hex(HMAC_SHA256(secret, t + '.' + body))`; the receiver recomputes and compares in constant time, and rejects if `t` is older than 5 minutes (**replay protection**). Per-endpoint secrets, rotate with overlap. HTTPS only. **SSRF protection** (critical): customers could register `http://169.254.169.254/` (cloud metadata) or internal hosts. Resolve DNS yourself, block private/loopback/link-local ranges, re-check after redirects (or disallow redirects), pin the resolved IP for the connection (defeats DNS rebinding), and send from an isolated egress network with no access to internal services. Stable source IPs let customers allowlist you.

**Idempotency for receivers.** At-least-once means duplicates. Include a stable `event_id` (the same across retries and across endpoints) and tell customers to dedupe on it. Ordering is **not guaranteed** (retries reorder); include `created_at` or a sequence so receivers can ignore stale updates, or advise fetching the latest resource state via API upon notification ('thin events').

**Data model.**

```sql
endpoints(endpoint_id PK, account_id, url, secret_hash, events TEXT[], status ENUM('ACTIVE','DISABLED','PAUSED'), created_at, consecutive_failures INT, disabled_reason)
events(event_id PK, account_id, type, payload JSONB, created_at)                 -- retained 30 days
deliveries(delivery_id PK, event_id, endpoint_id, status ENUM('PENDING','SUCCEEDED','FAILED'), attempt INT, next_attempt_at, last_status_code, last_error, updated_at)
delivery_attempts(delivery_id, attempt, started_at, duration_ms, status_code, response_snippet)
INDEX deliveries(status, next_attempt_at)                                         -- retry scanner
```

```java
class DeliveryWorker {
  void process(DeliveryTask t) {
    Endpoint ep = endpoints.get(t.endpointId());
    if (ep.status() != Status.ACTIVE) { deliveries.park(t); return; }
    if (!endpointLimiter.tryAcquire(ep.id())) { queue.requeueLater(t, Duration.ofSeconds(2)); return; }
    if (!breaker(ep).allowRequest()) { deliveries.scheduleRetry(t, nextBackoff(t)); return; }
    String body = events.payloadJson(t.eventId(), ep.apiVersion()); long ts = clock.epochSeconds();
    String sig = "t=" + ts + ",v1=" + Hex.encode(Hmac.sha256(ep.secret(), ts + "." + body));
    try {
      HttpResult r = safeHttp.post(ep.url(), body, Map.of("X-Signature", sig, "X-Event-Id", t.eventId()), Duration.ofSeconds(8));   // SSRF-safe client
      attempts.record(t, r);
      if (r.is2xx()) { deliveries.succeed(t); breaker(ep).recordSuccess(); }
      else if (r.status() == 410) endpoints.disable(ep.id(), "gone");
      else onFailure(t, ep);
    } catch (IOException | TimeoutException e) { attempts.recordError(t, e); onFailure(t, ep); }
  }
  private void onFailure(DeliveryTask t, Endpoint ep) {
    breaker(ep).recordFailure();
    if (t.attempt() >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) { deliveries.fail(t); alerts.notifyOwner(ep); }
    else deliveries.scheduleRetry(t, nextBackoff(t));
    if (endpoints.recordFailureAndCheck(ep.id()) >= 100) endpoints.disable(ep.id(), "too many failures");     // auto-disable
  }
  static Duration nextBackoff(DeliveryTask t) { long base = Math.min(43_200, (long) (5 * Math.pow(3, t.attempt()))); return Duration.ofSeconds(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(base / 2, base + 1)); }
}
```

**Failure cases.** Worker crash mid-request: task visibility timeout expires, redelivered (possible duplicate; receivers dedupe). Queue backlog after outage: autoscale workers, throttle per endpoint to avoid a retry storm on recovery. Poison endpoint returning 200 after 30 s: timeouts cap worker occupancy. Huge payloads: size cap (e.g. 256 KB), send thin events. Secret leak: rotation with dual validity. Region outage: events are durable in Kafka and DB, replay from the outbox. Customer requests bulk resend: rate-limited replay from stored events.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *Exactly-once?* Impossible over HTTP; at-least-once with event ids. (2) *How do you guarantee order?* You do not; use sequence/timestamps and state fetch; per-endpoint serial delivery if truly required at the cost of head-of-line blocking. (3) *How do you protect internal networks?* SSRF controls and egress isolation. (4) *How do you handle a customer endpoint taking 20 s?* Short timeout, treat as failure, retry later; encourage 'ack fast, process async'. (5) *How do customers test?* Test events, event log with resend, CLI tunnels.

**Summary.** Outbox to Kafka, per-endpoint tasks, isolated queues with concurrency and rate caps, signed requests with replay protection, exponential backoff for days with a circuit breaker, SSRF-safe HTTP client, delivery logs and replay, and receivers dedupe by event id.

## C. Social and communication

### Q35. Instagram

- **Idea:** photo/video sharing + follow graph + feed + stories. It is Q6 (feed) plus heavy media handling.
- **HLD:** upload -> object store -> async pipeline (resize to several sizes, strip metadata, moderation, thumbnails) -> CDN. Feed = hybrid fan-out (push for normal users, pull for celebrities) with ML ranking. **Stories** = items with 24-hour TTL stored per user, shown as a tray ordered by recency/affinity. Explore = recommendation system (Q67). Likes/comments counters via Redis + batched DB writes.
- **Data / LLD:** `posts(post_id Snowflake, user_id, media_refs, caption, created_at)`, `follows`, `likes(post_id, user_id)`; store only ids in feeds and hydrate.
- **Watch out:** media storage and egress cost, celebrity fan-out, hashtag search index, content moderation, stories expiry via TTL/lifecycle.

#### Q35 in depth: Instagram

**Scope.** Photo/video sharing with follow graph, home feed, stories (24 h), explore/recommendations, likes and comments, direct messages, notifications, search. The unique parts compared with the generic feed (Q6) are **media handling at scale, stories expiry, explore ranking, and the read-heavy image delivery path**.

**Requirements and scale.** 500M DAU, 100M photos/videos uploaded per day. Average photo 2 MB original; after processing (3-4 renditions + thumbnails) \~3 MB total: 100M x 3 MB = **300 TB/day, \~110 PB/year**. Views: each user opens the feed \~8 times/day x 20 items = 80B media views/day = 920k/s, almost all served by the CDN. Posting is rare compared with viewing (read:write about 100:1 or more).

**Upload flow (async, resumable).**

1. Client requests an upload slot: `POST /media` returns `media_id` and a pre-signed URL to object storage.
2. Client uploads directly (chunked, resumable) after on-device compression and EXIF stripping options; metadata call `POST /posts {media_id, caption, location, tags}` is made only after upload completes, with an idempotency key.
3. A message on Kafka triggers the **media pipeline**: virus/CSAM/nudity moderation scan (hash matching + classifier), resize into renditions (150, 320, 640, 1080 px), WebP/AVIF encoding, blurhash/dominant color placeholder, face/object tagging, video transcode (Q9) into HLS ladder. The post becomes visible when processing for the first rendition finishes (progressive availability).
4. Post metadata is written; fan-out workers update followers' feeds (hybrid push/pull as in Q6); search indexer and notification service consume the event.

**Storage layout.** Original in a durable bucket (kept for re-encoding), derived renditions in a CDN-fronted bucket keyed by content hash (`/m/ab/cd/<sha1>_640.webp`) with immutable cache headers. Metadata in sharded SQL/Cassandra: `posts(post_id, author_id, caption, created_at, media[], location)`; sharded by `author_id` for profile pages and indexed by time. Post ids are Snowflake-style (Q22) so id order equals time order.

**Feed.** Same hybrid fan-out as Q6 (push for normal accounts, pull-merge for celebrities), but ranking is dominant: candidate retrieval then a multi-stage ML ranker predicting like/comment/share/dwell time, with diversity rules and 'seen' suppression (a per-user Bloom filter or bitmap of recently seen post ids so the feed does not repeat). Pagination with cursors. Prefetch next page of metadata and the first rendition of the next images on the client for smooth scrolling.

**Stories.** Ephemeral media with a 24-hour TTL. Store in a time-bucketed table: `stories(author_id, story_id DESC, media, expires_at)` with TTL support (Cassandra TTL, or Redis sorted set with an expiry sweep). The **stories tray** (ordered row of friends with unseen stories) is built by: `followees with active stories` (a set per user updated on story post and expiry) ordered by affinity and unseen status. Seen state per viewer: `story_views(story_id, viewer_id)`; the author sees the viewer list. Delete media after expiry via a delayed job (Q24), but keep for archive if the user opted in.

**Explore.** Recommendation system (Q67): two-tower embeddings of users and posts, ANN retrieval of thousands of candidates, ranker, then policy filters. Fresh content needs an exploration budget (show new posts to a small audience, measure engagement, promote if good).

**Likes and comments.** Like: write `(post_id, user_id)` row (idempotent), increment a sharded counter asynchronously; show approximate counts; 'liked by friends' via intersection of the post's recent likers with the viewer's following (precomputed for hot posts). Comments: partitioned by post id, ordered by time or ranking, replies one level deep, with moderation and spam filters; load top comments first.

**Hot-key problem.** A celebrity post gets millions of likes in minutes: counters sharded across keys, writes batched, CDN caching of the post JSON, read-through cache with request coalescing, and per-user write rate limits.

**Search.** Users, hashtags, places: Elasticsearch fed by Kafka. Hashtag pages show top and recent posts: maintain per-hashtag sorted sets of top posts and a time-ordered stream; trending hashtags via windowed counts (Q68).

**Data model (core).**

```sql
users(user_id, handle UNIQUE, name, bio, avatar_media_id, is_private, follower_count, following_count)
follows(follower_id, followee_id, status ENUM('ACCEPTED','PENDING'), created_at)    -- two copies keyed by each direction
posts(post_id, author_id, caption, location_id, created_at, like_count, comment_count, deleted)
post_media(post_id, idx, media_id, type, width, height, blurhash)
likes(post_id, user_id, created_at) PRIMARY KEY (post_id, user_id) ; comments(comment_id, post_id, user_id, parent_id, text, created_at)
stories(author_id, story_id, media_id, created_at, expires_at) ; story_views(story_id, viewer_id, seen_at)
```

```java
class PostService {
  Post create(long author, UUID idemKey, CreatePostRequest req) {
    return posts.findByIdem(idemKey).orElseGet(() -> {
      Media m = media.requireReady(req.mediaId(), author);                       // uploaded + owned by author
      Post p = posts.insert(new Post(ids.next(), author, req.caption(), m.id(), clock.now()));
      outbox.add("post.created", p.id());                                         // fan-out, search, notifications consume this
      return p;
    });
  }
}
class StoryTray {
  List<StoryRing> build(long viewer) {
    List<Long> authors = graph.followeesWithActiveStories(viewer);                // maintained set per user
    Set<Long> seenAuthors = seenIndex.fullySeen(viewer, authors);
    return authors.stream().map(a -> new StoryRing(a, !seenAuthors.contains(a), affinity.score(viewer, a)))
                  .sorted(Comparator.comparing(StoryRing::unseen).reversed().thenComparing(StoryRing::score, Comparator.reverseOrder())).toList();
  }
}
```

**Failure cases.** Processing backlog: queue autoscale, serve original with lower priority renditions, show placeholder. CDN miss storms on viral posts: origin shield, coalescing. Partial upload: abandoned sessions garbage collected. Moderation false negatives: user reports, secondary asynchronous scans, takedown propagation by purging CDN keys. Feed cache loss: rebuild from graph + user posts. Privacy changes (account becomes private): filter at read time and purge fan-out entries asynchronously.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you store and serve billions of images?* Object storage, content-addressed renditions, CDN with long TTL. (2) *How do stories expire?* TTL storage plus a delayed cleanup job and read-time `expires_at` check. (3) *How do you avoid showing the same post twice?* Seen-state Bloom filters/bitmaps plus cursor pagination. (4) *How is the like count kept scalable?* Sharded async counters. (5) *Differences from Twitter?* Media-heavy, ranking-first, stories ephemeral, more private graph.

**Summary.** Direct-to-storage resumable uploads, async media pipeline with moderation and multiple renditions, hybrid fan-out feed with ML ranking and seen-suppression, TTL-based stories, explore via embeddings, CDN for nearly all bytes, sharded counters for hot posts.

### Q36. Slack / Discord

- **Idea:** workspace-scoped channels with real-time messages, threads, search, presence, file sharing.
- **HLD:** WebSocket gateways keep connections; messages written to a store partitioned by `channel_id` (Cassandra/Vitess-MySQL) then fanned out to online members via a **channel -> subscribers** routing layer (pub/sub over Redis/Kafka). Unread counts and last-read pointers per (user, channel). Search via Elasticsearch fed by Kafka. Large servers (Discord: millions of members): only fan out to *online and currently viewing* users, lazily load member lists.
- **Data / LLD:** `messages(channel_id, bucket(time), msg_id, author, content)` clustering by msg\_id; bucket by time window to avoid unbounded partitions.
- **Watch out:** huge channels (fan-out cost), hot partitions, message ordering by id, permissions per channel/role evaluated on every read, edit/delete propagation.

#### Q36 in depth: Slack / Discord

**What differs from WhatsApp (Q5).** Slack is a **workspace** product: channels with history, threads, search over everything, integrations/bots, permissions, retention and compliance, and many people in a channel (thousands). Discord adds huge servers (millions of members), voice channels and presence at scale. Messages are stored on the server in plaintext (or enterprise-key encrypted) so they can be searched, edited and exported. Real-time delivery still uses WebSockets, but the data model is channel-centric.

**Requirements and scale.** 20M DAU, 10M concurrent connections, 1B messages/day (\~12k/s average, 50k/s peak), channels up to 100k members, messages edited/deleted/pinned/reacted, threads, file uploads, full-text search across years, unread counts per user per channel, mentions and notifications, bots/webhooks/slash commands, message history load p99 under 300 ms.

**Core entities.** Workspace (tenant) -> channels (public, private, DM, group DM) -> messages (with thread parent, reactions, attachments, edit history). Everything is scoped by `workspace_id`; tenancy is the natural sharding key for Slack (a big enterprise is its own shard), while Discord shards by `channel_id`.

**Message path.** Client sends over WebSocket: `{channel_id, client_msg_id, text}` -> gateway -> **Message Service**: authorize (membership), sanitize, assign `message_id` (Snowflake, Q22) which is also the ordering key within the channel, persist, then publish `message.created` on a bus. -> **Realtime fan-out** pushes to every online member subscribed to that channel (via the gateway fleet; gateways keep a map channel -> local connections; a pub/sub topic per channel or per shard), -> **unread/mention service** updates counters, -> **notification service** (push/email for offline users and mentions, Q13), -> **search indexer** (Kafka consumer), -> **webhooks/bots** (Q34).

**Fan-out at scale.** A message in a 100k-member channel must not become 100k writes to inboxes. Use **subscription-based fan-out**: the message is written once to the channel log; each gateway server subscribes to the channels its connected users are viewing/members of; one publish to the bus reaches each gateway once (N gateways, not 100k users), and each gateway writes to its local sockets. Users not actively connected pull on next open. Presence and typing events for giant channels are sampled or limited to nearby/visible members.

**Storage (Discord's well-known path).** Messages table in a wide-column store partitioned by `(channel_id, bucket)` where bucket = a time window (e.g. 10 days of Snowflake ids) so a partition stays bounded; clustering by `message_id DESC`. Read recent N messages = one partition read. Discord moved from Cassandra to ScyllaDB for latency and hot-partition behavior. Slack uses sharded MySQL (Vitess) keyed by workspace/channel. Hot channels (a launch announcement channel) are read-heavy: cache recent messages per channel in Redis (last 50) with write-through.

```
messages: PRIMARY KEY ((channel_id, bucket), message_id)  CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC)
  columns: author_id, content, edited_at, thread_ts, attachments, reactions(map), mentions(set), deleted
channel_members: PRIMARY KEY (channel_id, user_id) -> role, notif_pref, last_read_id
read_state: PRIMARY KEY (user_id, channel_id) -> last_read_message_id, mention_count     -- unread count = messages after last_read_id
user_channels: PRIMARY KEY (user_id, channel_id)                                         -- sidebar
```

**Unread counts.** Store only `last_read_message_id` per (user, channel); unread = count of messages with id greater than that. Maintaining exact counts for 100k members on every message is too costly, so keep per-channel `latest_message_id` (one write per message) and compute the badge lazily: if `latest_message_id > last_read_id` show a dot; exact numbers only for DMs and mentions (increment mention counters for the mentioned users only, which are few). Mark-as-read updates `last_read_id` and clears counters; sync across devices via the realtime channel.

**Threads.** A thread reply stores `thread_root_id`; the root keeps `reply_count`, `last_reply_at`, participant list. Thread view = query by `thread_root_id` (secondary table `thread_messages` partitioned by root id). Replies can optionally also appear in the channel.

**Search.** Index messages into Elasticsearch/OpenSearch partitioned by workspace (routing key) so a query hits one shard group; fields: text, author, channel, time, has:link, in:channel; **ACL filtering** at query time (only channels the user can read) via a filter on channel ids (cached per user) or per-channel document-level security. Near-real-time indexing (1-2 s lag). Handle edits/deletes by updating the index; retention policies delete from index too.

**Permissions and compliance.** Public channels (anyone in workspace), private channels (explicit members), shared channels across workspaces; org-level retention (delete after N days), legal hold, eDiscovery export, audit logs, SSO/SAML/SCIM, data residency by region. Enforce permission on every read path including search results and file downloads (signed URLs with membership check).

**Integrations.** Incoming webhooks (POST to post), bots via Events API (subscribed events delivered like Q34), slash commands (synchronous HTTP call with a 3-second response budget, deferred responses via response URL), OAuth scopes per app, rate limits per app/workspace/method tiers (Q2).

**Presence and typing.** Ephemeral, TTL-based in Redis, delivered only to users currently viewing the relevant channel/contact list; batched every few seconds; for large servers show presence only for the visible slice.

**Voice (Discord).** Separate media plane: WebRTC/UDP to **SFU** media servers selected near participants; signaling over WebSocket; a channel's voice session is pinned to one SFU (cascaded SFUs across regions for large rooms); Opus audio at 32-64 kbps; only the speaking/active streams are forwarded (Q37).

```java
class MessageService {
  Message post(long userId, String channelId, UUID clientMsgId, String text) {
    access.requireMember(userId, channelId);
    return messages.findByClientId(channelId, clientMsgId).orElseGet(() -> {          // idempotent retry
      Message m = new Message(ids.next(), channelId, userId, sanitize(text), clock.now());
      messages.append(m);                                                              // durable
      recent.push(channelId, m);                                                       // Redis recent-N cache
      bus.publish("channel:" + channelId, new MessageCreated(m));                      // gateways fan out to their sockets
      mentions.extract(text).forEach(u -> readState.incrementMention(u, channelId));
      outbox.add("index", m.id());
      return m;
    });
  }
}
class Gateway {                                                                        // maintains channel -> local sessions
  private final Map<String, Set<Session>> byChannel = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
  void onSubscribe(Session s, String ch) { if (byChannel.computeIfAbsent(ch, c -> ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()).add(s) && byChannel.get(ch).size() == 1) bus.subscribe("channel:" + ch, this::deliver); }
  void deliver(MessageCreated evt) { for (Session s : byChannel.getOrDefault(evt.channelId(), Set.of())) s.send(evt); }
}
```

**Failure cases.** Gateway crash: clients reconnect and request `messages after last_seen_id`; no loss since persistence precedes fan-out. Bus lag: realtime delayed, history intact. Hot channel: Redis cache, bucketed partitions, sampled presence. Edit/delete races: versioned update with `edited_at`; deletes tombstone then purge. Thundering reconnect after outage: jittered backoff, resumable sessions (session id + sequence). Compliance deletion across stores: propagate to search index, caches, backups per policy.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How is ordering guaranteed?* Per-channel monotonic Snowflake ids assigned at the message service (single writer per channel shard). (2) *How do you handle a 1M-member server?* Subscription fan-out through gateways, lazy unread, sampled presence. (3) *Why not push to every user's inbox?* Write amplification; the channel log is the source of truth. (4) *How do you do search with permissions?* Workspace-routed index plus channel ACL filter. (5) *Edits and history?* Store edit versions; show latest, keep audit.

**Summary.** Channel log as the source of truth with Snowflake ids; WebSocket gateways subscribed per channel via a bus; unread via last-read pointers; bucketed wide-column or sharded SQL storage; permission-aware search; integrations as webhooks/events; SFU-based voice as a separate plane.

### Q37. Zoom / Google Meet

- **Idea:** real-time audio/video for many participants with latency under \~200 ms.
- **HLD:** signaling server (WebSocket) negotiates sessions (WebRTC SDP/ICE). Media goes over UDP. Topologies: **P2P** (2 people), **SFU** (Selective Forwarding Unit: each participant uploads once; the server forwards streams, no decoding; standard for group calls), **MCU** (server mixes into one stream; costly). Use **simulcast** (sender uploads 3 qualities; SFU picks per receiver) and adaptive bitrate. TURN servers relay when NAT blocks direct paths. Recording = SFU taps streams to a recorder -> transcoding -> object store.
- **Data / LLD:** `meetings(id, host, start, settings)`, participants, SFU assignment by region; cascade SFUs for very large meetings; only the active speaker + a few thumbnails are sent at high quality.
- **Watch out:** latency over throughput, packet loss concealment, bandwidth per receiver, geographic SFU placement, webinar mode with 10,000+ viewers via CDN/HLS.

#### Q37 in depth: Zoom / Google Meet

**The core problem.** Real-time audio/video between many participants over unreliable networks with latency under \~200 ms one-way. HTTP request-response is the wrong tool: media flows over **UDP** with **RTP/SRTP**, with adaptive quality and loss concealment instead of retransmission-based reliability (a retransmitted frame arrives too late to be useful).

**Requirements and scale.** 1:1 and group calls (up to 1,000 interactive, 10,000+ webinar viewers), screen sharing, chat, recording, mute/raise hand, virtual backgrounds, join by link/phone, waiting room, E2EE option. Scale example: 300M daily participants, 10M concurrent calls at peak; a typical 720p video stream \~1.5 Mbps, audio 40 kbps. 10M concurrent calls x 4 participants x 1.5 Mbps in = 60 Tbps ingest across regions, so media servers must be distributed globally and extremely efficient (forward packets, do not transcode).

**Topologies compared.**

| Topology | How | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Mesh (P2P)** | Every participant sends to every other | No servers for media, lowest latency for 2 | Upload = (N-1) streams; unusable beyond \~4 |
| **MCU** (Multipoint Control Unit) | Server decodes all streams, mixes into one, re-encodes per participant | Client downloads 1 stream, simple clients | Server CPU enormous (decode+encode), added latency, no per-viewer layout |
| **SFU** (Selective Forwarding Unit) | Each client sends 1 (or a few simulcast) stream(s) up; server forwards selected streams without decoding | Scales well, low latency, flexible layouts | Client downloads several streams; server bandwidth heavy |

Modern systems (Zoom, Meet, Teams, Discord) use **SFUs**, with MCU-like mixing only for legacy phones/recording.

**WebRTC building blocks.** *Signaling* (not standardized): clients exchange SDP offers/answers and ICE candidates over WebSocket/HTTP through your signaling service. *ICE/STUN/TURN:* find a network path through NATs: STUN reveals the public address (works for most home networks), **TURN relays** all media when direct paths fail (symmetric NATs, corporate firewalls; \~10-20 percent of calls). *DTLS-SRTP:* key exchange and media encryption. *Congestion control (GCC / transport-wide feedback):* the receiver reports packet arrival times; the sender adapts bitrate.

**Simulcast and SVC (the key to SFU quality).** Each sender encodes the video at 2-3 resolutions simultaneously (e.g. 180p, 360p, 720p simulcast) or as layered SVC. The SFU picks which layer to forward to each receiver based on that receiver's bandwidth and the tile size on screen: a participant shown as a thumbnail gets 180p; the active speaker gets 720p. When a receiver's bandwidth drops, the SFU switches to a lower layer on the next keyframe without involving the sender. **Active-speaker detection** uses audio levels (RFC 6464 header extension) so the SFU forwards only the top 3 audio streams and one or two high-res videos; others are paused to save bandwidth.

**Scaling beyond one server.** One SFU handles roughly 500-2,000 streams. A meeting is pinned to one SFU region node; large meetings use **cascaded SFUs**: participants connect to the nearest edge SFU; SFUs relay a limited set of streams between each other (tree topology), which cuts latency for geographically dispersed attendees. A **meeting router** (control plane) assigns the meeting to a data center and server based on organizer location, capacity and participant geography; it tracks load via heartbeats and can migrate meetings. Webinars (10k+): speakers via SFU, viewers via CDN with HLS/LL-HLS (5-10 s delay) or a WebRTC fan-out tree.

**Control plane.** Meeting service (create, schedule, links, passcodes, waiting room), auth, roster and permissions (host controls, mute-all), signaling gateway, presence, calendar integration. State per meeting (participants, host, recording) kept in memory on the SFU plus a replicated store (Redis/etcd) to recover if the SFU dies; clients auto-reconnect to a new SFU and renegotiate within a few seconds.

**Recording.** A recorder joins as a hidden participant (or the SFU forks streams), composes layout (grid/speaker) with FFmpeg/GPU, uploads segments to object storage, post-processes (transcode, thumbnails, transcript via speech-to-text, captions) and notifies the host. Cloud recording is queue-driven and idempotent (Q9 pipeline).

**Quality tricks.** Opus audio with in-band FEC and packet loss concealment; redundant audio packets (RED); jitter buffers (adaptive playout delay); NACK for small losses, FEC for bursts, PLI/FIR for keyframe requests; echo cancellation, noise suppression (ML), automatic gain control on the client; bandwidth estimation and resolution/frame-rate degradation order (keep audio first, drop video quality before audio, share screen at low fps/high resolution); network path probing and TURN over TCP/443 as last resort.

**Security.** Transport encryption (DTLS-SRTP) is hop-by-hop with SFUs seeing media; **E2EE** uses insertable streams: frames encrypted with a group key (derived via MLS or similar) that the SFU cannot read, at the cost of server-side features (cloud recording, transcription, some layouts). Waiting rooms, passcodes, host lock, authenticated joins; rate limit join attempts (Q2) to stop 'Zoom bombing'.

```java
class Sfu {
  private final Map<String, Meeting> meetings = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
  void onVideoPacket(String meetingId, Participant sender, RtpPacket pkt) {
    Meeting m = meetings.get(meetingId);
    for (Participant rcv : m.participants()) {
      if (rcv == sender) continue;
      Layer wanted = rcv.subscriptionFor(sender);                              // chosen from tile size + estimated bandwidth
      if (pkt.simulcastLayer() == wanted) rcv.send(rewrite(pkt, rcv, sender)); // rewrite SSRC/seq numbers so the switch looks seamless
    }
  }
  void onAudioLevel(String meetingId, Participant p, int level) { meetings.get(meetingId).speakers().update(p, level); }   // top-N speakers forwarded
}
class SubscriptionPlanner {
  Layer choose(double downlinkKbps, TileSize tile, boolean isActiveSpeaker) {
    Layer cap = tile.pixels() > 640 * 360 ? Layer.HIGH : tile.pixels() > 320 * 180 ? Layer.MID : Layer.LOW;
    Layer net = downlinkKbps > 2500 ? Layer.HIGH : downlinkKbps > 800 ? Layer.MID : Layer.LOW;
    return min(cap, net, isActiveSpeaker ? Layer.HIGH : Layer.MID);
  }
}
```

**Failure cases.** SFU crash: reconnect to another node, state from replicated store, 3-5 s interruption. Participant on bad network: downgrade to audio-only automatically. TURN overload: scale relay fleet, prefer direct paths. Region outage: meeting router steers new meetings elsewhere; live meetings reconnect. Echo/feedback loops: client-side AEC and mute-on-join. Abuse: reporting, host controls, ML moderation of shared content. Clock drift between audio and video: RTCP sender reports for lip-sync.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *Why UDP?* Late data is useless; retransmission harms latency. (2) *SFU versus MCU?* SFU forwards, MCU mixes; SFU scales better. (3) *How do you handle 50 participants?* Simulcast, active speaker, pagination of video tiles, forward only visible streams. (4) *What is TURN?* A relay used when direct NAT traversal fails. (5) *How do you support E2EE?* Insertable streams with group keys; lose cloud features. (6) *How do you minimize latency globally?* Edge SFUs, cascading, anycast/regional routing.

**Summary.** WebRTC over UDP; SFU architecture with simulcast layers chosen per receiver; active-speaker audio selection; ICE/STUN/TURN for connectivity; meeting router and cascaded SFUs for scale; control plane for rooms and permissions; recording as a hidden participant; adaptive bitrate, FEC and jitter buffers for quality.

### Q38. Tinder (matching)

- **Idea:** show nearby candidate profiles, record swipes, create a match when both swipe right.
- **HLD:** profile service + **geo-sharded** index (geohash/S2) to fetch candidates by distance/age/preferences; **recommendation/ranking** for the swipe deck, pre-generated and cached per user; swipe service writes `(swiper, target, direction)`; on right swipe check if the reverse right swipe exists (Redis set or KV lookup) -> create match -> notify both (push) and open chat (Q5).
- **Data / LLD:** `swipes` keyed by `(swiper_id, target_id)`; keep a Bloom filter or set of already-seen profiles per user to never show them again; `matches(user_a, user_b)` with `a < b` canonical order.
- **Watch out:** write-heavy swipes (billions/day), race when both swipe at the same instant (use atomic check-and-set or process by pair key to serialize), location privacy (fuzz distance), fake accounts.

### Q39. LinkedIn (connections, degrees of separation)

- **Idea:** 'Show 1st/2nd/3rd degree connections', 'people you may know', mutual connections.
- **HLD:** social graph store: adjacency lists in a sharded KV store or a graph DB (e.g. in-memory graph service partitioned by member id). Degree computation = bidirectional BFS limited to depth 2 or 3; mutual connections = set intersection of two adjacency lists. PYMK offline: friend-of-friend counts + ML scoring batch job (Spark), results cached.
- **Data / LLD:** `connections(member_a, member_b, created_at)` stored twice (a->b and b->a) so each direction is a single partition read.
- **Watch out:** super-nodes with 30K+ connections (cap, sample), 3rd-degree explosion (pre-limit depth or precompute counts), consistency for connect/accept, privacy settings.

#### Q39 in depth: LinkedIn (professional network)

**The core problem.** A **graph** product: members, connections (1st/2nd/3rd degree), a feed, 'People You May Know', jobs, search and messaging. The signature queries are graph traversals (mutual connections, degree of separation) which are expensive in a plain relational model at hundreds of millions of members.

**Requirements and scale.** 1B members, 300M MAU, avg 500 connections => 250B directed edges (connections are mutual, so \~125B undirected). Feed reads dominate (hundreds of thousands QPS), profile views, search, job applies, messaging. The connection graph must answer: is X connected to Y; mutual connections count; shortest path up to 3 degrees; 'People You May Know' (PYMK).

**Data model.**

```
member(id, name, headline, location, industry, ...)           -- sharded by member_id
connection(member_id, other_id, created_at)                  -- stored twice (both directions) so 'my connections' is one partition read
connection_request(from_id, to_id, status, created_at)
follow(member_id, target_id)                                  -- asymmetric, for creators/companies
position(member_id, company_id, title, start, end)            -- experience, drives PYMK/search
skill(member_id, skill_id, endorsement_count)
```

**Graph storage.** LinkedIn built a dedicated in-memory distributed **graph service** with the whole connection graph sharded by member id, replicated, and held in RAM (250B edges x 8 bytes per id is about 2 TB before replication). It answers `isConnected(a,b)`, `commonConnections(a,b)` and `distance(a,b,maxDepth=3)` in milliseconds. A 2nd-degree query is a set intersection or one-hop expansion: fetch A's connections (500), then each of their connections (500 x 500 = 250k ids) from the shards, deduplicated with a hash set. 3rd degree uses **bidirectional search** (expand about 1.5 hops from each side and intersect).

**Feed.** Similar to Facebook (Q35, Q11): candidates from connections, follows, groups and companies, plus out-of-network recommended posts, then **ML ranking** (Q67) using relationship strength, dwell time, comments and content type. Hybrid fan-out: normal members push posts to followers' feed stores; influencers are pulled at read time. The feed also dedupes seen posts, limits consecutive posts from one author, mixes ads (Q60) and applies integrity filters.

**PYMK (People You May Know).** Candidate generation: friends-of-friends ranked by **number of mutual connections**, plus shared company, school, location, imported contacts and profile views. Offline pipeline: a Spark job computes for every member the top-N 2nd-degree candidates using a self-join of the connection table, ranked by shared count, and stores them in a key-value store (`pymk:{member}`). An online service re-ranks with a model (probability that the invite is accepted) and filters blocked, dismissed or already-invited members. Incremental updates pick up new connections within minutes. Graph embeddings (node2vec, GNN) add candidates beyond two hops.

**Search.** *People search* ranks by network distance (1st degree first), name match, company, title, location and skills. It is a **federated search**: an inverted index (Elasticsearch or LinkedIn's in-house engine) partitioned by member id, with per-query graph-distance signals injected at query time (the searcher's 1st-3rd-degree set as a filter or boost). *Job search* has filters, location, seniority, recency and personalized ranking. Typeahead uses tries or prefix indexes (Q21).

**Jobs.** Job postings (employer/recruiter), job search and recommendations (member skills versus job requirements via embeddings), easy apply (application row, resume in object storage, status machine submitted -> viewed -> interview -> rejected/offer), alerts through the notification pipeline, and duplicate/fake job detection.

**Messaging.** InMail and chat built like Q5, with spam controls: rate limits on connection invitations and on messages to non-connections, premium credits.

**Data pipelines.** Everything emits events to **Kafka** (which LinkedIn created): profile views, impressions, clicks. Streaming jobs (Samza/Flink) maintain counters such as profile views and 'who viewed your profile'; batch jobs (Spark) do PYMK and model training; serving stores hold features for online ranking.

**Consistency.** Connections must be consistent for both parties: accepting creates both directed edges in one transaction, or via an outbox with an idempotent pair of writes. Counters like 'N connections' are eventually consistent.

```java
class GraphService {
  boolean isConnected(long a, long b) { return shardFor(a).contains(a, b); }
  Set<Long> mutual(long a, long b) {
    Set<Long> x = shardFor(a).neighbors(a), y = shardFor(b).neighbors(b);
    if (x.size() > y.size()) { Set<Long> t = x; x = y; y = t; }
    Set<Long> out = new HashSet<>();
    for (long id : x) if (y.contains(id)) out.add(id);                          // iterate smaller, probe larger
    return out;
  }
  int distance(long a, long b, int maxDepth) {                                    // bidirectional BFS
    Set<Long> fa = Set.of(a), fb = Set.of(b), va = new HashSet<>(fa), vb = new HashSet<>(fb);
    for (int d = 1; d <= maxDepth; d++) {
      if (fa.size() <= fb.size()) { fa = expand(fa, va); if (!Collections.disjoint(fa, vb)) return d; }
      else { fb = expand(fb, vb); if (!Collections.disjoint(fb, va)) return d; }
    }
    return -1;
  }
  private Set<Long> expand(Set<Long> frontier, Set<Long> visited) {
    Set<Long> next = new HashSet<>();
    for (long m : frontier) for (long n : shardFor(m).neighbors(m)) if (visited.add(n)) next.add(n);
    return next;
  }
}
```

**Failure cases.** Super-nodes (members with 30k connections): cap neighbor expansion or sample. Graph shard failure: replicas keep serving reads. Inconsistent connection state: reconcile via outbox and periodic audits. Spam invitations: limits and acceptance-rate signals. Fake profiles: detection models and verification. Search index lag: near-real-time indexing with bounded delay.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you compute mutual connections fast?* Sorted adjacency lists, iterate the smaller and probe the larger. (2) *How is the graph stored?* Sharded in-memory graph service with adjacency lists per member. (3) *How does PYMK work?* Offline 2nd-degree joins plus online ML re-rank. (4) *How would you show how you are connected to a 3rd-degree person?* Bidirectional BFS with caching. (5) *How does feed ranking differ from Facebook?* Professional intent, dwell time, creators. (6) *Why not just use a graph database?* Scale and latency; custom sharded adjacency stores beat generic graph DBs.

**Summary.** Sharded in-memory social graph for degree queries, offline Spark PYMK with online ranking, Kafka-driven pipelines, hybrid fan-out feed, federated people/job search with graph signals, and strict consistency only where two members' states must agree.

### Q40. Reddit (voting and ranking)

- **Idea:** posts and nested comments with upvotes/downvotes; ranked feeds (hot, new, top, controversial).
- **HLD:** votes are write-heavy: record vote events in Kafka, apply to counters in Redis; periodically recompute scores and write to DB; subreddit feeds are **sorted sets** (`ZSET`) keyed by score; comments stored as tree (parent id + materialized path) and loaded in pages with sorting.
- **Data / LLD:** **Hot ranking:** `score = log10(max(|ups-downs|,1)) + sign * (created_ts - epoch)/45000` favors new items that gain votes. Wilson score interval for 'best' comment ranking. One vote per user per item: `votes(user_id, item_id) UNIQUE`, update delta on change.
- **Watch out:** vote manipulation/brigading (rate limits, fuzzing counts), deep comment trees (collapse, lazy load), hot posts causing hot keys, eventual consistency of counts.

#### Q40 in depth: Reddit (voting, ranking, nested comments)

**The core problem.** Users post to communities (subreddits), vote up/down on posts and comments, and see lists sorted by **hot, new, top, controversial, best**. Comments are deeply nested trees. The hard parts: very high vote write rates on hot items, ranking formulas that change with time, rendering huge comment trees fast, and vote integrity (anti-brigading).

**Requirements and scale.** 500M MAU, 100M DAU, 20M posts/day is an upper bound but about 2M posts and 20M comments/day is realistic; 500M votes/day (\~6k/s average, 50k/s peak). Listing pages (home, subreddit, user) dominate reads: 100k+ QPS, almost all served from cache. Posts with 50k comments must still load in a second or two.

**Data model.**

```
post(id, subreddit_id, author_id, title, body/url, created_at, score, num_comments, hot_rank, removed)
comment(id, post_id, parent_id, author_id, body, created_at, score, depth, path)   -- path = materialized path '0001.0004.0012'
vote(user_id, thing_id, direction(-1,0,1), updated_at)    PK (user_id, thing_id)   -- one vote per user per item
subscription(user_id, subreddit_id)
```

**Voting path.** `POST /vote {thing_id, dir}`. Idempotent by design: the vote is 'set my vote to +1/-1/0', not 'increment'. Steps: upsert the row in `vote` (key user+thing); compute the delta versus the previous direction (e.g. from -1 to +1 is +2); apply the delta to the item's score. Writing the score directly on every vote is a hot row problem for a viral post (thousands of votes/s on one row). Solutions: (1) push votes to **Kafka** partitioned by `thing_id` and have a consumer **batch** them (aggregate deltas for 1-2 seconds, then one score update), (2) keep the live score in Redis (`INCRBY`) and flush to the DB periodically, (3) show approximate counts (Reddit even 'fuzzes' displayed scores to confuse vote-manipulators). The vote table remains the source of truth; counters can be rebuilt from it.

**Ranking formulas.**

- **Hot** (original Reddit): `hot = sign(s) * log10(max(|s|, 1)) + seconds_since_epoch_of_post / 45000`, where s = ups - downs. Log scale means the first 10 votes matter as much as the next 100; the time term means a post that is 12.5 hours newer (45000 s x 1) is worth 10x more votes. Because the formula uses the **post creation time**, not the current time, the hot score of a post is *static* once votes settle; no periodic recomputation needed except when votes change. That is why listings can be precomputed.
- **Top** (by period): sort by score within a time window (hour, day, week, year, all time).
- **New**: by created\_at.
- **Controversial**: high total votes with ups and downs close to each other, e.g. `magnitude = ups + downs; balance = min(ups, downs) / max(ups, downs); score = magnitude ^ balance`.
- **Best (comments)**: the **lower bound of the Wilson score confidence interval** for the up-vote fraction. It ranks a comment with 90 of 100 up-votes above one with 2 of 2, because it accounts for the uncertainty with few votes.

```java
static double wilsonLower(int ups, int downs) {              // z = 1.96 for 95% confidence
  int n = ups + downs; if (n == 0) return 0;
  double z = 1.96, phat = (double) ups / n;
  return (phat + z*z/(2*n) - z * Math.sqrt((phat*(1-phat) + z*z/(4*n)) / n)) / (1 + z*z/n);
}
static double hot(int ups, int downs, long createdEpochSec) {
  int s = ups - downs; int sign = Integer.signum(s);
  double order = Math.log10(Math.max(Math.abs(s), 1));
  return sign * order + (createdEpochSec - 1134028003) / 45000.0;
}
```

**Listings.** For each subreddit and sort, maintain a **sorted set in Redis** (`ZADD subreddit:{id}:hot score postId`), capped at the top 1,000 items (listings never paginate deeper). When a post's score changes materially, update its ZADD score. Top-by-time windows are rebuilt per window by a job. Home feed = merge of the user's subscribed subreddits' top slices (k-way merge by score, cached for a minute) plus a ranking/ads layer. Cache full rendered pages of anonymous traffic at the CDN with 30-60 s TTL; most traffic is logged-out.

**Comment trees.** Store as an **adjacency list plus materialized path**. To render, fetch the top N comments (e.g. 200) by sort order with limited depth, then show 'load more replies' stubs (`more children` placeholders) for the rest; clients fetch subtrees lazily by parent id. Pre-compute and cache the sorted tree per post (re-sorted every few minutes for hot threads). Collapse low-score branches. The tree is built in memory by grouping by `parent_id` in one query (`WHERE post_id = ? ORDER BY ...`), which beats recursive queries. Keep per-post comment counters via the batch counter path.

**Moderation and anti-abuse.** Per-subreddit mods with rules, removal queues, AutoModerator (rule engine on submit), spam filters (ML + link reputation), shadowbans, rate limits (Q2), karma thresholds for new accounts. **Vote manipulation / brigading:** detect vote rings (same IPs/devices voting together on the same targets, burst patterns), discount suspicious votes (still show them to the voter), and fuzz displayed counts. Votes of banned accounts are ignored in ranking.

**Search.** Elasticsearch over posts and comments, sharded by time and subreddit; near-real-time indexing via Kafka.

**Storage.** Reddit's well-known design uses Postgres with a generic 'thing/data' model, memcached and Cassandra for vote/listing data. A modern answer: sharded SQL or wide-column for posts/comments keyed by `post_id`, Redis for listings and counters, S3 for media, CDN for assets.

**Failure cases.** Hot post (front-page spike): vote batching, cached rendering, read replicas; degrade by freezing score refresh to every 30 s. Duplicate votes (retries): idempotent upsert on `(user, thing)`. Redis loss: rebuild sorted sets from DB by a background job; serve stale cache meanwhile. Comment tree explosion: depth and count limits with lazy loading. Race between delete and vote: removed items ignore votes. Clock skew in 'hot': use server time at creation only.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you rank 'hot'?* Log of net votes plus a recency term, computed from creation time so it is static between votes. (2) *How do you stop a viral post from killing the DB?* Queue plus batching plus Redis counters. (3) *Why Wilson score for comments?* Handles low-sample uncertainty. (4) *How do you store and load huge comment trees?* Adjacency list/path, top-N with lazy 'load more'. (5) *How do you prevent one user voting twice?* Primary key `(user_id, thing_id)` and set-semantics API. (6) *How do you detect brigading?* Graph/behavior clustering on voters, fuzzing, discounting.

**Summary.** Idempotent per-user vote rows as source of truth, batched counter updates, static-in-time hot formula, Redis sorted-set listings capped at 1,000, Wilson 'best' for comments, lazy-loaded comment trees, CDN caching for logged-out traffic, and layered anti-manipulation.

### Q41. Gmail (email service)

- **Idea:** send/receive email (SMTP), store mailboxes, search, spam filtering, labels.
- **HLD:** inbound: MX -> SMTP gateway -> spam/virus/phishing filters -> mailbox store; outbound: compose -> queue -> SMTP delivery with retries, DKIM/SPF/DMARC signing. Mailbox storage: per-user partition, messages as blobs in object store + metadata (labels, thread, flags) in Bigtable-like store. Search: per-user inverted index. Threading by `Message-ID`/`References` headers. Attachments to object storage with dedupe.
- **Data / LLD:** `messages(user_id, msg_id, thread_id, labels, flags, blob_ref, received_at)`; labels instead of folders (a message can have many).
- **Watch out:** spam (largest problem; ML + reputation), deliverability/reputation of sending IPs, strong durability (never lose mail), per-user quotas, IMAP/POP compatibility.

#### Q41 in depth: Gmail (email service)

**The core problem.** Email is an old, federated protocol (SMTP between domains, IMAP/POP3 or proprietary APIs to clients) wrapped around a modern product: huge per-user storage, powerful search, spam/phishing defense, conversation threading, labels, and very high reliability (never lose mail).

**Requirements and scale.** 1.8B users, 300B emails/day sent worldwide with Gmail handling a large share; a user stores up to 15 GB+ (avg maybe 5 GB) => exabytes in total. Per-user search in under a second across years of mail. Spam is about half of inbound traffic and must be blocked with very low false positives. Delivery guarantee: at-least-once with no loss, durable before acknowledging.

**Receiving mail (inbound path).**

1. Sender's MTA looks up the recipient domain's **MX record** (DNS) and connects to our **SMTP gateway** (many edge servers, anycast IPs, TLS via STARTTLS).
2. Connection-level checks: IP reputation, rate limits, **SPF** (is this IP allowed to send for the domain), **DKIM** (verify the signature over headers/body with the domain's public key), **DMARC** (policy when SPF/DKIM fail; alignment with the From domain), greylisting for suspicious senders, size limit (25 MB).
3. Content pipeline: virus scan, **spam/phishing classifier** (ML on content, headers, links, sender reputation, user-reported signals), attachment sandboxing, link rewriting/safe-browsing checks.
