**Requirements and scale.** 15M clients, 2M daily active traders, 10M orders/day (concentrated: 70% in the first and last hour), peaks \~5k orders/s, live ticks for 100k+ instruments streaming to 1M concurrent WebSocket clients, order placement p99 under 100 ms (platform side), exchange rate limits apply (e.g. orders per second per broker), regulations: audit trail, order and trade logs retained for years, margin rules (SPAN, peak margin), circuit-limit handling.

**Order path (OMS - Order Management System).** Client -> API gateway (auth, rate limit) -> **OMS**: validate (instrument active, lot size, price within circuit limits/price band, market hours) -> **Risk Management System (RMS)**: compute required margin/funds and check the user's available margin atomically -> blocks margin -> create order record (state OPEN/PENDING) -> send to the exchange via **exchange gateway** (FIX/binary over a leased line) -> asynchronous exchange acknowledgement (order id), then fills (trade confirmations) flow back -> OMS updates the order and **positions**, releases/adjusts blocked margin, notifies the user via WebSocket and push. States: PUT\_ORDER\_REQ\_RECEIVED -> VALIDATION\_PENDING -> OPEN -> PARTIALLY\_FILLED -> COMPLETE | CANCELLED | REJECTED, with a trigger-pending state for stop-loss orders.

**Margin and RMS (the correctness core).** Each user has a funds ledger (cash, collateral from pledged holdings with haircuts, margin used). Order placement must atomically `check available >= required` then `block`, otherwise two concurrent orders can both pass and over-leverage the account. Implement per-user serialization: keep each user's margin state on a single shard and process that user's risk checks in order (a per-user actor/queue or a row lock), so there are no cross-user locks and the hot path remains in-memory (Redis or an in-process cache with write-behind to the DB, or the DB as the lock). Margin recomputed on fills, on price moves for MTM, and at EOD; a **square-off** engine auto-liquidates intraday positions near close, and margin-shortfall positions get liquidated by risk rules. Options and futures need SPAN-style portfolio margin using exchange-provided risk arrays.

**Exchange connectivity.** One or a few persistent sessions per exchange (NSE/BSE), sequence-numbered FIX-like protocols with heartbeat and **resend-on-gap** semantics: the broker must maintain message sequence numbers and recover missed fills after a disconnect. The exchange rate-limits orders per second per member, so the broker needs a **throttler/queue** with priority (cancels and square-offs first) and a back-pressure message to the user when saturated. An order not acknowledged by the exchange has an **unknown state**: reconcile via the order-book/trade-book download API, never assume rejected (same lesson as payments, Q57).

**Live market data fan-out.** The exchange multicasts tick data (price/volume per instrument at up to many per second). A **tick processor** receives the feed, normalizes it, keeps the last tick and OHLC per instrument in memory, and publishes to a **pub/sub** layer (Kafka for history, Redis or a custom broker for live). **WebSocket servers** (e.g. 100-200 nodes at \~10k connections each) subscribe only to instruments that their connected users watch (subscription map: instrument -> set of sockets), and push binary-packed ticks (a compact format, not JSON) to the browser/app. Throttle to \~1 update/s per instrument per user for slow clients (conflation: send the latest value only), and send market depth only to users who opened that view. Because every user sees the same prices, the work scales with the number of (instrument, server) pairs, not (instrument, user) pairs, since each WebSocket server receives each tick once and fans it out locally.

**Charts and history.** Ticks are aggregated into candles (1m, 5m, daily) by a stream job (Flink or custom), written to a time-series store (TimescaleDB, ClickHouse, or a specialized columnar store) partitioned by instrument and time; the chart API reads from this store with aggressive caching of historical (immutable) candles in CDN/Redis. Live candle updates are appended from memory.

**Positions, holdings, P&L.** Positions (intraday/derivatives) update on each fill; holdings (delivery equity) update after settlement (T+1) from the depository (CDSL/NSDL) data. P&L = quantity x (LTP - avg price) is computed on the fly in the client/gateway from the latest tick (cheap), not stored per tick. Contract notes, tax P&L reports and ledger statements are batch-generated nightly.

**The market-open spike.** At 9:15 the system sees 10-50x normal traffic: logins, watchlists, order placements, chart loads. Defenses: pre-scaled fixed capacity (no autoscaling reliance), **aggressive caching** (instrument master, user watchlists loaded to memory at 8:45), stateless horizontal gateways, DB reads from replicas, avoiding heavy synchronous work on login, session tokens verified locally, rate limiting per user and per API, degraded modes (disable charts' indicators, limit heavy reports), and queue-based non-critical work. Order path is isolated on dedicated hardware so a flood of chart requests can never starve order placement (bulkheads).

**Data and compliance.** PostgreSQL as the system of record for orders, trades, ledger (partitioned by date), append-only audit tables, nightly archival, backups, strict access control, immutable logs for regulators, 2FA/TOTP and device binding for login, API keys with rate limits for algo traders, IP whitelisting for static IP rules, and kill switches.

```java
class OrderManagementService {
  OrderAck place(long userId, OrderRequest r) {
    validator.validate(r);                                                    // market open, lot size, circuit limits, tick size
    return userLanes.executeInOrder(userId, () -> {                           // per-user serialization (actor / striped lock)
      Margin required = rms.requiredMargin(r);
      if (!funds.tryBlock(userId, required)) throw new InsufficientMargin(required);
      Order o = orders.insertNew(userId, r, State.VALIDATION_PENDING);        // durable before sending
      exchangeQueue.submit(o, priorityFor(r));                                // throttled by exchange rate limit
      return OrderAck.accepted(o.id());
    });
  }
  void onExchangeEvent(ExchangeMsg m) {                                       // ack / fill / reject / cancel, sequence-numbered
    if (!dedupe.firstTime(m.exchangeSeq())) return;
    Order o = orders.byExchangeId(m.orderId());
    switch (m.type()) {
      case FILL -> { positions.apply(o.userId(), m); funds.adjustAfterFill(o, m); orders.markFilled(o, m); }
      case REJECT, CANCEL -> { funds.release(o.userId(), o.blockedMargin()); orders.close(o, m); }
      case ACK -> orders.markOpen(o, m.exchangeOrderId());
    }
    ws.pushToUser(o.userId(), OrderUpdate.of(o));
  }
}
```

**Failure cases.** Exchange session drop: reconnect, request retransmission from the last sequence, reconcile order/trade books. Order sent but no ack: unknown state until reconciled; block further actions on that order, never retry blindly (risk of double order). RMS cache loss: rebuild from the DB ledger before accepting orders (fail closed). Tick feed gap: use the sequence numbers to detect and request snapshots; display stale-data warnings. WebSocket node crash: clients reconnect and resubscribe with last-known state. DB failover during market hours: synchronous standby, drills before the market opens. Bad algos flooding orders: per-user rate limits and exchange-mandated algo controls.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you prevent over-leverage with concurrent orders?* Per-user serialized margin check-and-block, atomic with order creation. (2) *How do you stream prices to a million users?* Single feed ingest, per-server subscription maps, binary packing, conflation. (3) *What if the exchange doesn't acknowledge?* Unknown state, reconcile, never blind retry. (4) *How do you survive 9:15 AM?* Pre-scaling, caching, bulkheads, degradation, dedicated order path. (5) *Where is P&L computed?* On read from the latest tick and positions, not stored per tick. (6) *How do you handle square-off?* Scheduled engine with highest-priority order lane.

**Summary.** OMS plus RMS with atomic per-user margin blocking, throttled sequence-aware exchange gateway with reconciliation, tick fan-out via WebSocket servers using subscription maps and conflation, time-series candles, T+1 holdings from depositories, and a capacity-planned, bulkheaded design for the market-open spike.

### Q60. Ad click aggregation

- **Idea:** count clicks/impressions per ad per minute for billing and dashboards, accurately, at \~1M events/s.
- **HLD:** click servers -> Kafka (partition by ad\_id) -> **stream processor** (Flink) with tumbling windows (1 min), aggregating `(ad_id, window) -> count`, writing to an OLAP/time-series store (ClickHouse, Druid) -> query API. A parallel **batch path** (Lambda) reprocesses raw events from object storage to fix late/duplicate data (reconciliation); or use Kappa (replay the log).
- **Data / LLD:** dedupe with event ids (Bloom filter/state store); handle **late events** with watermarks and allowed lateness; fraud filters (bot clicks) applied before billing.
- **Watch out:** exactly-once effects for money (idempotent writes keyed by window), hot ad ids (salting then re-aggregate), time zones/windows, out-of-order events, storage of raw events for audits.

#### Q60 in depth: Ad click aggregation

**The core problem.** Count ad clicks (and impressions) per ad, campaign and time window, accurately enough to **bill advertisers**, fast enough for dashboards (seconds to a minute), at hundreds of thousands of events per second, while handling duplicates, late events, fraud and failures. Billing means the pipeline must be **exactly-once in effect** and reconcilable.

**Requirements and scale.** 1B ad clicks/day => \~12k/s average, 50k/s peak (impressions are 100x clicks: a billion-scale stream if included), queries: clicks per ad in the last M minutes at 1-minute granularity, top 100 most clicked ads in the last minute, filter by country/device/campaign; data latency under 1 minute for dashboards, billing accuracy and daily reconciliation, storage of raw events for audit and replay.

**Event and API.** Click arrives through a redirect: user clicks -> ad server logs the click and 302-redirects to the advertiser URL. Event: `{click_id (UUID), ad_id, campaign_id, user/cookie id, ts_click, ip, ua, country, placement, impression_id}`. The logging must be reliable and cheap: the log server writes to a local buffer, then to **Kafka** with `acks=all`; the redirect must not wait for downstream aggregation.

**Pipeline (lambda-style with raw log as truth).**

1. **Ingest:** click servers -> Kafka topic `clicks` partitioned by `ad_id` (so one ad's counts are processed on one consumer, but hot ads create hot partitions: add a salt `ad_id + random(0..k)` for hot keys and re-aggregate).
2. **Raw archive:** a consumer copies every event to object storage (Parquet, partitioned by date/hour) for audit, backfill and reconciliation. The raw log is the source of truth.
3. **Stream aggregation (Flink / Kafka Streams / Spark Structured Streaming):** deduplicate by `click_id` (keyed state with TTL, or a Bloom filter + state store), assign events to **event-time tumbling windows** (1 minute) using `ts_click`, aggregate counts per `(ad_id, minute[, dimensions])`, with **watermarks** (e.g. allowed lateness 5 minutes) to include late events; windows are emitted, then corrected by later updates within allowed lateness.
4. **Serving store:** write aggregates to an OLAP store (ClickHouse, Druid, Pinot) or a time-series table `agg(ad_id, minute, count)`; upserts are idempotent because the key is (ad\_id, minute\[, dims\]) and the value is the full window count (overwrite semantics), so reprocessing a window simply rewrites the same number.
5. **Top-K:** per minute, compute the top 100 ads: each aggregator keeps local counts, a global merge ranks them (Q68 for the sketch/heap approach; exact is feasible at this scale since distinct ads in a minute are bounded).
6. **Batch correction (reconciliation):** nightly Spark job recomputes exact counts from the raw archive, applies final fraud filtering and late data, and **overwrites** the aggregate tables and billing totals. Differences between the stream and batch results are monitored; billing uses the batch result.

**Exactly-once semantics.** Three places where duplicates arise: client retries/double clicks (dedupe by click\_id and a short cool-down per user+ad), Kafka producer retries (idempotent producer), and consumer reprocessing after failure. Solution: Flink checkpoints + transactional two-phase commit sink to Kafka/OLAP, or (simpler and robust) **idempotent writes**: since each aggregate row is a deterministic function of the events in its window, rewriting it is harmless. State: dedupe cache keyed by click\_id kept for the window plus lateness (memory bounded by \~ clicks in 6 minutes).

**Hot keys.** One viral ad could receive 10x average. Mitigation: two-stage aggregation: stage 1 partially aggregates by `(ad_id, salt)` in each worker, stage 2 combines partials per ad; a combiner reduces traffic before the shuffle.

**Late and out-of-order events.** Mobile clients may report clicks minutes late. Use event time, not arrival time. Watermark = max event time seen minus allowed lateness; events later than the watermark are sent to a **side output** (late stream) and applied by the nightly batch job. The dashboard shows the last few minutes labeled provisional.

**Fraud and invalid clicks.** Filters before billing: bot user-agents and known data-center IPs, abnormal click rates per IP/device/user (rate-based windows), click-farm patterns, impossible click-to-impression times, duplicate click\_ids, geography mismatches. Real-time rules flag in the stream (tag events `suspicious`), ML scoring in near-real-time, and the final decision in the batch job. Advertisers are billed only for valid clicks; invalid counts are retained for transparency. (Q61 expands on detection.)

**Query patterns and storage choices.** 'Clicks for ad X in the last 60 minutes' = 60 rows by key range; 'by country' requires dimensional rollups (pre-aggregate selected dimension combinations, or use an OLAP engine that stores raw-ish data and aggregates at query time with columnar scans). Retention: minute data for 7 days, hourly for 90 days, daily forever (downsampling jobs). Cache dashboard queries for 10-30 s.

**Capacity.** 50k events/s x 300 bytes = 15 MB/s on Kafka (trivial), 1.3 TB/day raw (compressed Parquet about 300 GB), aggregates: ad-minute rows, 10M active ads x 1,440 minutes = 14B rows/day if every ad is active all day, but sparse in practice; so choose a columnar store with good compression and TTL.

```java
// Flink-style pseudo-code
DataStream<Click> clicks = env.fromSource(kafka("clicks"), watermarks(Duration.ofMinutes(5)), "clicks");
clicks.keyBy(Click::clickId).filter(new DedupeWithTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(10)))       // keyed state, idempotent
      .keyBy(c -> c.adId() + "#" + (c.hashCode() % SALT))                              // hot-key salting
      .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1))).allowedLateness(Time.minutes(5))
      .aggregate(new CountAgg(), new WindowMeta())                                      // partial per salt
      .keyBy(PartialCount::adId).window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1)))
      .reduce(PartialCount::merge)                                                     // combine salts
      .addSink(new UpsertSink("agg(ad_id, minute)"));                                  // overwrite = idempotent
```

**Failure cases.** Consumer crash: restart from checkpoint, replay, idempotent upserts keep counts right. Kafka broker loss: replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2. Poison messages: dead-letter topic. Clock skew on clients: server-side receive time as a fallback and bounds check on ts. Skewed partitions: salting. Late data flood after an outage: batch correction. Double counting due to replays from archive plus stream: backfill jobs write to separate partitions then swap atomically. Billing dispute: re-run from raw logs for the contested window.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you ensure no double counting?* click\_id dedupe plus idempotent window upserts plus checkpointed processing. (2) *How do you handle late events?* Event-time windows with watermarks, allowed lateness, side output and nightly batch fix. (3) *What about hot ads?* Salted two-stage aggregation. (4) *Why keep the raw log?* Audit, replay, billing correctness. (5) *Stream or batch for billing?* Batch from raw for final numbers; stream for real-time views. (6) *How would you query by arbitrary dimensions?* OLAP engine (Druid/ClickHouse/Pinot).

**Summary.** Kafka ingestion with a raw archive as source of truth, deduplicated event-time windowed stream aggregation with watermarks and salting, idempotent upserts into an OLAP/time-series store, fraud tagging, and nightly batch reconciliation that produces the billable numbers.

### Q61. Fraud detection

- **Idea:** flag suspicious transactions in real time (under \~100 ms) with low false positives.
- **HLD:** transaction -> **feature service** (real-time features from a feature store: velocity counts last 1 min/1 h, device/IP reputation, geo distance from last txn, historical average amount) -> **rules engine** (hard blocks, e.g. blacklisted card) + **ML model** (gradient boosted trees) -> decision: approve / step-up auth (OTP) / decline / manual review. Features computed by streaming jobs; models trained offline on labeled outcomes (chargebacks), deployed with shadow mode then canary.
- **Data / LLD:** feature store with online (Redis/DynamoDB) and offline (warehouse) copies kept consistent to avoid train/serve skew; graph features for fraud rings.
- **Watch out:** latency budget, class imbalance, feedback delay (labels arrive weeks later), adversarial adaptation, explainability for regulators, fail-open vs fail-closed policy.

#### Q61 in depth: Fraud detection system

**The core problem.** Decide, in tens of milliseconds and before money moves, whether a transaction (payment, signup, login, order) is fraudulent, balancing **fraud loss** against **false declines** that lose good customers. Labels arrive late (chargebacks come weeks later), fraudsters adapt, and the base rate is tiny (0.1% or less), so the design combines rules, ML, graph signals and human review in a feedback loop.

**Requirements and scale.** 20k transactions/s peak, decision latency p99 under 100 ms in the synchronous path, features from the last seconds to the last years, explainable decisions for regulators and support, rules deployable by analysts without code releases, model retraining weekly or daily, case management for manual review, strict availability (a down fraud system must fail safe, not block all payments).

**Decision flow.**

1. Transaction request -> **Decision service** (called synchronously from checkout/payments, Q56/Q57).
2. **Feature assembly:** real-time features from a low-latency feature store (Redis/DynamoDB/Aerospike) plus request features (amount, merchant, device, IP, geo).
3. **Rules engine:** hard blocks (sanctioned entity, stolen-card list, velocity limits) and soft signals.
4. **ML scoring:** model returns a risk score 0-1.
5. **Policy layer:** combine score + rules -> `ALLOW`, `CHALLENGE` (3-D Secure/OTP/step-up), `REVIEW` (hold for manual), `DENY`; thresholds tuned per segment (amount, merchant risk, customer tenure) to hit a target precision/recall, expressed as expected cost: `cost = FN_loss * P(fraud) vs FP_cost * P(legit)`.
6. Decision, features and reasons are logged for audit, training and explanation.

**Features (the real differentiator).**

- **Velocity/aggregates:** count and sum of transactions per card/user/device/IP/email over 1 min, 1 h, 24 h, 7 d; number of distinct cards per device; distinct devices per card; failed attempts; new payee counts. Maintained by a stream processor (Flink) writing counters with sliding/tumbling windows into the feature store (key = entity+window). Computed in the stream and also exactly the same way in batch for training to avoid **training-serving skew** (use a shared feature definition / feature store).
- **Behavioral:** typing cadence, session length, navigation path, time of day, usual merchants/amount distribution (z-score vs the user's history).
- **Device and network:** device fingerprint, emulator/rooted flags, IP reputation, proxy/VPN/Tor, geo-velocity (impossible travel: two cities 2,000 km apart within an hour), SIM-swap signals.
- **Identity:** account age, KYC level, email/phone age and reputation, address/billing mismatch.
- **Graph features:** connected components of accounts sharing devices, cards, addresses or phone numbers; a new account linked to known fraud rings scores high. Computed offline (graph analytics, label propagation, GNN embeddings) and served as precomputed risk attributes per entity; fresh links updated incrementally.

**Models.** Gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost/LightGBM) are the workhorse (fast, tabular, explainable via SHAP); deep models/sequence models (RNN/Transformer over a user's event sequence) add lift; **anomaly detection** (isolation forest, autoencoders) for unseen patterns where labels are missing; a model per segment/region. **Class imbalance:** use stratified sampling, class weights, focal loss, and evaluate with precision-recall AUC and **recall at fixed false-positive rate**, not accuracy (a model saying 'never fraud' is 99.9% accurate).

**Labels and the feedback loop.** Labels: chargebacks (delayed 30-90 days), manual review outcomes (fast but biased), customer disputes, confirmed fraud ring takedowns. Problems: **delayed labels** (train on matured cohorts, correct for censoring), **selection bias** (you only learn about transactions you allowed; denied ones have no outcomes), mitigated by **exploration** (randomly allow a small percentage of borderline transactions to collect unbiased labels, with loss budgets) and counterfactual evaluation. Retrain regularly; monitor **drift** (feature distributions, score distribution, fraud rate) and use champion/challenger or shadow deployment before promoting a model.

**Rules engine.** Analysts write rules in a DSL/UI (`IF country != billing_country AND amount > 10000 AND account_age_days < 7 THEN REVIEW`); the engine compiles them to an efficient evaluation (e.g. Drools/Aviator or custom), supports versioning, simulation against historical data (backtest the rule: how many fraud caught, how many good customers hit), staged rollout (shadow, 1%, 100%), and instant kill switches. Rules complement ML for new attack patterns that appeared this morning before any model could learn them.

**Architecture.**

```
Checkout/Payments --> Decision Service --> [Feature Store (Redis)] + [Rules Engine] + [Model Server (ONNX/TF-Serving)]
        |                                  ^
        |                                  | real-time features
        +--> Kafka(events) --> Flink (windows, velocity, graph updates) --> Feature Store
                           --> Data lake (raw events, decisions, features at decision time) --> Training pipeline --> Model registry
Manual review UI <-- Case management <-- REVIEW decisions ;  analyst decisions --> labels --> training
```

The features used at decision time are **logged with the decision** (point-in-time correctness), so training sets reproduce exactly what the model saw, avoiding leakage from future data.

**Latency budget (100 ms).** Feature fetch 10-20 ms (parallel multi-gets, co-located cache), rules 1-5 ms, model 5-20 ms (small GBDT on CPU, or distilled NN), network 10-20 ms; use timeouts with default policies. **Fail-safe policy:** if the fraud service times out, fall back to a conservative rule set (e.g. allow low amounts for trusted customers, challenge others) rather than blocking everything or allowing everything.

**Similarity for fake content / reviews / duplicates (related use).** SimHash or MinHash with LSH over text; perceptual hashes for images; used for spam, fake reviews (Q51) and duplicate listings (Q55). SimHash: compute a 64-bit fingerprint where similar documents differ by few bits; candidate lookup via bit-sampling tables with Hamming distance threshold 3.

**Explainability and compliance.** Return reason codes (top contributing features via SHAP) for support agents and regulators; keep model cards and approval records; avoid prohibited features (protected attributes) and test for disparate impact; data retention and privacy controls.

```java
class DecisionService {
  Decision decide(TxnRequest r) {
    try {
      Features f = featureStore.assemble(r, Duration.ofMillis(25));                          // parallel gets with a timeout
      RuleResult rr = rules.evaluate(r, f);
      if (rr.hardBlock()) return log(Decision.deny(rr.reasons()), r, f);
      double score = model.score(f.vector());                                                // GBDT, ms-level
      Threshold t = policy.thresholdsFor(segmentOf(r));                                      // tuned on cost curves
      Decision d = score >= t.deny() ? Decision.deny(topFeatures(f)) : score >= t.review() ? Decision.review() : score >= t.challenge() ? Decision.challenge() : Decision.allow();
      return log(exploration.maybeOverride(d, score), r, f);                                 // small random allow for unbiased labels
    } catch (TimeoutException | RuntimeException e) {
      return log(fallbackPolicy.decide(r), r, null);                                         // fail safe, never block everything
    }
  }
}
```

**Failure cases.** Feature store outage: fallback rules; degrade to cached/segment-level features. Model drift after a new attack: monitor, ship an emergency rule, retrain. Label delay masking a new pattern: add short-horizon proxies (declined-then-retried, chargeback early signals). Adversarial adaptation (fraudsters probe thresholds): add randomness, rate limit probing, hide reasons from end users. Training-serving skew: single feature definitions, shadow comparisons. Over-blocking after a bad deployment: canary and auto-rollback on approval-rate drops.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you meet 100 ms?* Precomputed streaming features, parallel fetch, small models, timeouts. (2) *How do you deal with imbalance?* Weights/sampling and PR-AUC; recall at fixed FPR. (3) *How do you get labels?* Chargebacks, review outcomes, exploration for unbiased data. (4) *How do you catch new attacks quickly?* Rules with backtesting plus anomaly detection. (5) *What are graph features?* Shared device/card/address links, ring detection. (6) *What if the system is down?* Fail-safe fallback policy by risk tier.

**Summary.** Synchronous decision service combining a streaming feature store, a rules engine, ML scoring and a cost-based policy; delayed-label feedback with exploration; graph and behavioral features; point-in-time logging for training; and fail-safe operation with monitoring for drift.

### Q62. Coupon / discount engine

- **Idea:** apply promotions with rules (percent off, BOGO, min cart value, first order, per-user limits, global budget).
- **HLD:** promotion service stores rules (conditions + actions) in DB with caching; at checkout the engine evaluates applicable promotions on the cart and returns a discount breakdown; redemption is recorded atomically (counters per user and global).
- **Data / LLD:** **Strategy** for discount types, **Specification pattern** for eligibility rules (composable predicates), conflict resolution (stackable or best-of, priority). Redemption count: `UPDATE promo SET used = used + 1 WHERE id=? AND used < limit` (atomic). Single-use codes: unique-code table with `redeemed_by`.
- **Watch out:** race on limited-budget promos (atomic counter), abuse (multi-account, code sharing), rollback on payment failure/cancel (release redemption), explainability of the discount to the user.

#### Q62 in depth: Coupon and promotion engine

**The core problem.** Let marketing define discounts (10% off, flat 100 off, BOGO, free shipping, first order only, bank-card offers, user-specific codes) and apply them **correctly, fast and without abuse** at checkout. Hard parts: a flexible rules model, stacking and conflict resolution, **usage limits under concurrency** (only 1,000 redemptions of a flash coupon), per-user limits, budget caps, and preventing fraud, all inside the checkout latency budget.

**Requirements and scale.** 50M active users, 10k coupons/campaigns live, evaluation 20k/s at peak (cart view, checkout, and listing pages that show 'best offer'), flash coupons with a hard global cap, per-user once-only, validity windows, eligibility by user segment/product/category/payment method/city, p99 under 50 ms for evaluate, redemption must be exactly-once per order.

**Data model.**

```
promotion(id, type{PERCENT,FLAT,BOGO,FREE_SHIP,CASHBACK}, value, max_discount, min_cart_value,
          start_at, end_at, status, priority, stackable_group, budget_total, budget_used,
          total_usage_limit, per_user_limit, eligibility_rule_json, funding{PLATFORM,MERCHANT,BANK})
coupon_code(code PRIMARY KEY, promotion_id, assigned_user_id NULL, single_use BOOL, used_count)   -- generic or unique codes
redemption(id, promotion_id, code, user_id, order_id UNIQUE, amount, status{RESERVED,COMMITTED,RELEASED}, created_at)
user_promo_usage(user_id, promotion_id, count)                                                    -- per-user limit counter
```

**Rule model.** Eligibility is a boolean expression tree over a context: `cart.total >= 499 AND user.segment IN ('new') AND item.category = 'electronics' AND payment.bank = 'HDFC' AND city IN (...)`. Store as JSON/AST, compile to an in-memory predicate (Specification pattern, Part C), cache per promotion. Benefit calculation is a separate strategy (Strategy pattern): percent with cap, flat, tiered, BOGO per item, applied to eligible lines only. Keep **eligibility** and **benefit** decoupled so marketing can mix them.

**Evaluation flow (read path, no side effects).** Given `(user, cart, context)`: (1) fetch candidate promotions: auto-apply campaigns indexed by category/merchant/segment plus the entered code; (2) filter by validity window/status/budget remaining (approximate from cache); (3) evaluate eligibility; (4) compute discount per promotion; (5) resolve **stacking and conflicts**: each promotion has a `stackable_group` and `priority`; rules such as 'one coupon per order, plus one bank offer plus free shipping' are enforced by choosing the combination that maximizes customer benefit (or business margin) subject to constraints: a small knapsack/greedy search because the candidate set is tiny (under 20); (6) return applied list with amounts and reasons, and non-applicable codes with a human reason ('Add 120 more to unlock'). The evaluate call is idempotent and cached for a few seconds.

**Redemption flow (write path, must be exactly-once).** On order placement: **reserve** then **commit**.

1. *Reserve:* for each applied promotion atomically increment the global usage counter if below the cap and the per-user counter if below the limit. In Redis use a Lua script: `if used < cap and userUsed < perUser then INCR both; SADD reservations; return OK else return FAIL`. Because the script runs atomically, 10,000 concurrent requests for the last 100 slots yield exactly 100 successes. For code-level single-use codes, use `SET code:used orderId NX`.
2. *Commit* when payment succeeds (order CONFIRMED): mark redemption COMMITTED (durable in DB, unique constraint on `(order_id, promotion_id)` for idempotency).
3. *Release* on payment failure/timeout/cancel/return: decrement the counters, mark RELEASED. A TTL sweeper releases abandoned reservations (Q56 pattern). Returns/refunds can optionally restore the usage (policy-dependent, and some benefits are non-restorable).

Redis counters are the fast path; the database `redemption` table is the durable record and source for reconciliation (periodic job recomputes counters from COMMITTED rows and fixes drift). Budget caps work the same way with amounts: reserve `discount_amount` against `budget_total` atomically; with funding by merchant or bank, track spend per funding source for settlement.

**Flash coupons and hot keys.** A single counter key receiving 50k ops/s is a hot key. Options: shard the cap across N sub-counters (each with cap/N, with a fallback that steals from siblings when one is exhausted), pre-issue N **tokens** into a Redis list (`LPOP` = claim), or put an admission queue in front (Q42). Accept small under-use of the cap rather than any over-use.

**Unique and personalized codes.** Generate millions of single-use codes in bulk (random 8-10 chars from an unambiguous alphabet; collision-checked by unique index; or HMAC-signed so validity can be checked offline), pre-assign to users for referral or win-back campaigns; code lookup is a primary-key read. Rate limit code attempts per user/IP (Q2) to stop brute forcing. Referral programs: reward both referrer and referee after the first successful order (fraud checks on device/IP/payment instrument to stop self-referrals, Q61).

**Abuse prevention.** Per-user and per-device limits, new-account restrictions, same-address/payment-instrument detection, velocity limits on redemptions, anomaly alerts when redemption rate for a code spikes (leaked code posted on a deals forum), kill switch to disable a promotion immediately (status flag read from a cache with short TTL / pub/sub invalidation), and dynamic caps by risk score.

**Pricing integration.** Discounts are line-item allocations (proportionally distributed across items so returns/refunds and taxes compute correctly: e.g. 100 off a cart of 2 items priced 300 and 700 allocates 30 and 70), in integer minor units with deterministic rounding (largest remainder method so the allocations sum exactly). Tax is computed after or before discount per jurisdiction rules.

**Analytics and experimentation.** Every evaluation/redemption emits events to Kafka: uplift, incremental revenue, cannibalization, ROI per campaign; A/B test promotions (Q70) with holdout groups; budget pacing (spend evenly over the campaign window rather than exhausting in the first hour) via a pacing controller that adjusts eligibility probability.

```java
class PromotionService {
  EvalResult evaluate(Cart cart, User user, String enteredCode) {
    List<Promotion> cands = index.candidates(cart, user, enteredCode);
    List<Applied> ok = new ArrayList<>();
    for (Promotion p : cands) {
      if (!p.activeNow() || !p.eligibility().test(cart, user)) continue;
      ok.add(new Applied(p, p.benefit().compute(cart)));                       // Strategy: percent/flat/bogo
    }
    return stacking.resolve(ok);                                               // priority + stackable_group constraints, maximize benefit
  }
  boolean reserve(String orderId, Applied a, long userId) {
    Long r = redis.eval(RESERVE_LUA, keys(a.promoId(), userId, orderId), args(a.cap(), a.perUserLimit(), a.amount(), a.budget()));
    return r != null && r == 1;                                                // atomic: global cap, per-user cap, budget
  }
}
// RESERVE_LUA: if (GET used) < cap and (GET userUsed) < perUser and (GET spent)+amount <= budget then INCR/INCRBY all; SADD resv:{promo} orderId; return 1 else return 0
```

**Failure cases.** Redis loss: rebuild counters from the redemption table before serving (fail closed for capped promotions). Double submit of an order: unique `(order_id, promotion_id)` and idempotent reserve keyed by orderId (the Lua script checks `SISMEMBER resv orderId` first). Stale cache showing an expired promo: re-validate at checkout (authoritative). Race between evaluate and reserve (budget gone): reserve fails, checkout re-evaluates and informs the user. Misconfigured promotion (99% off): guardrails (max discount, approval workflow, anomaly alerts), staged rollout.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you stop a coupon being used more than its limit?* Atomic reserve in Redis Lua with durable reconciliation. (2) *How do you pick between stackable offers?* Constraint groups and priority; maximize benefit among valid combinations. (3) *How do you handle hot coupons?* Sharded counters or token pools plus admission control. (4) *How are discounts split across items?* Proportional allocation with largest remainder rounding. (5) *How do you prevent code brute-forcing/leaks?* Rate limits, long random codes, anomaly detection, kill switch. (6) *Evaluate vs redeem?* Evaluate is pure and cacheable; redeem is reserve/commit/release and idempotent.

**Summary.** Declarative eligibility rules plus pluggable benefit strategies, stacking resolution, atomic reserve-commit-release redemption with Redis fast path and DB truth, hot-key mitigation, abuse controls, and proportional discount allocation.

## G. Booking systems

All four share the BookMyShow pattern (Q11): **find availability -> temporarily hold -> pay -> confirm or release**, with an atomic conditional update on the scarce unit. What differs is the shape of the inventory.

### Q63. IRCTC train booking

- **Idea:** inventory is **seats per train, per date, per segment, per class**. A seat is free only for the segments of a passenger's journey; quotas (Tatkal, ladies, senior) and a **waiting list / RAC** that auto-promotes on cancellations.
- **HLD:** search trains between stations (precomputed route/schedule data, cached) -> availability query -> booking at the PNR level. Tatkal opens at a fixed time, so a **massive burst** (millions of users within a minute): virtual waiting room, captcha, rate limits, queue booking requests, heavy caching of availability (stale), and strict serialization of inventory per train+date.
- **Data / LLD:** `availability(train_id, journey_date, class, quota, available_count, waitlist_count)`; model each seat per segment as bits or use counters per class for simplicity. Booking = `UPDATE ... SET available_count = available_count - n WHERE available_count >= n` else waitlist. Cancellation triggers promotion: pick the next waitlisted booking (FIFO by booking time) and confirm it, with notification. Partition by `(train_id, date)`.
- **Watch out:** segment overlap logic (seat free for A->B but taken for B->C), payment timeouts holding seats, bots/agents, idempotent PNR generation, refund rules by cancellation time, CRIS-style legacy constraints.

#### Q63 in depth: IRCTC (railway ticket booking, Tatkal rush)

**The core problem.** A tiny, fixed inventory (seats on specific trains on specific dates) is demanded by a huge crowd at an announced moment (Tatkal opens at 10:00 AM sharp). The system must survive a **thundering herd**, never double-allocate a berth, support waitlist/RAC rules, and stay fair under extreme contention. This is the canonical **limited-inventory flash booking** problem (the same shape as Q65 hotels, Q64 flights, concerts).

**Requirements and scale.** 1M concurrent users at Tatkal open, \~25k booking attempts/s at the peak second, inventory for a train: \~1,000-1,500 berths per day over several classes (SL, 3A, 2A, 1A, CC); booking must be atomic across multi-leg journeys (a seat must be free on every segment between boarding and destination), payments via multiple gateways, bots/touts must be restrained, tickets issued exactly once, cancellations and refunds with rules, waitlist promotion.

**Inventory model: segment-based availability.** A train runs through stations S1..Sn. A passenger from Si to Sj occupies a berth for segments \[i, j). A berth is free for the request only if it is free on **all** segments in the range. Model: `seat_segment(train_id, date, coach, berth, segment_no, status)` or per-berth bitmask over segments (a 64-bit mask where bit k = segment k is booked): availability check = `(mask & requestMask) == 0`; booking = `mask |= requestMask` via compare-and-set on a version column. Berths are grouped by class and quota (General, Tatkal, Ladies, Senior citizen). Allocation algorithm picks a berth (preferring lower berth for seniors, contiguous for groups) among the free ones, minimizing fragmentation by choosing the berth whose free interval best fits the request (best-fit reduces future unsatisfiable splits).

**Booking state machine.** SEARCH -> SELECT -> HOLD (temporary lock on a berth for \~5-10 minutes while the user pays) -> PAYMENT\_PENDING -> CONFIRMED (PNR issued) | WAITLISTED | RAC | FAILED. Holds are atomic updates guarded by a version check and an expiry timestamp; expired holds are released by a sweeper and by lazy checking on read. Waitlist (WL) and RAC are queues per train/date/class with **chart preparation** hours before departure; on cancellation, the system promotes WL -> RAC -> CNF in order using the same atomic mechanism. PNR = unique booking reference; passenger records with ID type, age (age-based concessions and berth rules), and so on.

**Surviving the herd.** The tactics, in order of importance:

1. **Admission control / virtual waiting room:** at 9:58, users enter a queue with a randomized or first-come position; only N users per second are admitted to the booking flow (token bucket at the edge, Q2). This protects the core from 1M simultaneous requests and offers fairness; display position/estimated wait to reduce refresh storms.
2. **Separate read and write paths:** train search and availability display (reads, 95% of traffic) are served from an eventually consistent cache/read replicas (availability counts refreshed every few seconds, with 'subject to change' semantic), while booking writes go to the strongly consistent inventory store.
3. **Static content on CDN;** lightweight pages for Tatkal window; defer heavy features (offers, ads, history).
4. **Partition inventory by train/date:** every (train, date) is an independent shard; the hot trains (Delhi-Mumbai at 10:00) are contention hotspots, so give them dedicated capacity; use an in-memory/Redis-backed inventory service for hold decisions with a write-behind to the database, or the DB with row-level optimistic locking on small rows (bitmask per berth), which scales because contention is spread over \~1,000 berth rows rather than one counter.
5. **Short critical sections:** the hold step is a single conditional update; no network calls inside a lock.
6. **Anti-bot measures:** CAPTCHA (hard to be both secure and accessible), per-user session limits, device and IP rate limits, behavioral checks, identity-verified accounts, limits on tickets per user per month/Tatkal window, Aadhaar-linked quotas, and blocking known automation signatures; also detect agent/tout networks via shared payment instruments.
7. **Graceful failure:** fast clear errors beat timeouts. Failing fast frees resources. Retry-After hints and exponential backoff on clients. Idempotent booking requests with a booking-attempt id so refreshes don't double-hold.

**Payment handling is the weak link.** Gateways have limits; a payment taking 3 minutes can hold a berth. Mitigations: multiple gateways with routing and circuit breakers, a short hold time (e.g. 5-7 minutes), instant-payment methods (UPI/wallet balance/pre-loaded e-wallet to skip redirects), asynchronous confirmation with reconciliation (Q57 unknown state), and auto-refund when payment succeeds after the hold expired and no berth remains.

**Consistency of the critical step.** Pseudocode for hold with optimistic concurrency:

```java
class InventoryService {
  Optional<Hold> hold(TrainDate td, ClassType cls, Quota q, int fromSeg, int toSeg, int pax, String attemptId) {
    long req = segmentMask(fromSeg, toSeg);
    List<Berth> picked = new ArrayList<>();
    for (Berth b : candidates(td, cls, q)) {                                   // ordered by best-fit / preferences
      if ((b.mask() & req) != 0) continue;                                     // segment overlap -> not free
      boolean ok = db.update("UPDATE berth SET mask = mask | ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ? AND (mask & ?) = 0",
                             req, b.id(), b.version(), req) == 1;              // atomic compare-and-set on one berth row
      if (ok) { picked.add(b); if (picked.size() == pax) break; }
    }
    if (picked.size() < pax) { rollback(picked, req); return waitlistOrFail(td, cls, q, pax); }
    return Optional.of(holds.create(attemptId, picked, req, Instant.now().plusSeconds(420)));   // expiry
  }
  void release(Hold h) { for (Berth b : h.berths()) db.update("UPDATE berth SET mask = mask & ~?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ?", h.mask(), b.id()); }
}
```

Because each berth is a separate row, thousands of concurrent requests contend on different rows and only collide when targeting the same berth, in which case the loser simply tries the next candidate. Candidate lists are randomized slightly per request to spread contention (avoid everyone fighting for berth #1).

**Cancellation and refunds.** Refund = fare minus cancellation charges by time-to-departure rules; computed in a rules table; cancelling releases segment bits and triggers waitlist promotion in the same transaction/outbox sequence (promotion events processed per train/date in order using a single consumer partition to preserve queue order).

**Reliability.** Active-active across two data centers is hard with a strongly consistent inventory; use a single primary region per train-date shard with synchronous standby and a clear failover runbook; the cache layer and read replicas are replicated freely. Capacity is planned for the Tatkal burst and load-tested with realistic bot traffic; autoscaling won't react in seconds, so pre-provision at 9:30.

**Failure cases.** Duplicate booking via refresh: attempt id idempotency. Hold leak (user closes browser): expiry sweeper. Double allocation: eliminated by compare-and-set on mask+version. Payment succeeded after hold expiry: auto-refund or re-hold if available. Hot train DB overload: queue-based admission, shed load. Partial multi-passenger failure: all-or-nothing rollback. Chart prep errors: audit and idempotent promotion jobs.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you represent multi-leg availability?* Segment bitmask per berth; free iff mask AND request is zero. (2) *How do you avoid double booking?* Optimistic compare-and-set per berth row inside a short critical section. (3) *How do you survive the 10 AM rush?* Waiting room, admission control, read/write separation, pre-scaling, fail fast. (4) *How do you handle slow payments?* Short holds, fast payment options, reconciliation and auto-refund. (5) *How do you stop bots?* CAPTCHA, rate limits, device/identity checks, per-user quotas. (6) *How does the waitlist work?* Per train/date/class ordered queue, promoted on cancellation using ordered event processing.

**Summary.** Segment-bitmask inventory with per-berth optimistic locking, hold-pay-confirm state machine with expiry, waiting-room admission control and read/write path separation for the Tatkal herd, anti-bot controls, resilient payments with reconciliation, and ordered waitlist promotion.

### Q64. Airline reservation

- **Idea:** flights have fare classes (buckets) with seat inventory; overbooking is deliberate; pricing is dynamic (revenue management).
- **HLD:** search against schedule + availability (cached from the airline's inventory system / GDS); booking creates a **PNR** with held seats and a **ticketing time limit**; payment -> ticket issue; seat selection as a separate step. Revenue management service adjusts fare bucket availability from demand forecasts. Codeshare/interline add partner calls (Q4 adapters).
- **Data / LLD:** `flights(flight_id, origin, dest, departure, aircraft)`, `fare_inventory(flight_id, fare_class, seats_left)`, `pnr(pnr, passengers[], segments[], status)`, `seat_assignments(flight_id, seat, pnr)`. Seat map conditional update like Q11.
- **Watch out:** overbooking and denied-boarding compensation, schedule changes (re-accommodate), multi-leg itinerary atomicity (all legs or none), name change/refund fare rules, strict audit.

#### Q64 in depth: Airline reservation system

**The core problem.** Search flights across itineraries (multi-leg, connections), price them with **fare classes** that change with demand, hold a seat while the passenger pays, issue tickets, and handle changes, cancellations and overbooking. Two things make it different from IRCTC (Q63): **pricing is dynamic and rule-heavy** (fare buckets, taxes, ancillaries) and inventory is **counted per fare bucket**, not per physical seat, until check-in.

**Requirements and scale.** 1,000 flights/day per large airline, aggregators (GDS, metasearch) query 100x more than they book (look-to-book ratio 500:1), search must return in 1-2 s across many airlines, booking exactly-once, PNR (Passenger Name Record) lifecycle, seat selection, baggage and meals, schedule changes, codeshares, payments with 3-D Secure, regulatory data (API/PNR).

**Core entities.**

```
flight(id, airline, number, origin, dest, dep_time, arr_time, aircraft_type, status)           -- a scheduled instance per date
inventory(flight_id, cabin, fare_bucket{Y,B,M,H,K,...}, seats_available, seats_total, authorization_level)
fare(origin, dest, airline, bucket, base_price, rules{refundable, change_fee, min_stay, advance_purchase}, valid_from, valid_to)
seat_map(flight_id, seat_no, class, status{FREE,HELD,ASSIGNED,BLOCKED}, attributes{window,exit,extra_legroom})
pnr(id, contact, status, passengers[], segments[], total, payment_id, ticket_numbers[], created_at)
```

**Inventory by fare bucket.** An aircraft has 180 economy seats but the airline sells them in buckets at different prices: Y (full fare, always available), B, M, H, K (cheapest, limited). The **revenue management** system sets `seats_available` per bucket using demand forecasts so cheap seats sell out first: 'only 3 left at this price'. This is a *counter* per (flight, bucket), decremented atomically on booking (`UPDATE inventory SET seats_available = seats_available - :n WHERE flight_id=:f AND bucket=:b AND seats_available >= :n`). Physical seat assignment is separate and can happen later (seat selection, check-in). Overbooking: the airline sells more than capacity based on no-show forecasts (e.g. 105%), and denied-boarding compensation is a modeled cost.

**Search architecture.** Searching A to B on a date: find direct flights and **connections** (A to H to B) with minimum connect time and maximum layover rules. Pre-compute a **flight graph / schedule index** (nodes = airports, edges = flights by date), search with constrained shortest path (limit to 1-2 stops, respect minimum connection times, same-airline or interline agreements). Prices: do not call the fare engine for every candidate in real time. Maintain a **price cache** of lowest fares per route-date-cabin refreshed by pricing jobs and by real searches; availability is checked live only for the top candidates just before display (look-to-book ratio is huge, so caching dominates). Rank by price, duration, stops, airline preferences, and deliver in 1-2 seconds with a time budget per supplier (stop waiting for slow airlines and show what you have).

**Pricing engine.** Fare = base fare for the bucket + taxes and fees (per airport/country) + fuel surcharge + ancillaries. Rules: advance purchase (21 days), minimum stay, Saturday-night stay, refundability, change penalties, child/infant discounts. Dynamic pricing reacts to demand via the revenue management system adjusting bucket availability (and sometimes the fare itself). The result of a search is a **priced offer** with an `offer_id` and expiry (usually 15-30 minutes); booking references the offer so the price is honored, but availability is re-confirmed at booking time.

**Booking flow.**

1. Select an offer -> **price/availability recheck** (airline inventory call; offers can become stale).
2. Create a **PNR** in HOLD status: decrement bucket counters for each segment atomically (all segments or none; multi-segment booking is a mini-saga: if segment 2 fails, release segment 1 inventory). Hold timer (e.g. 15 min to 24-48 h for 'hold fare' products).
3. Collect passenger data (names as on passport, DOB, passport details, contact), ancillaries, seats.
4. Payment (Q57) with 3-D Secure; on success **issue tickets** (e-ticket numbers) and mark PNR CONFIRMED; on failure/expiry release the inventory.
5. Notifications (confirmation, itinerary, calendar), loyalty accrual.

Idempotency key per booking attempt; payment-uncertain handling as in Q56/Q57; if payment succeeds but the inventory was lost during a long hold, the system re-checks and either re-books at the same price or refunds automatically.

**Seat selection.** Seat maps are a per-flight grid; selecting a seat uses a short lock (hold 5-10 min) via compare-and-set on the seat row `status FREE -> HELD(user, expiry)`, then ASSIGNED when the PNR is confirmed. Paid/preferred seats are priced individually. Auto-assignment at check-in fills gaps and keeps families together. Same optimistic-locking pattern as Q63.

**Distribution and consistency across systems.** Airlines expose inventory through GDS (Amadeus, Sabre) or direct NDC/API channels. Inventory is held in the airline's **PSS** (passenger service system), the source of truth; aggregators cache and revalidate. Always treat external inventory as eventually consistent and handle `SOLD_OUT` responses at the last step with fallback offers. Schedule changes (retiming, cancellations) arrive as events and trigger re-accommodation workflows and notifications.

**Changes, cancellations and disruptions.** Change = cancel+rebook with fare-rule calculation (difference + penalty); refund by rules into original payment (ledger entries, Q57); airline cancellations trigger bulk re-accommodation: find alternatives for thousands of passengers, prioritize by status/fare/connection, send self-service links; compensation rules by regulation.

**Scaling and reliability.** Shard inventory and PNRs by flight (inventory) and by PNR id (bookings); read-heavy search on replicas/caches; strict ACID for inventory decrements within a flight (counter rows are modest contention: use per-bucket counters and optimistic retries, or serialize per flight through a partitioned queue). Peak events (sale launches) use a waiting room (Q42/Q63). Geographic redundancy with a primary region per flight shard.

```java
class BookingService {
  @Transactional
  Pnr hold(OfferId offer, List<Passenger> pax, String idemKey) {
    return pnrs.byIdem(idemKey).orElseGet(() -> {
      Offer o = offers.requireValid(offer);                                                   // price lock window
      List<SegmentInventory> taken = new ArrayList<>();
      for (Segment s : o.segments()) {
        int rows = inventory.decrement(s.flightId(), s.bucket(), pax.size());                  // conditional UPDATE (>= n)
        if (rows == 0) { taken.forEach(t -> inventory.increment(t.flightId(), t.bucket(), pax.size())); throw new SoldOut(s); }
        taken.add(new SegmentInventory(s.flightId(), s.bucket()));
      }
      return pnrs.create(o, pax, Instant.now().plus(Duration.ofMinutes(15)), idemKey);          // status = HELD
    });
  }
  void ticket(Pnr p, PaymentResult pay) {
    if (p.expired()) { refunds.auto(pay); return; }
    tickets.issue(p); pnrs.confirm(p.id()); outbox.add(new Ticketed(p.id()));
  }
}
```

**Failure cases.** Offer stale at booking: recheck and present the new price. Partial multi-segment failure: compensating increments. Double booking on retries: idempotency key. Payment after hold expiry: re-check or auto-refund. GDS timeouts: circuit breaker, show cached results flagged 'price may change'. Duplicate passenger bookings: duplicate PNR detection rules. Overbooked flight at departure: voluntary compensation workflow first.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How is inventory modeled?* Counters per fare bucket per flight; seats assigned later. (2) *How do you search connections quickly?* Schedule graph with constraints plus a price cache; live recheck of the top results. (3) *How do you keep prices honest?* Offers with expiry; recheck at booking. (4) *How do you handle multi-leg atomicity?* Mini-saga with compensating releases. (5) *What is overbooking?* Selling beyond capacity using no-show forecasts. (6) *How do you scale search vs booking?* Cache and replicas for search; consistent counters for booking.

**Summary.** Fare-bucket counters with revenue management, cached price/schedule search with live revalidation, priced offers with expiry, PNR hold-pay-ticket state machine with multi-segment compensation, optimistic seat locking, and external-system eventual consistency handling.

### Q65. Hotel booking (MakeMyTrip / Booking.com)

- **Idea:** inventory = **room types per night**, not specific rooms (assign the room at check-in). A stay of N nights needs availability on all N dates.
- **HLD:** supply via channel managers/APIs (rate and availability pushed or pulled) + own contracts; search by city + dates + guests with filters (Elasticsearch + availability service + price cache); booking: hold -> pay -> confirm with the hotel's system. Rates vary by date, occupancy, meal plan, cancellation policy.
- **Data / LLD:** `room_inventory(hotel_id, room_type, date, total, booked)` PK(hotel, room\_type, date). Book N nights = update N rows each `booked < total` in one transaction (all or nothing). Rate plans separate from inventory.
- **Watch out:** overbooking policy (some hotels allow), stale cached rates (re-validate at checkout), time zones for date boundaries, partial-night failures, payments at hotel vs prepaid, commission/ranking incentives.

#### Q65 in depth: Hotel booking (rooms, dates, overbooking)

**The core problem.** Sell hotel rooms by **room type per night** over date ranges. Search shows availability and price per night; booking must not oversell a room type on any night in the stay; rates vary by day, channel and rules; cancellations and modifications are common. Structurally similar to Airbnb (Q50) and flights (Q64), but inventory is **fungible per room type** (any Deluxe room, not a specific one until check-in).

**Requirements and scale.** 1M hotels, 50 room types each, 365-day horizon => \~18B (hotel, room type, date) inventory cells at most; search QPS 50k (look-to-book 100:1), bookings 100/s average and 1k/s at peak sales, multi-night stays (1-30), exactly-once bookings, overbooking policy, rate plans (refundable, non-refundable, breakfast included), multi-currency, channels (direct, OTAs, corporate), and integration with each hotel's property management system (PMS).

**Inventory model: counters per room type per night.**

```
room_type(id, hotel_id, name, capacity, total_rooms)
inventory(hotel_id, room_type_id, date, total, booked, held, blocked)            -- PK (room_type_id, date)
   available = total - booked - held - blocked   (+ overbooking allowance)
rate(room_type_id, date, rate_plan_id, price, min_stay, max_stay, closed_to_arrival)
reservation(id, hotel_id, room_type_id, check_in, check_out, rooms, guest, status, rate_plan_id, total_price, version)
```

Because rooms of a type are interchangeable, a **counter per (room type, date)** is enough, and a booking decrements every night in the stay in one transaction:

```sql
UPDATE inventory SET held = held + :n
 WHERE room_type_id = :rt AND date >= :checkin AND date < :checkout AND total - booked - held - blocked >= :n;
-- success iff updated_rows == number_of_nights  (otherwise ROLLBACK)
```

If any night lacks capacity the row count is short and the whole transaction rolls back (all-or-nothing). Dates for one room type live in one shard (partition by `room_type_id` or hotel), so the multi-night update is a single-shard transaction. Contention occurs per (room type, night); popular nights on popular hotels are the hot rows, but the update is tiny; use short transactions and retries with jitter.

**Hold, confirm, release.** Booking path: HOLD (increment `held`, reservation PENDING with expiry 10-15 min) -> payment (Q57) -> CONFIRM (decrement `held`, increment `booked`) or RELEASE (decrement `held`) on failure/expiry. A sweeper releases expired holds; it must be idempotent. Cancellation: decrement `booked` for each night; refund per rate-plan rules (non-refundable gets nothing, free cancellation until 24-48 h before check-in); late cancellation fees calculated from rules tables.

**Overbooking.** Hotels expect cancellations and no-shows, so they allow `booked` to exceed `total` by an overbooking factor per hotel/room type/date (e.g. 3-5% on high-demand nights, learned from historical no-show rates). Implementation: `available = total * (1 + overbookingFactor) - booked - held - blocked`. At check-in, if all rooms are taken, the hotel 'walks' the guest to a comparable hotel at the hotel's cost. Revenue management tunes the factor to maximize expected revenue minus walk cost. Keep this configurable per property and visible to the booking engine only, never to guests.

**Pricing.** Price per night per rate plan from the rate table, with rules: minimum stay, closed to arrival/departure, day-of-week and seasonality, length-of-stay discounts, early-bird, last-minute, member rates, taxes, resort fees. Dynamic pricing from demand forecasts adjusts rates (price API for revenue managers; changes pushed via the hotel's channel manager). Prices shown at search time come from a **price cache**; the exact quote (including taxes) is recomputed and locked at checkout with expiry (Q56 pattern).

**Search.** Query: destination (geo/city/POI), dates, guests, filters. Two-phase: (1) candidate hotels from a geo+attribute search index (Q50/Q51) ranked by quality; (2) for the top few hundred, check **availability and the cheapest rate for the whole stay** from a denormalized `availability_summary(hotel_id, date -> min_price, available_flag by room type)` cache (Redis or in-memory). For a stay of k nights, compute availability as the AND over nights (bitmaps per room type, compressed) and total price as the sum of per-night min prices. The cache is updated by events from inventory/rate changes within seconds and accepted as slightly stale; availability is **re-verified at booking**.

**Hotel integrations (the messy reality).** Hotels use a PMS and a channel manager that sync inventory to all OTAs (Booking.com, Expedia, direct site). The system of record for availability is often external, so integrations use push (availability/rate updates, ARI = availability, rates, inventory) and pull, with reconciliation jobs; bookings are sent to the PMS and may fail asynchronously (the hotel cannot honor it): handle with retries, escalation, alternatives and free cancellation. Idempotent booking messages with the reservation id.

**Group bookings and special cases.** Blocks for conferences (allotments with release dates), corporate negotiated rates, multi-room bookings (n rooms in the same update), assigning specific room numbers at check-in (an offline assignment algorithm satisfying preferences; fits the interval-scheduling/graph-coloring family), mixed room types, no-show handling, early checkout adjustments.

**Consistency and scaling.** Strong consistency for inventory updates within a hotel shard, eventual consistency for search caches and read models; use CQRS: write model = inventory/reservations (SQL), read model = search index/caches updated through events (outbox + Kafka). Shard by hotel\_id (or region); replicas for reads. Peak sales (Black Friday, flash deals): rate-limit, queue holds, show 'x people viewing' only as a UI nudge.

```java
class HotelBookingService {
  @Transactional
  Reservation hold(long roomTypeId, LocalDate in, LocalDate out, int rooms, String idemKey) {
    return reservations.byIdem(idemKey).orElseGet(() -> {
      int nights = (int) ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(in, out);
      int updated = jdbc.update("UPDATE inventory SET held = held + ? WHERE room_type_id = ? AND date >= ? AND date < ? " +
                                "AND total + overbook - booked - held - blocked >= ?", rooms, roomTypeId, in, out, rooms);
      if (updated != nights) throw new NoAvailability();                          // @Transactional rolls the partial update back
      return reservations.insertPending(roomTypeId, in, out, rooms, Instant.now().plus(Duration.ofMinutes(12)), idemKey);
    });
  }
  @Transactional void confirm(long resId) {
    Reservation r = reservations.lock(resId);
    if (r.status() != PENDING || r.expired()) { release(r); return; }
    jdbc.update("UPDATE inventory SET held = held - ?, booked = booked + ? WHERE room_type_id = ? AND date >= ? AND date < ?", r.rooms(), r.rooms(), r.roomTypeId(), r.checkIn(), r.checkOut());
    reservations.setStatus(resId, CONFIRMED); outbox.add(new ReservationConfirmed(resId));
  }
}
```

**Failure cases.** Concurrent bookings of the last room: the conditional update admits exactly one. Payment after hold expiry: re-hold if still available, else refund. PMS rejects a confirmed booking: alternative property workflow with compensation. Search cache stale (sold out): rejection at hold, show next best. Rate parity issues across channels: rate integrity checks. Clock/time-zone errors in dates: store dates as hotel-local calendar dates (not instants) because check-in is a property-local concept.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you avoid overselling a night?* Conditional counter updates for every night in a single transaction. (2) *Why counters and not rows per room?* Fungible rooms; assignment happens later. (3) *How do you search availability for a date range across many hotels?* Denormalized per-night summary with AND across nights; verify at booking. (4) *How do you handle overbooking?* Per-property factor from no-show history; walk policy. (5) *How do you integrate with PMS/channel managers?* ARI push/pull, idempotent messages, reconciliation. (6) *How is this different from Airbnb?* Airbnb's listing is a unique unit per night; hotels sell counts of interchangeable units.

**Summary.** Per-night inventory counters with all-or-nothing multi-night conditional updates, hold-confirm-release lifecycle, overbooking allowance, cached availability and price summaries with booking-time verification, CQRS read models, and robust PMS/channel integrations.

### Q66. Doctor appointment booking (Practo)

- **Idea:** doctors publish availability; patients book time slots; reminders; teleconsultation.
- **HLD:** doctor schedule (working hours, breaks, leave) generates **slots** (e.g. 15-minute) either materialized for the next N days or computed on the fly from rules + existing bookings. Booking = atomic claim of the slot (unique constraint `(doctor_id, slot_start)`), hold during payment, confirm, remind via notifications (Q13), reschedule/cancel. Search = doctors by specialty, location (geo), rating, next available slot.
- **Data / LLD:** `slots(doctor_id, start, end, status)` with UNIQUE(doctor\_id, start); `appointments(id, patient_id, slot, status)`. Variable-length appointments: range-overlap check using an exclusion constraint (Postgres) or lock the doctor's day row.
- **Watch out:** double booking from concurrent patients (DB constraint is the safeguard), no-shows/overbooking policy, time zones for tele-visits, waitlists, privacy (health data compliance), emergency slot priority.

#### Q66 in depth: Practo (doctor appointment booking)

**The core problem.** Match patients with doctors by specialty, location, availability and quality; let them book a **time slot** that is guaranteed not to be double-booked; support video consults, reminders, reschedules and no-shows; store sensitive health data safely. It is a scheduling problem (like Calendar, Q47, and meeting rooms, Q93) wrapped in a marketplace (Q50) with healthcare-grade privacy.

**Requirements and scale.** 300k doctors, 30M MAU, 500k appointments/day, search QPS 5k, booking QPS peaks \~200/s (morning slots open), slot granularity 10-30 min, clinics with multiple doctors/rooms, doctors with irregular schedules and breaks, walk-ins, same-day cancellations, SMS/WhatsApp reminders, video consults with a call link, ratings, payments (prepaid or pay-at-clinic), compliance (HIPAA/GDPR-like consent, India's DPDP), audit logs of data access.

**Data model.**

```
doctor(id, name, specialties[], qualifications, languages[], experience_yrs, rating_avg, rating_count, fee, consult_modes{CLINIC,VIDEO})
clinic(id, name, geo, address, phone) ; doctor_clinic(doctor_id, clinic_id, fee, working_hours_template)
schedule_template(doctor_id, clinic_id, weekday, start, end, slot_minutes, break_ranges)     -- recurring weekly rules
schedule_exception(doctor_id, date, type{LEAVE,EXTRA_HOURS,HOLIDAY}, ranges)                -- overrides
slot(id, doctor_id, clinic_id, start_utc, end_utc, status{OPEN,HELD,BOOKED,BLOCKED}, version)  -- materialized for the next N days
appointment(id, patient_id, slot_id UNIQUE, doctor_id, mode, status, reason, created_at, fee, payment_id)
patient(id, ...), consent(patient_id, doctor_id, scope, granted_at), medical_note(...)       -- encrypted, access-controlled
```

**Slots: generate, don't compute on the fly.** Weekly templates plus exceptions are the source of truth for the doctor's availability. A **slot generator** job materializes concrete `slot` rows for the next 30-60 days (and tops up daily), splitting working ranges minus breaks into fixed-length slots and marking blocked ones. Materializing makes booking a single-row compare-and-set and makes search simple. When a doctor edits their schedule, regenerate affected future slots: slots that already have appointments are kept and the doctor is prompted to reschedule conflicting patients (never silently delete booked slots).

**Preventing double booking.** The invariant is one active appointment per slot. Enforce it in the database: `appointment.slot_id` unique for active statuses (a partial unique index `WHERE status IN ('CONFIRMED','PENDING')`), plus a conditional slot update: `UPDATE slot SET status='HELD', version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND status='OPEN'` and check rows == 1. The flow mirrors Q63/Q65: HOLD for 5-10 minutes while the patient completes details or payment, then CONFIRM, otherwise a sweeper reopens the slot. If the same patient already has an overlapping appointment, warn (a patient-side overlap check). Rows are naturally partitioned by doctor, so contention only arises on a popular doctor's popular slots.

**Search and ranking.** Search by specialty/symptom/doctor name/clinic plus location and 'available today/tomorrow' filters. Index doctors in Elasticsearch with geo-points of their clinics, specialty tags, languages, fees, rating, experience, and a derived **next available slot** field per doctor (updated by events from the slot service, refreshed every minute; a rolling summary rather than the full slot list). Ranking blends relevance (specialty/symptom match: map symptoms to specialties with a lookup or ML classifier), distance, rating with Bayesian damping (Q51), availability soon, response/cancellation rate, and profile completeness; sponsored placement is clearly labeled. Query results show the next three slots from a cache; selecting a doctor loads fresh slots from the slot service.

**Time zones and display.** Store slot times in UTC with the clinic's IANA timezone; show local times; avoid DST bugs by generating slots in local time then converting (Q47). Video consults across regions use each participant's local zone.

**Video consultations.** Booking creates a video room via a third-party or in-house WebRTC service (Q37): a short-lived signed join link for doctor and patient, valid from 10 minutes before the slot to the end; join token authenticated; recording off by default; fallback to phone; waiting-room logic; if the doctor does not join within N minutes, auto-refund/reschedule.

**Reminders and no-shows.** Notifications at booking, 24 h before, 2 h before, with one-tap confirm/reschedule/cancel (Q13). No-show reduction is a major business metric: confirmation prompts, cancellation windows, deposits for high-demand doctors, prediction models flagging likely no-shows for overbooking policies (some clinics intentionally double-book a fraction of slots; model it as a slot `capacity` > 1 with a small probability weighting).

**Reschedule/cancel.** Cancel releases the slot (status OPEN) and may trigger a **waitlist**: patients wanting earlier slots subscribe; on release, notify the first waitlisted patient with a time-limited claim link (compare-and-set claim, same atomic pattern). Reschedule = atomic swap: hold the new slot then release the old one in a transaction/saga so the patient never loses their slot.

**Privacy and security (a differentiator in this question).** Health data is highly sensitive: encrypt at rest and in transit; field-level encryption for notes and prescriptions with per-tenant keys in a KMS; role-based access (patient, doctor, clinic staff, support) with least privilege and break-glass access logged; consent records; immutable audit trail of every read of a medical record; data minimization in search indexes (never index diagnoses or private notes); pseudonymous ids in analytics; data residency; right to erasure workflows; secure messaging between doctor and patient; compliance reviews. Phone/OTP login with rate limits; protect against enumerating patients.

**Doctor-side tooling.** Practice management: daily schedule view, patient history, e-prescriptions with templates and drug-interaction checks, billing, follow-up scheduling; sync with external calendars; clinics may use a queue/token system for walk-ins where the system estimates waiting time from average consult duration and current queue length.

```java
class AppointmentService {
  @Transactional
  Appointment hold(long patientId, long slotId, String idemKey) {
    return appointments.byIdem(idemKey).orElseGet(() -> {
      if (appointments.patientHasOverlap(patientId, slots.get(slotId))) throw new OverlapWarning();
      int rows = jdbc.update("UPDATE slot SET status='HELD', held_until=?, version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND status='OPEN'", Instant.now().plusSeconds(480), slotId);
      if (rows != 1) throw new SlotTaken();                               // someone else won the slot
      return appointments.insert(patientId, slotId, Status.PENDING, idemKey);
    });
  }
  @Transactional
  void confirm(long apptId, PaymentResult pay) {
    Appointment a = appointments.lock(apptId);
    if (!pay.ok() || slots.holdExpired(a.slotId())) { slots.reopen(a.slotId()); appointments.cancel(apptId, "PAYMENT_OR_EXPIRY"); return; }
    slots.markBooked(a.slotId()); appointments.confirm(apptId);
    outbox.add(new AppointmentConfirmed(apptId));                         // notifications, video room, calendar sync
  }
}
```

**Failure cases.** Double booking race: conditional slot update and unique index. Doctor schedule changed after booking: conflict workflow to reschedule affected patients with priority. Payment outage: pay-at-clinic fallback. Video provider down: phone consult fallback. Notification failures: multi-channel retry. Stale search availability: verify at slot load and hold time. Sensitive data leak risk: strict access control, audit alerts.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you represent availability?* Templates plus exceptions generating materialized slots. (2) *How do you prevent double booking?* Conditional slot update plus unique active-appointment constraint with hold expiry. (3) *How do you show 'next available' in search?* Derived field updated from slot events. (4) *How do you reduce no-shows?* Reminders, confirmations, deposits, predictive overbooking. (5) *How do you secure health data?* Encryption, RBAC, consent, audit logs, data minimization. (6) *How do waitlists work?* Subscribe, notify on release, time-limited atomic claim.

**Summary.** Template-based schedules materialized into slots, atomic hold-confirm booking with unique constraints, search index with next-available summaries, WebRTC video consults, reminder and waitlist workflows, and privacy-by-design data handling.

## H. Data, ML, and search

### Q67. Recommendation system

- **Idea:** suggest items (videos, products, songs) a user is likely to engage with.
- **HLD:** two-stage funnel. **Candidate generation** narrows millions of items to hundreds using fast methods: collaborative filtering (users who liked X also liked Y), item/user **embeddings** with approximate nearest neighbor search (ANN: FAISS/ScaNN/HNSW), popularity and recency, content similarity. **Ranking** scores those hundreds with a heavier ML model (features: user history, item features, context like time/device) predicting click/watch/purchase probability. **Re-ranking** applies business rules: diversity, freshness, remove seen/blocked items, ads. Offline: training pipelines on logged interactions; online: feature store + model serving (under \~100 ms). Feedback loop: log impressions and outcomes.
- **Data / LLD:** `interactions(user_id, item_id, type, ts)`; embedding tables; precompute recommendations for inactive users in batch, compute in real time for active ones.
- **Watch out:** cold start (new users/items: use content features, popularity, exploration/bandits), feedback loops and filter bubbles, offline vs online metric mismatch (validate with A/B, Q70), latency budget, position bias in training data.

#### Q67 in depth: Recommendation system

**The core problem.** From millions of items and millions of users, show each user a short ranked list they are likely to engage with, in under 100-200 ms, learning continuously from behavior. The standard answer is a **multi-stage funnel**: candidate generation (millions to hundreds), ranking (hundreds to tens), re-ranking with business rules, because you cannot run a heavy model over every item for every request.

**Requirements and scale.** 100M users, 10M items, 50k recommendation QPS, latency p99 under 150 ms, freshness (new items and recent behavior must matter within minutes), cold start (new users/items), diversity and fairness, explanation, offline and online evaluation, multiple surfaces (home, similar items, email, notifications).

**Signals.** Explicit: ratings, likes. Implicit (far more plentiful): views, clicks, dwell time, add-to-cart, purchases, skips, shares, searches. Context: time, device, location. Item content: text, image, category, price, embeddings. Weight implicit signals by strength (purchase > add-to-cart > click > view) and decay them by recency.

**Stage 1: candidate generation (recall).** Run several cheap generators in parallel and union their outputs:

- **Collaborative filtering:** users with similar histories like similar items. *Item-item* (similar items by co-occurrence: `sim(i,j) = co(i,j) / sqrt(n_i n_j)`, precomputed top-K neighbors per item, served from a KV store) is robust and explainable ('because you viewed X'). *Matrix factorization* (ALS/SVD): learn `d`-dimensional user and item vectors so that `u . i` predicts affinity.
- **Two-tower neural retrieval:** a user tower (history, context) and an item tower (content, ids) produce embeddings trained with sampled-softmax/contrastive loss on engagement; items are indexed in an **ANN index** (HNSW/ScaNN/Faiss, see Q71) and the user vector retrieves the top few hundred in milliseconds.
