- **Popularity/trending** (global and per segment), **recently viewed / continue where you left**, **content-based** (items similar to what the user liked by embedding), **graph/session-based** (next item given the session: item2vec or sequence models), and **business-driven** (new arrivals, promotions).
- Cold start: for new users use onboarding choices, location/device defaults and popularity; for new items use content embeddings and an **exploration budget** (show to a small sample, bandit-style, to learn quality).

**Stage 2: ranking.** A heavier model scores each of \~500 candidates using rich features: user features (embeddings, historical CTR by category), item features (price, freshness, quality), cross features (user-item affinity, category match), context. Models: GBDT for strong tabular baselines, or deep models (Wide & Deep, DeepFM, DLRM, transformer sequence models) predicting multiple objectives (click, purchase, watch time). Final score = weighted combination of objectives, e.g. `p(click)^a * p(purchase)^b * value`, weights tuned by experiments. Latency control: features come from an online **feature store** (Redis/DynamoDB), batch features computed nightly, streaming features (last 5 clicks) updated in near-real time; model served via a model server with batching or on GPUs.

**Stage 3: re-ranking.** Apply constraints that a pointwise model cannot: remove already-seen/purchased/blocked items, enforce **diversity** (maximal marginal relevance: pick items balancing relevance and dissimilarity; limit repeats of the same category/creator), freshness boosts, fairness/exposure for small sellers, ad slots, inventory/availability, safety/policy filters, and **exploration** (epsilon-greedy or Thompson sampling in a few slots to gather unbiased feedback and surface new items).

**Offline pipeline.** Event logs -> data lake -> feature and training-set generation (join labels with features **as of impression time**, point-in-time correctness) -> model training (daily/weekly; embeddings and item-neighbor tables nightly) -> evaluation -> model registry -> deployment (canary, A/B test Q70). Precompute heavy things offline (item-item neighbors, popular lists, user embeddings for batch users) and store as KV for instant lookup; compute light personalized pieces online.

**Evaluation.** Offline: AUC/log-loss for rankers; recall@K, NDCG, MAP for retrieval; always check calibration and slice metrics. But offline gains do not guarantee online wins (feedback loops, position bias). **Online A/B tests** measure CTR, conversion, watch time, retention, revenue, plus guardrails (diversity, complaint rate, latency). Beware **position bias** (top slots get clicks regardless; correct with randomization buckets or position features) and **feedback loops/popularity bias** (rich get richer; mitigate with exploration and debiasing).

**Serving architecture.**

```
Request(user, context) -> Recommendation Service
   |-> fetch user profile/features (feature store)       ~10 ms
   |-> candidate generators in parallel (ANN, item-item KV, trending cache)   ~20-30 ms, each with a timeout; union + dedupe -> ~500
   |-> ranking model on features (batch inference)       ~30-50 ms
   |-> re-rank rules + diversity + filters               ~5 ms
   '-> log impressions (ids, features, model version, scores) to Kafka for training   (async)
Fallback: if anything times out -> cached per-segment popular list.
```

Cache final lists for anonymous or low-personalization surfaces (per segment, TTL minutes); never cache personalized lists beyond short TTLs without invalidation on strong actions (a purchase should remove that item). Pre-warm lists for notification/email campaigns in batch.

**Real-time adaptation.** Stream processing updates session features (last N clicked items, category affinity) within seconds so the next page reflects behavior; item-level counters (CTR, stock status) update continuously; model parameters update periodically, with embedding refresh for new items hourly.

```java
class Recommender {
  List<Item> recommend(long userId, Context ctx, int n) {
    UserFeatures uf = featureStore.user(userId);
    List<Candidate> pool = Stream.of(
          annIndex.nearest(uf.embedding(), 300),            // two-tower retrieval
          itemNeighbors.forRecent(uf.recentItems(), 200),    // item-item CF
          trending.forSegment(uf.segment(), 100))             // popularity fallback / exploration
        .flatMap(List::stream).distinct().filter(c -> !seen.contains(userId, c.itemId())).toList();
    List<Scored> ranked = ranker.score(pool, uf, ctx);                        // multi-objective model
    return reranker.diversify(ranked, n, /*lambda*/ 0.7, exploration.slots(ctx));   // MMR + exploration slots
  }
  // Maximal Marginal Relevance: pick argmax( lambda*score(i) - (1-lambda)*max_{j in picked} sim(i,j) )
}
```

**Failure cases.** Feature store outage: fall back to cached/segment recs. Model regression: shadow/canary, auto-rollback on guardrail drops. Cold start flood (new catalog): content embeddings plus exploration. Training-serving skew: shared feature definitions and logged serving features. Echo chambers/filter bubbles: diversity constraints and exploration. Data poisoning/fake engagement: fraud filtering of signals (Q61). Latency spikes: per-stage timeouts and degraded paths.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *Why a multi-stage funnel?* Compute budget: cheap recall over millions, expensive ranking over hundreds. (2) *How do you solve cold start?* Content-based embeddings, popularity, onboarding signals, exploration. (3) *Collaborative vs content-based?* CF captures taste patterns but needs data; content handles new items; hybrid wins. (4) *How do you evaluate?* Offline metrics then online A/B with guardrails; handle position bias. (5) *How do you keep it fresh?* Streaming features, frequent embedding refresh, exploration. (6) *How do you ensure diversity?* MMR/re-ranking constraints.

**Summary.** Multi-stage funnel with parallel candidate generators (CF, two-tower ANN, trending), feature-store-backed multi-objective ranking, re-ranking for diversity/exploration/business rules, offline training with point-in-time features, online A/B evaluation, and robust fallbacks.

### Q68. Trending topics (Top-K heavy hitters)

- **Idea:** find the top K hashtags/queries in the last N minutes at massive event rates.
- **HLD:** events -> Kafka (partition by term) -> stream processors maintain counts per term in **sliding or tumbling windows** (e.g. 5-min buckets, sum the last 12 for an hour) -> merge partial top-K from each partition into a global top-K every few seconds -> cache -> API. For huge cardinality use **Count-Min Sketch** (approximate frequency in fixed memory) plus a small heap of candidates; Space-Saving algorithm is another heavy-hitter method.
- **Data / LLD:** per node a min-heap of size K keyed by count; the global stage merges K lists (k-way merge). Trending (not just popular) = **growth versus baseline** (count now / typical count), otherwise 'the' always wins; filter spam and stop-words.
- **Watch out:** approximate vs exact tradeoff, bursty sources, geo/personalized trends (separate aggregation per region), abuse (coordinated hashtag spam), window boundaries.

#### Q68 in depth: Trending / Top-K (heavy hitters)

**The core problem.** Continuously find the K most frequent items (hashtags, searches, videos, products) in a sliding time window over a stream of millions of events per second, with bounded memory and results fresh within seconds. Counting everything exactly in one place does not scale; the question tests **streaming algorithms and distributed aggregation**.

**Requirements and scale.** 500k events/s (1M peak), hundreds of millions of distinct keys per day, K = 10-100, windows: last 1 minute, 1 hour, 24 hours (also 'trending now' = velocity versus baseline), results refreshed every 5-10 s, per-region and global views, p99 read latency under 50 ms (reads are a lookup of a precomputed list), accuracy: exact for small K is ideal, approximate within 1% error is acceptable at scale, abuse resistance (bots pumping a hashtag).

**Naive approach and why it fails.** A hash map `key -> count` per window on one server: 100M distinct keys x 50 bytes = 5 GB, and one machine cannot ingest 500k writes/s of updates plus window expiry. And sorting 100M entries every few seconds is far too slow. Use partitioned counting plus a small heap.

**Exact approach with partitioning (when keys are bounded or hardware is generous).**

1. **Partition the stream by key hash** (Kafka partitions keyed by item id) so each aggregator owns a disjoint set of keys and counts them exactly in memory (or in RocksDB state for larger sets).
2. Each aggregator keeps a **min-heap of size K** over its local keys' counts for the current window and publishes its local top-K every few seconds.
3. A **merger** takes N local top-K lists and computes the global top-K: because partitions are disjoint by key, the global top K is contained in the union of local top K's, so merge N x K candidates with another heap: O(NK log K).
4. Write the result to a cache/KV (`topk:{window}:{region}`), served by the read API.

This is exact and simple but memory scales with distinct keys per partition and window handling needs care. Hot keys (one hashtag at 100k/s) overload one partition: split a hot key across salts and sum partials in a second stage (Q60).

**Approximate approach with sketches (memory bounded).**

- **Count-Min Sketch (CMS):** a `d x w` matrix of counters; to add an item, increment one counter per row using d independent hash functions; the estimate is the **minimum** across rows. Never underestimates; overestimates by at most `epsilon * N` with probability `1 - delta` when `w = e/epsilon` and `d = ln(1/delta)`; e.g. epsilon = 0.001, delta = 0.01 gives w = 2,718, d = 5, about 13.6k counters (\~54 KB) independent of the number of distinct keys. Sketches are **mergeable** (add matrices element-wise), so each ingest node keeps a sketch and the merger sums them.
- A sketch alone cannot list the top K (it doesn't store keys). Pair it with a **min-heap of K candidates**: on each item, update the sketch, read its estimate, and if the estimate beats the heap minimum, insert/update the heap. This is the standard heavy-hitters pipeline: sketch for counts, heap for identities.
- **Space-Saving / Misra-Gries:** maintain exactly m counters for the m most likely heavy hitters; when a new key arrives and the table is full, replace the minimum counter's key and inherit its count + 1. Guarantees any item with frequency above N/m is retained, with bounded overestimation. Often more accurate than CMS for top-K with the same memory, and also mergeable.
- **HyperLogLog** is for distinct counts (unique viewers), not top-K, but pairs with it when 'trending' means unique users, not raw events (to defeat one bot spamming).

**Sliding windows.** Options: (1) **Tumbling buckets**: maintain one sketch/counter set per minute; the 1-hour view merges the last 60 buckets; the 24-hour view merges 24 hourly rollups; expiring a window = dropping the oldest bucket (cheap and exact in time). (2) **Hopping windows** in Flink/Kafka Streams (window size 1 h, slide 1 min). (3) **Exponential decay**: `score = score * e^{-lambda dt} + 1` per event, so recent events dominate and no explicit expiry is needed (a single number per key), ideal for 'trending now'. Decay-based counters with a Space-Saving table are a compact production pattern.

**Trending is not just count.** A constantly popular term (the word 'the', #love) is popular but not trending. Trending = **surge relative to baseline**: score = `(count_now - expected_count) / sqrt(expected_count)` (z-score), or ratio `count_last_10min / (avg_count_same_slot_last_weeks + smoothing)`. Store baseline averages per key per time-of-day/day-of-week (decayed history). Add filters: minimum volume threshold, stop-word and spam blocklists, unique-user normalization (count distinct accounts via HLL), geographic scoping, dedupe of near-identical content, and abuse detection (new accounts, coordinated posting).

**Architecture.**

```
Events -> Kafka (partition by key) -> Aggregators (per-partition state: count map or SpaceSaving + per-minute buckets)
      -> every 5 s: local top-K + sketch snapshot -> Kafka 'partials'
      -> Merger (Flink job, parallelism 1 per window/region): merge partials -> global top-K
      -> Redis/KV: topk:{region}:{window}  (value = JSON list with scores, TTL ~30 s)
Read API: GET /trending?region=IN&window=1h -> single KV lookup (cacheable at the CDN for 5-10 s)
Batch path: hourly/daily exact recompute from the data lake corrects sketches and writes authoritative 24h/7d lists.
```

Handle late events with event-time bucketing and small allowed lateness; keep the real-time list approximate and the batch list exact for reports.

**Memory example.** Per-minute CMS of 54 KB x 1,440 minutes/day = 78 MB per partition, tiny. A Space-Saving table of 10,000 counters x 40 bytes = 400 KB. Compare to exact counting of 100M keys at 5 GB per window.

```java
class SpaceSaving<K> {                                   // finds heavy hitters in O(1) amortized with m counters
  private final int m; private final Map<K, long[]> counts = new HashMap<>();
  SpaceSaving(int m) { this.m = m; }
  void add(K key) {
    long[] c = counts.get(key);
    if (c != null) { c[0]++; return; }
    if (counts.size() < m) { counts.put(key, new long[]{1, 0}); return; }
    Map.Entry<K, long[]> min = Collections.min(counts.entrySet(), comparingLong(e -> e.getValue()[0]));   // use a min-heap/bucket list in production
    counts.remove(min.getKey());
    counts.put(key, new long[]{min.getValue()[0] + 1, min.getValue()[0]});     // inherit count; error bound = old min
  }
  List<Map.Entry<K, long[]>> topK(int k) { return counts.entrySet().stream().sorted((a, b) -> Long.compare(b.getValue()[0], a.getValue()[0])).limit(k).toList(); }
}
class CountMinSketch {
  final int d, w; final long[][] t; final int[] seeds;
  CountMinSketch(int d, int w) { this.d = d; this.w = w; t = new long[d][w]; seeds = new Random(42).ints(d).toArray(); }
  void add(String x, long c) { for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) t[i][idx(x, i)] += c; }
  long estimate(String x) { long m = Long.MAX_VALUE; for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) m = Math.min(m, t[i][idx(x, i)]); return m; }
  void merge(CountMinSketch o) { for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) for (int j = 0; j < w; j++) t[i][j] += o.t[i][j]; }
  private int idx(String x, int i) { return Math.floorMod(x.hashCode() * 31 + seeds[i] * 0x9E3779B1, w); }
}
```

**Failure cases.** Aggregator crash: restore state from checkpoint/changelog and replay from Kafka offsets; the list may lag by seconds. Hot key skew: salting and combiners. Clock skew: event time plus watermarks. Sketch saturation (too small): error grows with total volume N, so size by epsilon and rotate sketches per window. Manipulation (bots): unique-user counting, account-age weighting, rate limits, manual blocklists. Cold start after deploy: empty windows, so warm from the last hour of Kafka.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *Why not sort all counts?* Too much data; use heaps and partitioned aggregation. (2) *Why is merging local top-K correct?* With key partitioning, a global top-K item is in its partition's local top-K. (With non-partitioned data, local top-K is not enough; use mergeable sketches or counter tables.) (3) *CMS vs Space-Saving?* CMS supports arbitrary frequency queries and merges; Space-Saving gives better top-K accuracy per byte. (4) *How do you do sliding windows?* Bucketed sketches or exponential decay. (5) *How do you separate trending from popular?* Compare to baseline; z-score or ratio. (6) *How do you stop bots?* Unique counts, reputation weighting, filters.

**Summary.** Partition the stream by key, maintain per-partition exact counters or Space-Saving/CMS sketches with small heaps, merge partial top-K lists, use bucketed or decayed windows, rank by surge versus baseline, and serve the precomputed list from a cache with batch correction for exactness.

### Q69. Real-time leaderboard

- **Idea:** rank millions of players by score; show top N and 'my rank' in real time.
- **HLD:** **Redis Sorted Set** (`ZADD leaderboard score userId`; `ZREVRANGE 0 99` for top 100; `ZREVRANK userId` for rank) -- skip-list backed, O(log n). Scores updated by game servers via events. For many leaderboards (daily/weekly/per-country) use separate keys with TTLs. Persist to DB asynchronously for durability.
- **Data / LLD:** if the set outgrows one node: **shard by score range** (rank = sum of counts in higher shards + rank in shard) or hash-shard users and compute global top-K by merging each shard's top-K; for 'my rank' on huge sets, approximate with percentile buckets (count users per score bucket).
- **Watch out:** ties (break by earliest achievement: encode `score*1e6 + (max_ts - ts)`), hot leaderboard key (replicas for reads), cheating/validation of scores server-side, reset at period boundaries.

#### Q69 in depth: Leaderboard

**The core problem.** Maintain a ranking of players by score with millions of updates, answering three queries in milliseconds: **top N**, **a player's rank**, and **players around a given player** (ranks r-5 to r+5). A SQL `ORDER BY score DESC` or `COUNT(*) WHERE score > x` per request is O(n) or at best O(log n) with indexes, which fails at game scale.

**Requirements and scale.** 50M players, 100k score updates/s peak, 20k leaderboard reads/s, rank lookup under 10 ms, global plus regional plus friends leaderboards, time-bounded boards (daily, weekly, seasonal reset), ties handled deterministically, anti-cheat, durability of scores (cache loss must not lose points).

**Redis sorted set (the standard answer).** A sorted set (`ZSET`) stores `member -> score` in a skip list plus a hash map. Operations are O(log N): `ZADD board score userId` (insert/update), `ZINCRBY board delta userId`, `ZREVRANK board userId` (0-based rank from the top), `ZREVRANGE board 0 99 WITHSCORES` (top 100), `ZREVRANGE board r-5 r+5` (neighbors), `ZCOUNT board min max` and `ZREMRANGEBYRANK` for trimming. For 50M members the memory is about 50M x 80-100 bytes = 4-5 GB, which fits on a single large Redis node, but a single node's throughput (\~100k ops/s) and failure domain are limits, so plan for sharding and replication.

**Ties.** Equal scores need a deterministic order (first to reach the score ranks higher). Encode the score and tie-break into one double or sorted-set score: `composite = score * 2^k + (MAX_TS - timestamp)` where the latter orders earlier achievers first; keep composite within 53 bits of double precision (e.g. score up to 2^31, timestamp seconds in the lower 22 bits), or store the tie-break in the member (lexicographic ordering within equal scores in a ZSET is by member string, which you can design as `paddedTimestamp:userId`).

**Sharding when one node is not enough (50M-1B players).**

- **By score range:** shard i holds scores in a range (e.g. 0-1000, 1001-5000, ...). Rank of a player = (count of players in all higher-score shards, a small precomputed array refreshed every second) + (rank within the local shard). Top N = read from the highest shard(s) first. Works nicely because top ranks are queried most, and hot shards are small (few players with high scores). Requires moving players between shards when scores cross boundaries (delete in the old, add in the new; make it idempotent and ordered), and rebalancing boundaries.
- **By user hash:** each shard holds a random subset; top N = merge the top N from every shard (scatter-gather with k-way merge): fine for top 100 but exact rank needs counts from all shards: `rank = sum over shards of ZCOUNT(shard, score+, +inf)` = N parallel O(log) calls, acceptable for individual rank lookups (tens of ms) but costly at high read rates; cache results for a few seconds.
- **Approximate rank for huge boards:** for a player not in the top N, show a percentile ('top 3%') computed from a histogram or sampled/sketch data (t-digest, or fixed buckets of score counts: `rank ~ sum counts of buckets above + position within bucket`), which is cheap and good enough for the product (exact ranks matter only near the top).

**Write path and durability.** Score updates: game server -> validation (anti-cheat, plausibility) -> **Kafka** (`score_events`, partitioned by user) -> leaderboard updater consumer -> `ZADD`/`ZINCRBY` in Redis; and in parallel persist to the DB (source of truth: `player_score(user_id, season, score, updated_at)`). Redis is a derived, rebuildable index: after a crash, rebuild from the DB or from a snapshot (RDB/AOF) plus replay from Kafka. Use idempotency: the consumer applies `ZADD` with absolute scores (idempotent) rather than `ZINCRBY` deltas (not idempotent on replay), or keep per-event ids to dedupe. For 'best score' semantics use `ZADD GT` (update only if greater) in modern Redis.

**Time-bounded boards.** One key per period: `lb:daily:2026-11-10`, `lb:weekly:2026-W46`, `lb:season:12`; set TTL after the period ends (keep archives in the DB); on each score event update the relevant boards (a pipeline of ZADDs); resets are free because a new key starts empty. Aggregate boards (weekly) can be computed by `ZUNIONSTORE` over daily keys (with weights) periodically instead of double-writing.

**Friends leaderboard.** The friend set is small (hundreds): fetch the friends' scores with a pipelined `ZMSCORE board friend1 friend2 ...` (or a separate per-user structure) and sort in the application. No dedicated global structure is required.

**Around-me query.** `rank = ZREVRANK board userId`; then `ZREVRANGE board max(0, rank-5) rank+5 WITHSCORES`. Two O(log N + M) calls, or one Lua script for atomicity so the window matches the rank.

**Read scaling.** Replicas serve reads; cache the top-100 page (identical for everyone) in memory/CDN for 1-5 s, which turns 20k reads/s into a handful of Redis hits; only the personalized rank call hits Redis per user, and it is cheap. Push updates for top-of-board changes via pub/sub to connected clients if live display is needed.

**Anti-cheat and integrity.** Score submissions are validated server-side (game server authoritative, replay or signature verification), rate-limited, with anomaly detection (impossible jumps, repeated identical scores), shadow-banning cheaters off the public board, an admin tool to remove a user from boards (`ZREM`) and re-rank, and audit logs of score changes.

**Alternatives and why not.** SQL with an index on `(season, score DESC)`: top N is fast, but rank requires `COUNT(*) WHERE score > x` (index range count O(rows) or O(log n) with order-statistics support only in some engines) and heavy update churn on the index; fine to 1M users, not at 50M with 100k writes/s. Segment tree or order-statistic tree (balanced BST augmented with subtree sizes) provides O(log n) rank in memory: that is what a ZSET's skip list does with span counters. A **Fenwick tree (BIT) over score values** works when scores are bounded integers (e.g. 0..1M): `update(score, +1/-1)` and `rank = total - prefixSum(score)`, giving O(log S) rank, trivially mergeable and shardable.

```java
class Leaderboard {
  private final RedisCommands redis; private final String key;
  void submit(String userId, long score, long tsMillis) {
    double composite = score * 1e6 + (1e6 - (tsMillis % 1_000_000));          // earlier timestamp wins ties (keep < 2^53)
    redis.zadd(key, ZAddArgs.Builder.gt(), composite, userId);                // keep best score only; idempotent on replay
  }
  List<Entry> top(int n) { return redis.zrevrangeWithScores(key, 0, n - 1); }
  Long rank(String userId) { return redis.zrevrank(key, userId); }           // 0-based; null if absent
  List<Entry> around(String userId, int radius) {
    Long r = redis.zrevrank(key, userId); if (r == null) return List.of();
    return redis.zrevrangeWithScores(key, Math.max(0, r - radius), r + radius);
  }
}
class FenwickRank {                                                           // rank for bounded integer scores
  final long[] bit; final int max;
  FenwickRank(int max) { this.max = max; bit = new long[max + 2]; }
  void add(int score, int delta) { for (int i = score + 1; i <= max + 1; i += i & -i) bit[i] += delta; }
  long countLE(int score) { long s = 0; for (int i = score + 1; i > 0; i -= i & -i) s += bit[i]; return s; }
  long rankOf(int score, long total) { return total - countLE(score) + 1; }   // 1-based, ties share a rank
}
```

**Failure cases.** Redis node loss: replica promotion; rebuild from DB/Kafka. Replays double-counting increments: use absolute `ZADD` or event ids. Hot shard at top: smaller score ranges for top shards, replicas. Rank skew while moving players across shards: read both shards during migration, tolerate brief inconsistency. Cheaters: validation and removal. Season reset load: pre-create keys; archive old boards asynchronously.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *Why a sorted set?* O(log N) updates and rank via skip list with spans. (2) *How do you shard?* By score range (rank = higher-shard counts + local rank) or scatter-gather for hash sharding; percentiles for the long tail. (3) *How do you handle ties?* Composite score with timestamp. (4) *What if Redis dies?* Rebuild from the DB and Kafka replay; idempotent writes. (5) *How do you do weekly boards?* Key per period, TTL, or ZUNIONSTORE of dailies. (6) *Alternative structures?* Fenwick tree over bounded scores, order-statistic tree.

**Summary.** Redis ZSETs per board and period for top-N, rank and neighbor queries; deterministic tie-breaking; durable scores in the DB with Kafka-fed idempotent updaters; sharding by score range or hash with approximate ranks for the tail; cached top pages; server-side anti-cheat.

### Q70. A/B testing platform

- **Idea:** run controlled experiments, assigning users to variants and measuring metric impact with statistical rigor.
- **HLD:** **assignment:** deterministic hash `bucket = hash(userId + experimentId) % 10000`; ranges map to variants, so assignment is stateless, stable, and consistent across services (SDK evaluates locally from experiment config; config service Q28). **Exposure logging:** log when a user actually sees the variant. Pipeline: events -> Kafka -> warehouse/stream -> metrics computation per variant (conversion, revenue, latency) -> statistical engine (t-test/z-test, confidence intervals, sequential testing, variance reduction like CUPED) -> dashboard.
- **Data / LLD:** `experiments(id, layers, traffic_pct, variants, start, end, targeting_rules)`; **layers/namespaces** keep concurrent experiments orthogonal by using different hash salts per layer.
- **Watch out:** sample-ratio mismatch (assignment bug), peeking (stopping early inflates false positives), novelty effects, network effects/interference (marketplaces), multiple-comparison corrections, guardrail metrics.

#### Q70 in depth: A/B testing / experimentation platform

**The core problem.** Let teams run many controlled experiments at once on live traffic: assign users to variants **consistently and independently**, log exposures, compute metrics, and decide with **statistical rigor** whether a change helped. The system is half infrastructure (assignment, config, logging at huge scale) and half statistics (power, significance, peeking, multiple tests).

**Requirements and scale.** 500M users, 1,000 concurrent experiments, assignment decision on every request (200k QPS) with under 5 ms added latency and no network call on the hot path, sticky assignment (a user stays in the same variant), mutually exclusive experiments where needed, targeting (country, platform), gradual rollout and instant kill switch, exposure and metric logging with near-zero loss, daily metric computation with confidence intervals, guardrail metrics.

**Assignment by deterministic hashing.** Variant = function of `(user_id, experiment_salt)`: `bucket = hash(user_id + ':' + experiment_id) mod 10000`; allocate bucket ranges to variants (control 0-4999, treatment 5000-9999 for a 50/50 split; or 0-99 for a 1% ramp). Properties: no storage needed, stateless and consistent across servers and languages (agree on the hash: murmur3), sticky, adjustable allocation by changing ranges (ramp-ups keep earlier users in treatment because ranges expand, not reshuffle, when you add bucket ranges at the end). A different salt per experiment makes assignments **independent** across experiments (no correlation between being in A in experiment 1 and in experiment 2).

**Layers for mutual exclusion.** Experiments that touch the same surface (two checkout button tests) must not overlap. Use **layers/domains**: users are hashed into 1,000 layer buckets once; each experiment in the layer owns a disjoint bucket range; users fall into at most one experiment per layer. Independent layers (search ranking, UI theme) overlap freely. Holdout groups (a permanent 1-5% not receiving any new features) measure long-term cumulative impact.

**Config distribution.** Experiment definitions (id, salt, layer, ranges, targeting rules, status, allocation) live in a config service; SDKs embedded in app servers/clients **poll or stream** them (every 10-30 s, via push or ETag polling) into local memory so assignment is a local computation. Client-side SDKs (mobile/web) fetch assignments from an edge service at session start, or evaluate rules locally from a signed config. Kill switch propagates in seconds (push) and defaults to control when config is unavailable (fail-safe).

**Exposure logging.** Log an **exposure event** only when the user actually *sees/uses* the treatment (e.g. the checkout page rendered), not at assignment, otherwise analysis dilutes with users who never encountered the change. Event: `{user_id, experiment_id, variant, timestamp, context}`. Send asynchronously to Kafka; dedupe on analysis (first exposure per user). Keep assignment, exposure and metric events joinable by user id. Log also the **assignment reason** (targeting match, holdout) for debugging.

**Metrics pipeline.** Business events (clicks, orders, revenue, latency, crashes) flow to the data lake. A daily (and hourly for fast experiments) batch job joins exposures with metric events per user: for each experiment compute per-variant metric values per *user* (sum or mean over the experiment window **after first exposure**), then aggregates and statistics. Metric types: conversion rate (binary), average revenue per user (continuous, heavy-tailed: winsorize or use log/CUPED), counts per user, ratio metrics (CTR = clicks/impressions needs the **delta method** because users have varying denominators), retention curves. **Guardrails**: latency, error rate, unsubscribes, support tickets; an experiment that wins on conversion but breaks guardrails is not shipped.

**Statistics you must know.**

- **Hypothesis test:** H0 = no difference. For a conversion metric use a two-proportion z-test: `z = (p_t - p_c) / sqrt(p(1-p)(1/n_t + 1/n_c))`; for continuous use Welch's t-test. Report the effect, a **confidence interval**, and the p-value. Significance level alpha = 0.05 (false-positive rate); **power** = 0.8 (chance to detect a real effect of the minimum size).
- **Sample size** per variant for proportions: `n = 2 * (z_{1-alpha/2} + z_{power})^2 * p(1-p) / delta^2`. Example: baseline conversion 10%, want to detect a 0.5 pp absolute lift: `n = 2 * (1.96 + 0.84)^2 * 0.1*0.9 / 0.005^2 = 2 * 7.84 * 0.09 / 0.000025 = 56,448` users per variant. Small effects need large samples; duration = n / daily eligible traffic, rounded up to full weeks to cover weekly seasonality.
- **Peeking problem:** checking results daily and stopping when p < 0.05 inflates false positives (up to 30%+). Remedies: fixed-horizon tests (decide the sample size in advance), **sequential testing** (mSPRT, group-sequential alpha spending), or Bayesian approaches with proper decision rules.
- **Multiple comparisons:** many metrics and variants raise false discoveries; use Bonferroni/Holm for few tests or Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR) for many; designate a single primary metric ahead of time.
- **Variance reduction:** **CUPED** (regress out pre-experiment behavior: `Y' = Y - theta (X - mean(X))`) can cut variance 30-50%, shortening tests; stratification by platform/country.
- **Sample ratio mismatch (SRM):** if a 50/50 split shows 50.5/49.5 with a chi-square p < 0.001, something is broken (assignment bug, bot filtering differences, logging loss); results are invalid until explained. Always run an SRM check automatically.
- **Novelty/primacy effects, interference:** novelty fades; network effects (social features, marketplaces) violate independence (treated users affect control): use cluster-randomized or switchback designs (time-based alternation for marketplaces like ride-hailing).

**Analysis service and UI.** A results store keyed by `(experiment, variant, metric, date)` with sufficient statistics (n, sum, sum of squares, covariances) so intervals can be recomputed cheaply and incrementally; dashboards show lift, CI, p-value, SRM status, guardrails, segment breakdowns (with a warning about slicing), and ship/iterate/stop recommendations. Governance: experiment registry with owner, hypothesis, primary metric, planned duration, review, and a decision log.

```java
class ExperimentSdk {
  Variant assign(String userId, Experiment e, Context ctx) {
    if (!e.status().running() || !e.targeting().matches(ctx)) return Variant.CONTROL_NOT_ENROLLED;
    int layerBucket = Math.floorMod(Hashing.murmur3(userId + ":" + e.layerId()), 1000);
    if (!e.layerRange().contains(layerBucket)) return Variant.NOT_IN_LAYER_RANGE;          // mutual exclusion within the layer
    int b = Math.floorMod(Hashing.murmur3(userId + ":" + e.salt()), 10_000);
    for (Allocation a : e.allocations()) if (a.range().contains(b)) return a.variant();   // sticky, stateless
    return Variant.CONTROL_NOT_ENROLLED;
  }
  void expose(String userId, Experiment e, Variant v) { events.sendAsync(new Exposure(userId, e.id(), v, clock.now())); }   // log on actual use
}
static double sampleSizePerVariant(double p, double deltaAbs, double alpha, double power) {
  double za = normInv(1 - alpha / 2), zb = normInv(power);
  return 2 * Math.pow(za + zb, 2) * p * (1 - p) / (deltaAbs * deltaAbs);
}
```

**Failure cases.** Config service outage: SDK uses the last known config, defaults to control. Assignment drift because of salt reuse or code differences: cross-language test vectors for the hash. Logging loss in one variant: SRM alarms. Bot traffic skews metrics: filter before analysis. Concurrent experiments interacting: layers plus interaction checks for known conflicts. Ramp-up that reshuffles users: only extend ranges. Ending an experiment: remove the code path, document the result, stop logging.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you assign users consistently without a database?* Deterministic hash of user and experiment salt into buckets. (2) *How do you run non-overlapping tests?* Layers with disjoint bucket ranges. (3) *How long should a test run?* Sample size from baseline, minimum detectable effect, alpha and power; full weeks. (4) *What is peeking and how do you avoid it?* Repeated looks inflate false positives; use sequential methods or fixed horizons. (5) *What is SRM?* Imbalance versus the intended split signals a bug. (6) *How do you test in a marketplace?* Switchback or cluster randomization to avoid interference.

**Summary.** Stateless hash-based assignment with layers and holdouts, locally cached experiment configs with kill switches, exposure logging, a batch metrics pipeline with correct statistics (power, sequential tests, CUPED, SRM, FDR), guardrails, and governance around decisions.

### Q71. RAG chatbot / enterprise search

- **Idea:** answer questions over private documents by retrieving relevant passages and having an LLM write an answer grounded in them, with citations.
- **HLD:** **Ingestion:** connectors (Drive, Confluence, Slack) -> parse (PDF/HTML) -> **chunk** (200 to 500 tokens with overlap, respecting headings) -> embed with an embedding model -> store in a **vector DB** (HNSW index) alongside metadata and **ACLs**; also keep a keyword index (BM25) for **hybrid search**. **Query:** rewrite query (use chat history) -> hybrid retrieve top \~50 -> **rerank** with a cross-encoder to top \~5 -> build prompt with passages -> LLM (Q20) -> answer with citations -> optional groundedness check.
- **Data / LLD:** `chunks(chunk_id, doc_id, text, embedding, acl_groups, version, ts)`; incremental re-indexing via document change events and content hashes; delete propagation.
- **Watch out:** **permissions** (filter by the user's ACL at retrieval time, never after generation), hallucination (require citations, say 'I don't know' when retrieval is weak), chunking quality (largest lever on answer quality), stale index, prompt injection from retrieved documents, evaluation sets (retrieval recall, answer faithfulness).

#### Q71 in depth: RAG chatbot (retrieval-augmented generation)

**The core problem.** Answer questions about a private or fast-changing corpus (company docs, tickets, product manuals) using a large language model **without fine-tuning**, by retrieving relevant passages and putting them in the prompt. Goals: grounded answers with citations, low hallucination, respect for **access permissions**, acceptable latency and cost, and measurable quality.

**Requirements and scale.** 100M document chunks, 1k QPS peak, time to first token under 1.5 s, full answer in 5-10 s, document updates visible within minutes, per-user permissions (only retrieve what the user may read), multi-tenant isolation, conversation history, feedback, evaluation, cost control (tokens are the bill).

**Indexing pipeline (offline/near-line).**

1. **Connectors** pull from sources (Drive, Confluence, Slack, S3, databases) with incremental sync (change tokens/webhooks) and keep an **ACL** (who can read) per document.
2. **Parse and clean:** extract text from PDF/DOCX/HTML/slides (layout-aware parsing, OCR for scans, table handling), remove boilerplate, keep structure (headings, page numbers, URLs).
3. **Chunking:** split into passages of \~200-800 tokens with 10-20% overlap, preferably along semantic boundaries (headings, paragraphs); attach metadata (doc id, title, section, url, author, updated\_at, ACL, tenant). Chunk size is a trade-off: small chunks are precise but lose context; large chunks dilute relevance and cost tokens. Variants: parent-child chunking (retrieve small, feed the parent), sentence-window retrieval, contextual headers prepended to each chunk.
4. **Embedding:** run an embedding model to get a vector per chunk (e.g. 768-3072 dimensions); batch on GPUs/API; store `(chunk_id, vector, text, metadata)`.
5. **Index:** vector index (HNSW / IVF-PQ in Faiss, pgvector, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch kNN, Pinecone, Milvus, Qdrant) **plus** a lexical BM25 index for keyword precision. Updates: upsert changed chunks, delete removed ones (tombstones then compaction), re-embed when the embedding model changes (blue/green index versions).

**Vector search basics.** Exact nearest-neighbor over 100M x 1,024 floats (400 GB) is too slow, so use **ANN**. *HNSW*: layered proximity graph; query greedily walks from top layers down; very high recall (95-99%) at \~1-10 ms, memory heavy (graph + vectors). *IVF*: cluster vectors with k-means, search the closest `nprobe` clusters. *PQ* (product quantization): compress vectors to \~64 bytes (8x-32x smaller) with some accuracy loss, often with re-scoring on full vectors. Typical trade-off knobs: `efSearch`/`nprobe` (recall vs latency), quantization (memory vs accuracy). Similarity: cosine/dot product on normalized vectors. Shard the index by tenant/hash and replicate for QPS.

**Query path (online).**

1. **Authenticate, load ACL principals** (user id, groups).
2. **Query understanding:** rewrite follow-up questions using conversation history into a standalone query ('and what about its price?' -> 'what is the price of Product X?'), optionally expand/decompose multi-part questions, classify intent (small talk vs knowledge vs tool call).
3. **Hybrid retrieval:** embed the query; run vector kNN (top 50-100) and BM25 (top 50-100) **with metadata filters**: tenant, ACL, recency, source; combine with **reciprocal rank fusion** `score(d) = sum 1/(k + rank_i(d))`. Doing ACL filtering **inside** the search (pre-filter or filtered ANN) is essential: post-filtering top-K can return nothing visible, and unfiltered retrieval risks leaking data.
4. **Re-ranking:** a cross-encoder reranker scores (query, chunk) pairs jointly (more accurate than embedding similarity) on the top \~100 and keeps the best 5-10. This single stage often improves answer quality the most.
5. **Prompt assembly:** system instructions (answer only from sources, cite, say 'I don't know' if unsupported), conversation summary, retrieved chunks with ids, the question; respect the context-window budget (truncate, order by relevance, dedupe near-duplicates).
6. **Generation** with streaming tokens to the UI; temperature low for factuality.
7. **Post-processing:** verify citations map to provided chunks, run guardrails (PII, policy), attach source links, log everything (query, retrieved ids, prompt version, model version, latency, tokens) for evaluation.

**Hallucination control.** Ground via strict prompts; require quotations or chunk ids per claim; abstain when top retrieval scores are below a threshold; **self-check/verification** pass (a second call asks whether each claim is supported by the sources); constrained output formats; show sources so users verify. Retrieval failures are the dominant cause of bad answers, so measure retrieval separately from generation.

**Evaluation (what interviewers love).** Build a golden set of questions with reference answers and relevant chunk ids. Retrieval metrics: recall@k, MRR, nDCG. Generation metrics: faithfulness (is every claim supported by retrieved context?), answer relevance, completeness; LLM-as-judge with calibration against human labels; online feedback (thumbs, edits), rate of 'no answer'. Regression-test every change (chunking, embedding model, prompt) on the golden set before rollout; A/B test (Q70).

**Latency and cost.** Latency budget: embed query 20-50 ms, vector+BM25 30-60 ms, rerank 100-200 ms, LLM first token 400-800 ms, then streaming. Cost levers: **caching** (exact-match and semantic caches of question embeddings for repeated questions, with ACL-aware keys), smaller models for routing/rewriting, limiting retrieved tokens, prompt caching of static prefixes, batching embeddings, quantized indexes, shorter outputs, and tiered models (cheap first, escalate for hard questions).

**Security and permissions.** Never rely on the model to enforce access; enforce ACLs in retrieval. Prevent **prompt injection** from documents ('ignore previous instructions...'): treat retrieved text as untrusted data (delimiters, instruction hierarchy, no tool execution driven by content without confirmation), sanitize, scan, and limit tool permissions. Tenant isolation in storage and caches; audit logs; PII redaction; data residency; encryption; retention/deletion propagation (deleting a document must delete its chunks, embeddings and cache entries).

**Beyond basic RAG.** Agentic RAG (the model decides to search multiple times, call tools/SQL), query decomposition for multi-hop questions, knowledge graphs, summarization indexes for long documents, structured data via text-to-SQL, freshness boosting, per-source weighting, conversation memory, multilingual embeddings.

```java
class RagService {
  Answer answer(User u, String question, List<Turn> history) {
    String standalone = rewriter.standalone(question, history);
    float[] qv = embedder.embed(standalone);
    Filter acl = Filter.and(Filter.tenant(u.tenantId()), Filter.anyOf("acl", u.principals()));      // enforced inside the index
    List<Hit> dense = vectorIndex.search(qv, acl, 80), sparse = bm25.search(standalone, acl, 80);
    List<Hit> fused = Rrf.fuse(List.of(dense, sparse), /*k*/ 60);
    List<Hit> top = reranker.rerank(standalone, fused.subList(0, Math.min(100, fused.size()))).subList(0, 8);
    if (top.isEmpty() || top.get(0).score() < MIN_RELEVANCE) return Answer.noAnswer();           // abstain rather than guess
    String prompt = prompts.build(standalone, history, ContextBudget.fit(top, 6000));
    Stream<String> tokens = llm.stream(prompt, 0.1);
    return Answer.streaming(tokens, citations.from(top)).logTo(telemetry);
  }
}
```

**Failure cases.** Irrelevant retrieval: hybrid search, reranker, thresholds, query rewriting. Stale docs: incremental sync, freshness filters, TTL checks. Permission drift: ACL sync on change events and periodic reconciliation. Context overflow: dynamic budgeting and parent-child chunk trimming. LLM provider outage or rate limit: fallback model, queue, cached answers. Prompt injection: untrusted-content handling. Embedding model upgrade: parallel index build and cutover. Cost spikes: quotas per tenant, caching, small-model routing.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *RAG vs fine-tuning?* RAG for fresh/private knowledge and citations; fine-tuning for style/skills; they combine. (2) *How do you choose chunk size?* Evaluate on a golden set; \~300-500 tokens with overlap as a start; structure-aware. (3) *Why hybrid search and reranking?* Dense captures semantics, BM25 captures exact terms; the cross-encoder fixes ordering. (4) *How do you enforce permissions?* Filter at retrieval with ACL metadata; never trust the model. (5) *How do you evaluate and reduce hallucination?* Separate retrieval and generation metrics, faithfulness checks, abstention. (6) *How do you scale the vector index?* ANN (HNSW/IVF-PQ), sharding by tenant/hash, replicas, quantization.

**Summary.** Ingest, chunk and embed with ACL metadata into a hybrid (vector + BM25) index; at query time rewrite, retrieve with permission filters, rerank, assemble a budgeted prompt, generate with citations and abstention; evaluate retrieval and generation separately; control latency and cost with caches and tiered models; defend against prompt injection and data leaks.

### Q72. Web search engine (Google)

- **Idea:** crawl the web, build an index, answer queries in \~200 ms with relevant ranked results.
- **HLD:** pipeline: **crawler** (Q15) -> content store -> **indexer** builds an **inverted index** (term -> postings list of doc ids, positions, frequencies), sharded by **document** (each shard indexes a subset of docs; a query goes to all shards in parallel and merges the top results) with replicas for throughput; link graph -> **PageRank** (offline iterative computation); **query serving:** parse, spell-correct, expand synonyms, fan out to index shards, each returns top-k by a cheap score (BM25 + signals), aggregator re-ranks the best few hundred with a heavy ML ranker (freshness, quality, links, click data, personalization), then snippets are generated. Caches: results for popular queries at the front; postings lists in memory. Tiered index: hot/high-quality docs in fast tier, long-tail in slower tier.
- **Data / LLD:** postings compression (delta encoding + variable-byte); skip pointers for fast intersection of lists (AND queries: intersect the shortest list first); `index segments` merged in the background (LSM-like), near-real-time index for fresh news.
- **Watch out:** tail latency (hedged requests, timeouts with partial results), spam/SEO manipulation, freshness vs depth, index size (billions of docs) and cost, query understanding (intent, entities).

#### Q72 in depth: Web search engine

**The core problem.** Crawl a huge, ever-changing web, build an index that can answer a query over billions of documents in about 200 ms, and rank the results by relevance and quality. Four subsystems: **crawler, indexer, query serving, ranking**, plus freshness and spam control.

**Requirements and scale.** 50B pages indexed, 10B pages recrawled per day for freshness (news in minutes, static pages weekly), 100k queries/s, p99 under 300 ms, index size in the petabytes, polite crawling (respect robots.txt, rate limits per host), duplicate and spam handling, multilingual, safe search, spelling correction and autocomplete (Q21).

**Crawler.** Architecture: a **URL frontier** (priority queues) -> **fetcher workers** (distributed, DNS-cached, HTTP/2, per-host connection pools) -> **parser** (extract text, links, metadata, canonical tag) -> **dedupe** -> store raw content (object store) and emit new links back to the frontier. Frontier design: two layers. *Priority* (front queues by importance score such as PageRank, update frequency, user demand) and *politeness* (back queues, one per host, with a minimum delay between requests to the same host, e.g. 1 req/s, and crawl-delay from robots.txt). Workers pick the next host whose delay has elapsed (a heap keyed by next-allowed time). Shard the frontier by host hash so each host is handled by exactly one machine (politeness is then a local decision). Handle traps: infinite calendars, session ids in URLs, soft 404s: depth limits, URL normalization (lowercase host, sort query params, strip tracking params), duplicate pattern detection. Dedupe URLs with a Bloom filter (`seen`) and dedupe content with SimHash (near-duplicate pages differ by few bits, Hamming distance <= 3) or shingling+MinHash. **Recrawl scheduling:** estimate each page's change rate from past crawls (conditional GET with ETag/If-Modified-Since to save bandwidth), recrawl frequently changing and important pages more often, solve as a bandit/optimization problem to maximize freshness per fetch budget. Special pipelines for news/social (feeds, sitemaps, push APIs).

**Indexing.** Build an **inverted index**: `term -> posting list` of `(docId, positions, term frequency, field flags)` sorted by docId and **delta/variable-byte/PFOR compressed** (typically 4-8x). Steps: tokenization (language-specific; CJK segmentation), normalization (lowercase, accent folding), stemming/lemmatization, stop-word handling (keep in phrase indexes), n-grams for prefix/typo. The corpus is split into **shards** by document id (document partitioning): each shard indexes a subset and can answer any query on its subset; queries scatter to all shards and gather top results. Alternative term partitioning (each machine holds some terms) causes heavy cross-machine posting list transfer and hot terms, so document partitioning dominates in practice. Add **tiering**: a small, fast tier with high-quality pages in RAM/SSD (most queries are answered here), and lower tiers for the long tail, queried only when the top tier yields too few results.

**Index building and updates.** Large-scale batch with MapReduce-style pipelines (parse -> invert -> merge -> compress) produce immutable index segments. Freshness requires an **incremental** path: a small real-time index (in memory, recent crawls) is merged with the main index at query time and periodically compacted (like LSM segments). Deleted/updated docs use tombstones/liveness bitmaps. Build in the background and swap atomically (blue/green index versions).

**Query serving.** Flow: frontend -> **query understanding** (spell correction using query logs and edit distance, synonyms, entity detection, language detection, intent classification such as navigational/informational/local/shopping, query rewriting) -> **scatter** to all shards (or to the relevant tier) in parallel with a tight deadline -> each shard retrieves candidates by intersecting/unioning posting lists (conjunctive AND with skip pointers and **early termination**: process documents in descending static-quality order or use WAND/MaxScore dynamic pruning to skip documents that cannot enter the top-K) and scores them with a cheap ranker (BM25 + static rank) -> returns its local top few hundred -> **aggregator** merges, applies a heavier re-ranker (machine-learned) to the top \~1,000 -> final page assembly (snippets, titles, rich results, ads, related searches, knowledge panel). Use **hedged requests** to tame tail latency (resend a slow shard request to a replica after the p95 delay) and return partial results if a shard misses the deadline. Replicas of each shard serve load; cache popular queries' results (the head of the distribution is heavily repeated: 15-30% of queries are new each day, but the top queries are cached for seconds to minutes with freshness caveats).

**Ranking.** Signals: *text relevance* (BM25/TF-IDF over title, anchor text, body, URL with field weights, proximity of query terms, phrase matches), *link analysis* (**PageRank**: a page is important if important pages link to it; compute iteratively on the link graph, `PR(p) = (1-d)/N + d * sum_{q->p} PR(q)/outdeg(q)`, d = 0.85, via distributed MapReduce/Pregel; anchor text as extra document text), *quality* (site authority, content depth, spam score, page speed, mobile friendliness, HTTPS), *freshness* for time-sensitive queries, *personalization and context* (location, language, history, device), and *user behavior* (click-through, dwell time, pogo-sticking, aggregated and debiased). Final ranking is a **learning-to-rank** model (LambdaMART gradient-boosted trees or neural rankers, and embedding-based semantic retrieval for meaning-based matches, merged with lexical results) trained on human relevance labels (rater guidelines, side-by-side tests) and click data; evaluated with NDCG, and online experiments (Q70).

**Spam and quality.** Link farms, keyword stuffing, cloaking, scraped content. Defenses: spam classifiers, link-graph analysis (TrustRank propagates trust from a seed of good sites), manual actions, content-quality models, penalties, and crawl-time filters. This is an adversarial game, so continuous model updates are needed.

**Autocomplete and spelling.** Prefix trie/FST of popular queries with weights (decayed popularity, personalization, locale), top-K per prefix precomputed, updated hourly from logs (Q21). Spelling: candidate generation by edit distance within a dictionary of queries/terms plus a noisy-channel model with the query log language model.

**Storage and infrastructure.** Raw page store (distributed file system, compressed), link graph store (adjacency lists, billions of nodes, hundreds of billions of edges), index shards on SSD/RAM with replication across clusters/regions; DNS and fetch infrastructure; GPU/TPU clusters for ranking models and embeddings; query logs in a data lake for training and analytics; strict privacy handling (anonymization, retention limits).

**Capacity sketch.** 50B docs x average 5 KB text = 250 TB raw text (compressed \~60 TB); inverted index roughly 10-30% of raw size per replica => \~50 TB per replica; at 100 docs/ms per core... the point is: 50B docs / 10M docs per shard = 5,000 shards x \~3 replicas = 15,000 machines for the main index. A query fans out to 5,000 shards in parallel, which is why tail-latency control (hedging, deadlines, tiering, caching) is the central problem rather than raw throughput.

```java
class ShardSearcher {
  List<ScoredDoc> search(Query q, int topK) {
    List<PostingIterator> its = q.terms().stream().map(index::postings).sorted(comparingLong(PostingIterator::cost)).toList();   // rarest first
    PriorityQueue<ScoredDoc> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(topK, comparingDouble(ScoredDoc::score));
    long doc = its.get(0).next();
    while (doc != NO_MORE) {
      boolean all = true;
      for (PostingIterator it : its) { long d = it.advance(doc); if (d != doc) { doc = d; all = false; break; } }      // skip-pointer leapfrog (AND)
      if (all) {
        double s = bm25(doc, its) + staticRank[(int) doc];
        if (heap.size() < topK) heap.add(new ScoredDoc(doc, s)); else if (s > heap.peek().score()) { heap.poll(); heap.add(new ScoredDoc(doc, s)); }
        doc = its.get(0).next();
      }
    }
    return heap.stream().sorted(comparingDouble(ScoredDoc::score).reversed()).toList();
  }
}
class Frontier {                                                          // politeness: one back-queue per host
  private final PriorityQueue<HostQueue> ready = new PriorityQueue<>(comparingLong(HostQueue::nextAllowedMillis));
  Optional<Url> next() { HostQueue h = ready.peek(); if (h == null || h.nextAllowedMillis() > now()) return Optional.empty(); ready.poll(); Url u = h.pop(); h.setNextAllowed(now() + h.crawlDelayMillis()); if (!h.isEmpty()) ready.add(h); return Optional.of(u); }
}
```

**Failure cases.** Slow or dead shard: hedged requests and partial results. Crawler stuck in a trap: per-host budgets and depth caps. Index corruption: checksums, immutable segments, rebuild from raw store. Bad ranking release: interleaving experiments, instant rollback. Spam wave: rapid classifier/rule updates, demotion. Hot query surge (breaking news): caching, freshness index, query rate limits. Data center outage: replicated shards across clusters with global load balancing.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you avoid hammering a website?* Per-host back queues with delays, robots.txt, shard by host. (2) *How do you detect duplicates?* URL normalization + Bloom filter; SimHash for content. (3) *How is the index partitioned?* By document into shards, replicated, tiered; scatter-gather. (4) *How do you keep latency low across thousands of shards?* Deadlines, hedging, early termination, tiering, caching. (5) *What is PageRank?* Link-based importance computed iteratively on the web graph. (6) *How do you stay fresh?* Change-rate-based recrawl, incremental real-time index, news-specific pipelines.

**Summary.** Polite, prioritized distributed crawler with dedupe and recrawl scheduling; compressed inverted index sharded by document with tiers and an incremental fresh index; scatter-gather query serving with pruning, hedging and caches; multi-stage ranking combining text, link and behavior signals with learned models; spam control and continuous evaluation.

# Part C: LLD classics (Q73 to Q100)

For each: requirements in one line, the classes and why, then the core code. In an interview, say the entities and patterns out loud first, then code the main flow. Follow the LLD script from Part 4.

### Q73. Parking lot

- **Requirements:** multiple floors; spot types (compact, regular, large, EV); vehicle types (bike, car, truck); issue ticket on entry, compute fee on exit; find nearest free suitable spot; payment.
- **Classes:** `ParkingLot` (singleton), `Floor`, `ParkingSpot` (type, occupied), `Vehicle` (abstract; `Car`, `Bike`, `Truck`), `Ticket` (id, vehicle, spot, entryTime), `SpotAllocationStrategy` (Strategy: nearest-to-entrance, lowest floor), `PricingStrategy` (Strategy: hourly, flat, by vehicle type), `Payment`.
- **Patterns:** Strategy (allocation, pricing), Factory (vehicle/spot creation), Singleton (lot).

```java
class ParkingLot {
  private final List<Floor> floors; private final Map<String, Ticket> active = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
  private final SpotAllocationStrategy allocator; private final PricingStrategy pricing;

  Ticket park(Vehicle v) {
    Optional<ParkingSpot> spot = allocator.find(floors, v.getType());
    if (spot.isEmpty()) throw new LotFullException();
    ParkingSpot s = spot.get();
    if (!s.tryOccupy(v)) return park(v);              // another thread took it; retry
    Ticket t = new Ticket(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), v, s, Instant.now());
    active.put(t.id, t); return t;
  }
  Money exit(String ticketId) {
    Ticket t = active.remove(ticketId);
    Money fee = pricing.fee(t, Instant.now());
    t.spot.free(); return fee;
  }
}
class ParkingSpot {
  private final SpotType type; private Vehicle current;
  synchronized boolean tryOccupy(Vehicle v) { if (current != null || !type.fits(v.getType())) return false; current = v; return true; }
  synchronized void free() { current = null; }
}
```

- **Watch out:** concurrency on spot assignment (atomic `tryOccupy`), a large spot may host a smaller vehicle (fit rules), lost-ticket fee, adding a new vehicle type without editing old code (Open/Closed).

#### Q73 in depth: Parking lot (LLD)

**How to approach any LLD question (use this script).** (1) Clarify requirements and scope in 3 minutes. (2) List entities (nouns) and behaviors (verbs). (3) Identify what varies (pricing, slot choice, payment) and put each behind an interface (Strategy). (4) Draw the class diagram and relationships. (5) Walk through the main flows. (6) Handle concurrency and edge cases. (7) Mention extensions. Clean code with SOLID matters more than cleverness.

**Requirements to confirm.** Multi-floor lot; vehicle types (motorcycle, car, bus/truck) mapped to compatible slot types (small, medium, large, also EV charging, handicapped); entry and exit gates (multiple); ticket issued at entry, fee computed at exit by duration and vehicle type; payment by cash/card/UPI; capacity display per floor; concurrent entries must not assign the same slot; lost-ticket policy; reservations optional. Non-goals: hardware drivers, camera ANPR (mention as an adapter).

**Entities.** `ParkingLot` (singleton-per-site facade), `ParkingFloor`, `ParkingSlot` (id, type, status, floor), `Vehicle` (plate, type), `Ticket` (id, vehicle, slot, entryTime, gateId, status), `Gate` (Entry/Exit), `Payment` and `PaymentProcessor`, `PricingStrategy`, `SlotAllocationStrategy`, `DisplayBoard` (observer).

**Class diagram (text).**

```
ParkingLot 1---* ParkingFloor 1---* ParkingSlot
ParkingLot ---> SlotAllocationStrategy (interface)  <|-- NearestToEntryStrategy, FirstFitStrategy, LeastLoadedFloorStrategy
ParkingLot ---> PricingStrategy (interface)         <|-- HourlyPricing, FlatPlusHourly, SurgePricing(decorator)
ParkingLot ---> PaymentProcessor (interface)        <|-- CardPayment, UpiPayment, CashPayment      (Factory creates by type)
ParkingLot ---> TicketRepository ; ParkingLot ---> List<ParkingObserver>  (DisplayBoard, Analytics)
Slot compatibility: VehicleType -> Set<SlotType>   (data-driven, not if/else)
```

**Design decisions and patterns.** *Strategy* for slot allocation and pricing so new rules (EV first, cheapest, surge) need no change to `ParkingLot` (Open/Closed). *Factory* creates `Vehicle`/`PaymentProcessor`. *Observer* updates display boards when availability changes. *Singleton* only for the lot facade if truly one (prefer dependency injection to ease tests). *State* for `ParkingSlot`/`Ticket` lifecycle (AVAILABLE -> OCCUPIED -> AVAILABLE; ticket ACTIVE -> PAID -> CLOSED, or LOST). Keep entities as data holders and put logic in services (`TicketService`, `FeeCalculator`) to respect Single Responsibility.

**Core flows.** *Entry:* gate asks `lot.park(vehicle)`: pick compatible slot via strategy -> **atomically mark OCCUPIED** -> create ticket -> notify observers -> print ticket/open gate. If no slot: return a clear `LotFullException`. *Exit:* scan ticket -> compute fee `pricing.calculate(ticket, exitTime)` -> process payment -> on success mark ticket PAID, free slot (atomic), open gate. Idempotent exit: scanning an already closed ticket returns the previous receipt. Lost ticket: lookup by plate, charge the max daily fee plus penalty.

**Concurrency.** Two entry gates may race for the same slot. Options: (1) a lock per floor/slot-type pool (`ReentrantLock`) around select-and-mark; (2) per-slot compare-and-set (`AtomicReference<SlotStatus>` / `AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true)`) and retry with the next candidate when CAS fails (finer-grained and scalable); (3) maintain per-type free queues (`ConcurrentLinkedQueue<ParkingSlot>`) so allocation is `poll()` and release is `offer()` (O(1), naturally atomic) but nearest-slot ordering needs a `PriorityQueue` under a lock or a `ConcurrentSkipListSet` ordered by distance. Never check-then-act without atomicity.

**Pricing examples.** `HourlyPricing`: rate per hour per vehicle type, rounded up to the next hour with a grace period; `FlatPlusHourly`: first 2 hours flat, then per hour; `DailyCap`: max per day; decorators (`PeakHourSurge`, `MemberDiscount`) wrap a base strategy (Decorator pattern), composing rules without subclass explosion.

```java
enum VehicleType { MOTORCYCLE, CAR, TRUCK }
enum SlotType { SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE, EV }
class ParkingSlot {
  private final String id; private final SlotType type; private final int floor; private final AtomicBoolean occupied = new AtomicBoolean(false);
  boolean tryOccupy() { return occupied.compareAndSet(false, true); }          // atomic claim
  void release() { occupied.set(false); }
  SlotType type() { return type; }  int floor() { return floor; }  String id() { return id; }
}
interface SlotAllocationStrategy { Optional<ParkingSlot> pick(List<ParkingFloor> floors, VehicleType v); }
class NearestFloorStrategy implements SlotAllocationStrategy {
  private static final Map<VehicleType, List<SlotType>> COMPAT = Map.of(
      VehicleType.MOTORCYCLE, List.of(SlotType.SMALL, SlotType.MEDIUM, SlotType.LARGE),
      VehicleType.CAR, List.of(SlotType.MEDIUM, SlotType.LARGE), VehicleType.TRUCK, List.of(SlotType.LARGE));
  public Optional<ParkingSlot> pick(List<ParkingFloor> floors, VehicleType v) {
    for (ParkingFloor f : floors)                                              // floors ordered by distance from the entry
      for (SlotType t : COMPAT.get(v))                                         // prefer the tightest fit first
        for (ParkingSlot s : f.slots(t)) if (s.tryOccupy()) return Optional.of(s);   // CAS: safe under concurrency
    return Optional.empty();
  }
}
interface PricingStrategy { Money fee(Ticket t, Instant exit); }
class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy {
  private final Map<VehicleType, Money> perHour;
  public Money fee(Ticket t, Instant exit) {
    long minutes = Math.max(0, Duration.between(t.entryTime(), exit).toMinutes() - 15);           // 15-minute grace
    long hours = Math.max(1, (minutes + 59) / 60);
    return perHour.get(t.vehicle().type()).times(hours);
  }
}
class ParkingLot {
  private final List<ParkingFloor> floors; private final SlotAllocationStrategy alloc; private final PricingStrategy pricing; private final TicketRepository tickets;
  private final List<ParkingObserver> observers = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
  Ticket park(Vehicle v) {
    ParkingSlot s = alloc.pick(floors, v.type()).orElseThrow(LotFullException::new);
    Ticket t = tickets.save(new Ticket(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), v, s, Instant.now()));
    observers.forEach(o -> o.onChange(snapshot())); return t;
  }
  Receipt exit(String ticketId, PaymentProcessor pay) {
    Ticket t = tickets.find(ticketId).orElseThrow(InvalidTicketException::new);
    if (t.isClosed()) return t.receipt();                                        // idempotent exit
    Money fee = pricing.fee(t, Instant.now());
    pay.charge(fee, t.id());                                                     // throws on failure -> slot stays occupied
    t.slot().release(); t.close(fee);
    observers.forEach(o -> o.onChange(snapshot())); return t.receipt();
  }
}
```

**Edge cases.** Lot full; ticket lost or damaged; vehicle exits without paying (gate stays closed until payment); payment failure retries without double charging (idempotency by ticket id); clock changes (use monotonic/instants from a Clock abstraction for tests); a vehicle already parked tries to enter again (check by plate); slot out of service (status MAINTENANCE excluded from allocation); EV vehicles prefer EV slots but may use regular ones; reservation expiry.

**Testing.** Inject `Clock` and strategies; unit-test pricing boundaries (exactly 60 minutes, grace period), concurrency test with N threads claiming M slots (assert no slot assigned twice and exactly M successes), and slot release after failed payment.

**Extensions.** Reservations (hold a slot with expiry), multi-lot chain with a central service (then it becomes an HLD problem: availability service, payments, sharded by lot), dynamic pricing by occupancy, license-plate recognition adapter, monthly passes (a different `Ticket` type via the same interface), valet mode, analytics.

**Follow-ups.** (1) *How do you add EV charging slots?* New `SlotType` and compatibility entry; allocation strategy prefers them for EVs; no changes to `ParkingLot`. (2) *How do you prevent two cars getting the same slot?* CAS on the slot (or per-pool lock). (3) *How do you change pricing at runtime?* Inject a different `PricingStrategy`, or decorator for peak hours. (4) *How would you scale to 1,000 lots?* Move to services: per-lot inventory with a store, central ticket/payment services, event-driven availability (HLD view). (5) *Why Strategy over if/else?* Open/Closed; each rule isolated and testable. (6) *How do you test it?* Fake clock, deterministic strategies, thread-safety test.

**Summary.** Entities plus Strategy-based allocation and pricing, atomic slot claiming, ticket lifecycle with idempotent exit, observers for display boards, and a clear extension story.

### Q74. Elevator system

- **Requirements:** N elevators, M floors; hall calls (up/down) and in-car floor selection; efficient scheduling; doors, capacity, emergency stop.
- **Classes:** `ElevatorController` (dispatcher), `Elevator` (state, currentFloor, direction, pending stops as TreeSets), `Request` (floor, direction), `DispatchStrategy` (Strategy: nearest idle / SCAN-aware cost), `ElevatorState` (State: `IDLE`, `MOVING_UP`, `MOVING_DOWN`, `DOORS_OPEN`, `MAINTENANCE`).
- **Algorithm (SCAN / LOOK):** keep serving requests in the current direction, then reverse. Maintain `upStops` (min-order) and `downStops` (max-order).

```java
class Elevator {
  int floor; Direction dir = Direction.IDLE;
  TreeSet<Integer> up = new TreeSet<>(), down = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
  synchronized void addStop(int f) { if (f > floor) up.add(f); else if (f < floor) down.add(f); else openDoors(); }
  synchronized void step() {
    if (dir == Direction.UP || (dir == Direction.IDLE && !up.isEmpty())) {
      if (!up.isEmpty()) { floor++; dir = Direction.UP; if (up.remove(floor)) openDoors(); }
      if (up.isEmpty()) dir = down.isEmpty() ? Direction.IDLE : Direction.DOWN;
    } else if (dir == Direction.DOWN || !down.isEmpty()) {
      if (!down.isEmpty()) { floor--; dir = Direction.DOWN; if (down.remove(floor)) openDoors(); }
      if (down.isEmpty()) dir = up.isEmpty() ? Direction.IDLE : Direction.UP;
    }
  }
  int cost(Request r) { /* distance + stops in the way, penalty if direction differs */ return Math.abs(floor - r.floor) + (sameDirectionOrIdle(r) ? 0 : 10); }
}
class ElevatorController { Elevator assign(Request r) { return Collections.min(elevators, Comparator.comparingInt(e -> e.cost(r))); } }
```

- **Watch out:** a request exactly at the current floor, overload (reject extra stops), starvation (SCAN avoids it), zoning for tall buildings, simulate time with a tick loop for testing.

#### Q74 in depth: Elevator system (LLD)

**Requirements to confirm.** A building with N floors and M elevators; hall calls (up/down buttons on a floor) and car calls (floor buttons inside); a **dispatcher** assigns hall calls to a car; each car moves, stops, opens doors, handles weight limit and emergency stop; minimize average wait time; handle peak patterns (morning up-peak, lunch). Non-goals: physical control (motor, sensors) which sits behind an interface.

**Entities.** `Building`, `ElevatorController` (the dispatcher), `ElevatorCar` (id, currentFloor, direction, state, door, load, stop set), `Request` (floor, direction, timestamp; `HallCall` and `CarCall`), `Door`, `Display`, and strategies `DispatchStrategy` and `StopSchedulingStrategy`.

**State machine of a car.** States: IDLE, MOVING\_UP, MOVING\_DOWN, DOORS\_OPEN, MAINTENANCE/EMERGENCY. Transitions are driven by events: `requestAdded`, `arrivedAtFloor`, `doorTimerExpired`, `overload`, `emergencyStop`. Implement with the **State pattern** (each state object handles events) or an enum-based switch with a transition table; this removes tangled boolean flags like `isMoving && !doorsOpen`.

**The scheduling algorithm inside one car: SCAN / LOOK (the 'elevator algorithm').** A car keeps moving in its current direction, serving stops in order (floors above while going up), then reverses when no stops remain ahead. Maintain two sorted sets: `upStops` (TreeSet ascending) and `downStops` (TreeSet descending). Going up: next stop = `upStops.ceiling(currentFloor)`; if none, switch direction and use `downStops`. This avoids starvation better than FIFO (which zigzags) and is simple.

**Dispatch across cars.** For a hall call at floor f going direction d, compute a **cost** for each car and assign the minimum:

- A car that is idle: cost = |car.floor - f|.
- A car moving toward f in the same direction d and not yet past f: cost = |car.floor - f| (it will pick it up on the way).
- A car moving away or in the opposite direction: cost = distance to its last committed stop + distance back to f (it must finish and turn around).
- Add penalties for load (nearly full cars skip), and for cars with many pending stops.

This is the standard 'nearest car with direction awareness' approach; alternatives are zoning (cars own floor ranges), destination dispatch (passengers choose destination at the lobby kiosk and the system groups people going to the same floors, reducing stops), and ML-predicted traffic. Make it a `DispatchStrategy` so they are swappable.

**Concurrency.** Calls arrive from many threads (buttons) while each car runs its own control loop. Model each car as an **actor-like single-threaded executor** with a thread-safe request queue: the dispatcher only enqueues commands (`addStop(floor)`), and the car's loop applies them, so no shared mutable state between cars; the dispatcher reads a volatile snapshot (position, direction, number of stops) for cost computation. This avoids locks inside car logic. Use `ConcurrentSkipListSet` if stops are modified from outside.

**Class sketch.**

```java
enum Direction { UP, DOWN, IDLE }
enum CarState { IDLE, MOVING, DOORS_OPEN, MAINTENANCE }
record HallCall(int floor, Direction dir) {}
class ElevatorCar implements Runnable {
  private final int id; private volatile int floor = 0; private volatile Direction dir = Direction.IDLE; private volatile CarState state = CarState.IDLE;
  private final NavigableSet<Integer> upStops = new ConcurrentSkipListSet<>();
  private final NavigableSet<Integer> downStops = new ConcurrentSkipListSet<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
  private final int capacityKg = 800; private volatile int loadKg;
  void addStop(int target) { if (target > floor) upStops.add(target); else if (target < floor) downStops.add(target); else openDoors(); }
  int costFor(HallCall c) {
    if (state == CarState.MAINTENANCE || loadKg > capacityKg * 0.9) return Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    if (dir == Direction.IDLE) return Math.abs(floor - c.floor());
    if (dir == c.dir() && ((dir == Direction.UP && c.floor() >= floor) || (dir == Direction.DOWN && c.floor() <= floor))) return Math.abs(floor - c.floor());   // on the way
    int farthest = dir == Direction.UP ? (upStops.isEmpty() ? floor : upStops.last()) : (downStops.isEmpty() ? floor : downStops.last());
    return Math.abs(floor - farthest) + Math.abs(farthest - c.floor()) + 5 * (upStops.size() + downStops.size());
  }
  public void run() {                                           // control loop
    while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
      Integer next = nextStop();
      if (next == null) { dir = Direction.IDLE; state = CarState.IDLE; sleepQuietly(100); continue; }
      moveTo(next);                                             // updates floor step by step, checking emergency stop
      openDoors(); upStops.remove(next); downStops.remove(next); // door timer, then close (reopen if obstruction)
    }
  }
  private Integer nextStop() {
    if (dir != Direction.DOWN) { Integer n = upStops.ceiling(floor); if (n != null) { dir = Direction.UP; return n; } }
    Integer d = downStops.ceiling(floor);                       // downStops ordered descending -> ceiling gives next lower floor
    if (d != null) { dir = Direction.DOWN; return d; }
    if (!upStops.isEmpty()) { dir = Direction.UP; return upStops.first(); }
    return null;
  }
}
class ElevatorController {
  private final List<ElevatorCar> cars;
  void onHallCall(HallCall c) {
    ElevatorCar best = cars.stream().min(Comparator.comparingInt(car -> car.costFor(c))).orElseThrow();
    best.addStop(c.floor());                                    // dispatcher only enqueues; the car owns its movement
  }
}
```

**Edge cases.** Overload: refuse to close doors, buzz, ignore new stops until load drops; door obstruction sensor reopens; emergency stop/fire mode (recall all cars to the ground floor, ignore calls); a car in maintenance excluded from dispatch; duplicate button presses ignored (sets dedupe); request for the current floor opens doors; a hall call assigned to a car that later fails: **reassign** (keep outstanding hall calls in the controller until served and re-dispatch on car failure); starvation prevention (age requests: cost decreases with waiting time); simultaneous calls from the same floor.

**Testing.** Deterministic simulation with a fake clock and a scripted request stream; assert wait times, no skipped stops, direction-respecting service; property tests that every request is eventually served.

**Extensions.** Destination dispatch, express cars/zones for tall buildings, VIP/service modes, energy saving (park idle cars at lobby or mid-height, power down idle cars), predictive pre-positioning from traffic history, multiple elevators per shaft, integration with access control (floor authorization).

**Follow-ups.** (1) *Which algorithm schedules stops?* SCAN/LOOK with up and down ordered sets. (2) *How does the dispatcher pick a car?* Cost function with direction awareness, load and queue length; pluggable strategy. (3) *How do you avoid race conditions?* One control loop per car; dispatcher only enqueues. (4) *What if a car breaks?* Reassign its pending hall calls. (5) *How would you reduce average wait time?* Destination dispatch, zoning, pre-positioning. (6) *Why State pattern?* Behavior depends on state; avoids flag soup and illegal transitions.

**Summary.** Per-car state machine with SCAN stop scheduling, controller using a swappable cost-based dispatch strategy, single-writer control loops for thread safety, and explicit handling of overload, emergency and failure cases.

### Q75. Tic-tac-toe

- **Requirements:** NxN board, two players alternate, win by filling a row, column, or diagonal; detect draw.
- **Classes:** `Game`, `Board`, `Player` (symbol), `Move`, `GameStatus`.
- **Key idea:** O(1) win check using counters: per player keep `rows[N]`, `cols[N]`, `diag`, `antiDiag`; add +1 for player X and -1 for player O; if any counter reaches N in absolute value, that player wins.

```java
class Board {
  final int n; final char[][] cells; int[] rows, cols; int diag, anti; int moves;
  Board(int n) { this.n = n; cells = new char[n][n]; rows = new int[n]; cols = new int[n]; }
  boolean place(int r, int c, int delta, char sym) {         // delta = +1 for X, -1 for O
    if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= n || c >= n || cells[r][c] != 0) throw new InvalidMoveException();
    cells[r][c] = sym; moves++;
    rows[r] += delta; cols[c] += delta;
    if (r == c) diag += delta; if (r + c == n - 1) anti += delta;
    return Math.abs(rows[r]) == n || Math.abs(cols[c]) == n || Math.abs(diag) == n || Math.abs(anti) == n;
  }
  boolean isFull() { return moves == n * n; }
}
```
